# Tuning capture on a busy server

Use this page when a live capture drops packets.

- sipnab's defaults already suit a busy production link.
- So check first whether you are dropping anything at all.
- If you are, change the settings below in the order they appear. That is the
  order that helps most.

**Start here, always:** find out whether you are actually dropping packets.
Every other decision on this page depends on that number, and sipnab reports it.

---

## Are you dropping packets?

sipnab polls libpcap's kernel counters once a second and reports two numbers.

```text
PACKETS ARE BEING DROPPED on 'eth0' (kernel buffer: 18432, interface/driver: 0).
The analysis for this run is INCOMPLETE — dialogs may be missing messages and
RTP loss figures will overstate what was on the wire. This run's kernel capture
buffer is 64 MiB: raise it with -B/--buffer, narrow the capture with a BPF
filter, or reduce --snaplen. Interface drops are not fixed by a bigger buffer;
they point at the NIC or driver.
```

You get that warning the moment the first drop happens. You also get a summary
at the end of the capture:

```text
Live capture on 'eth0' finished: 4821003 packets captured, but 18432 dropped by
the kernel buffer and 0 by the interface — THIS ANALYSIS IS INCOMPLETE
```

A run with no drops ends with this line:

```text
Live capture on 'eth0' finished: 4821003 packets, no drops
```

### The two counters mean different things

| Counter | libpcap field | What it means | What fixes it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **kernel buffer** | `ps_drop` | The ring was full when the packet arrived. sipnab was not draining fast enough. | [The kernel capture buffer](#the-kernel-capture-buffer--b----buffer) (`-B`), [Capture less: BPF filters](#capture-less-bpf-filters) (BPF), [Snapshot length](#snapshot-length---snaplen--and-why-it-decides-your-ring-capacity) (`--snaplen`), [Which interfaces](#which-interfaces-any-versus-named) (device) |
| **interface/driver** | `ps_ifdrop` | The NIC or its driver discarded the packet before libpcap ever saw it. | ["Interface and driver drops"](#interface-and-driver-drops) — **a bigger buffer cannot fix this** |

Read the two counters before you change anything. A larger `-B` reduces
`kernel buffer` drops only. It has no effect on `interface/driver` drops.

### Both numbers describe a capture handle, not an interface

sipnab reads libpcap's counters for each capture handle this run opened.
libpcap keeps those counters per handle.

- A *handle* is one capture socket.
- An *interface* is the NIC every process on the host shares.

The difference changes what a zero means and what a total covers.

- **Zero drops means this run missed nothing.**
  - It says nothing about the interface.
  - Another sniffer on the same NIC keeps its own counters.
  - Neither run can read the other's.
- **One run can hold several handles.**
  - `--multi-device` opens one per named interface.
  - `--cores N` on a live device opens N sockets on one interface
    ([On a live device it means capture sockets, not workers](#on-a-live-device-it-means-capture-sockets-not-workers)).
  - sipnab adds each handle's increment to one process-wide pair. So the
    totals cover the whole run rather than any single socket.
  - The first-drop warning names the device that dropped. That tells you where
    to act.
- **The packet count beside them is sipnab's own tally**, not a libpcap
  counter.
  - It counts frames sipnab read.
  - The drop pair is what says how many more the wire carried.

### Where the two numbers appear

sipnab reports both counters on four surfaces. It keeps them apart on every one
of them. So whichever you are looking at can answer "which kind of drop is
this?"

| Surface | How they appear |
|---|---|
| Live warning | `PACKETS ARE BEING DROPPED on 'eth0' (kernel buffer: N, interface/driver: M)`, the moment the first drop happens |
| End-of-run summary | `... N dropped by the kernel buffer and M by the interface`, or `no drops` |
| `--report` | one sentence each, and each names only the fixes that apply to it |
| `--metrics` (Prometheus) | `sipnab_capture_kernel_dropped_packets_total` and `sipnab_capture_interface_dropped_packets_total`, as separate counters |

Alert on each Prometheus counter separately. Each one has its own fix, and a
sum of the two does not say which fix applies.

The REST API and MCP report the same pair on the capture-quality object:

- `kernel_dropped_packets` and `interface_dropped_packets`.
- They sit beside the `invalid_timestamps`, `undecodable_frames` and
  snapped-frame counts. Those make up the rest of a capture's quality.
- See [`GET /v1/stats`](rest-api.md#get-v1stats).

> **What a drop does to the analysis.**
>
> - A dropped SIP message means a dialog reconstructs wrong.
>   - A missing `BYE` leaves a call that never ends.
>   - A missing `200 OK` leaves one that never answered.
> - A dropped RTP packet counts as network loss that did not happen on the
>   wire. MOS and loss figures read worse than the call was.

---

## The kernel capture buffer (`-B` / `--buffer`)

**Default: 64 MiB per capture device.**

This is the ring libpcap fills and sipnab drains. It absorbs the difference
between two times:

- when packets arrive (bursty, driven by your traffic);
- when sipnab gets scheduled to read them (jittery, driven by your kernel).

Change it first.

Busy trunk — give it room for a bigger burst:

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 -B 256
```

Small or embedded host — cap the memory instead:

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 -B 8
```

> **The packet count a buffer holds depends on other settings.**
>
> - On the TUI's ring, libpcap divides the buffer into fixed-size slots. Their
>   size comes from `--snaplen`.
> - So how many *packets* 64 MiB holds depends on:
>   - the snapshot length;
>   - whether NIC offloads are on — anywhere from ~1,000 to ~41,000;
>   - whether you named an interface at all.
> - Read [Snapshot length](#snapshot-length---snaplen--and-why-it-decides-your-ring-capacity) and [Which interfaces: `any` versus named](#which-interfaces-any-versus-named) before concluding that a bigger `-B` did not help.

Rules of thumb:

- **Raise it** when `kernel buffer` drops are non-zero and CPU is *not* pinned.
  - Dropping with idle CPU means bursts.
  - Bursts are exactly what a ring absorbs.
- **Do not raise it** when the drops persist and a core is at 100%.
  - A bigger ring buys a longer burst, not more throughput.
  - You are not keeping up on average, and no buffer size fixes that.
  - Go to [Capture less: BPF filters](#capture-less-bpf-filters).
- **Lower it** on `--multi-device` runs.
  - The cost is **per device**.
  - Eight interfaces at the default reserve half a gigabyte of kernel memory.

### It degrades rather than failing

Asking the kernel for a large ring can fail with `ENOMEM` on a small or loaded
host. sipnab does not treat that as fatal. Instead it:

- halves the request and retries, down to a 2 MiB floor;
- tells you when it settled for less:

```text
'eth0': the kernel refused a 64 MiB capture buffer; capturing with 16 MiB
instead. This host will tolerate a smaller burst before dropping — watch the
drop counters, and set -B/--buffer explicitly to pin a size.
```

sipnab honors an explicit small `-B` exactly and never promotes it upward.
`-B 1` on a constrained box means 1 MiB.

### Request a buffer larger than 2047 MiB

The largest buffer sipnab can request is 2047 MiB. sipnab reduces a larger `-B`
to 2047 MiB and logs a warning before it opens the device:

```text
-B/--buffer 5000 MiB exceeds the 2047 MiB ceiling (pcap_set_buffer_size takes a
C int); capturing with 2047 MiB instead.
```

The run continues with 2047 MiB. To use more memory for capture, open more
than one ring: name several interfaces with `--multi-device`, or spread one
interface across sockets with
[`--cores`](#on-a-live-device-it-means-capture-sockets-not-workers).

### `--buffer-budget` is a different buffer

Two settings carry the word. They sit on opposite sides of the kernel boundary.

- `-B` sizes the kernel ring.
- `--buffer-budget` sizes the in-process queue between the capture thread and
  the processing loop.
  - It is in MiB, and it defaults to 64.
  - sipnab turns that budget into a packet count at an assumed 2 KiB average.
  - It then clamps the result to between 10,000 and 5,000,000 packets.

Raise it when processing lags behind a bursty capture the ring is already
absorbing. It does nothing for a ring that overflows. The kernel discards those
packets before this queue ever sees them.

---

## Capture less: BPF filters

A BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) expression selects packets in the kernel.

- A BPF filter runs **in the kernel**, before the ring.
- So filtered traffic costs no buffer space, no copy, and no parse.

**A live capture already has one.** Give sipnab no expression of your own, and
it does this:

- It compiles one from `--portrange` (default 5060-5061).
- It then adds an arm that reaches SIP inside one VLAN tag, QinQ, a PPPoE
  Session header or an MPLS label stack.
- It logs the expression it installed. So `-v` shows you exactly what the
  kernel is running.

The baseline is therefore signaling-only already. This section is about
narrowing further or about letting media back in.

**Your expression replaces that one entirely.** sipnab never edits what you
typed.

- So an expression of your own drops the encapsulation arm.
- It also makes `--capture-tunnels` inert.
- Two warnings cover that:
  - one when a port-based expression shows no sign of handling encapsulation;
  - one naming `--capture-tunnels` as ignored when you passed it beside a
    filter of your own.

Careful with the flag name:

- `--filter` is sipnab's own matching language, applied to messages after
  capture.
- The BPF expression is the trailing argument, or a file named by
  `--bpf-file`.

Only SIP signaling, and nothing tagged:

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 "port 5060 or port 5061"
```

Signaling plus one media range:

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 "port 5060 or (udp portrange 10000-20000)"
```

One customer's traffic:

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 "host 203.0.113.10"
```

Use a narrower filter first when drops persist while a core is at 100%. A
larger buffer does not raise the rate at which sipnab reads packets. A filter
lowers the number it has to read.

> **Careful with RTP.**
>
> - Filtering to `port 5060` alone gives you signaling with no media.
> - So every stream turns orphan and every MOS figure disappears.
> - If you want quality metrics, the filter must admit the negotiated media
>   ports too.

---

## Snapshot length (`--snaplen`) — and why it decides your ring capacity

**Default: 65535** — the whole frame.

`--snaplen` sets how many bytes of each packet sipnab captures. On Linux it
also sets how many packets the TUI's capture ring holds.

- The TUI uses libpcap's TPACKET_V2 ring. Every slot in that ring has the same
  size, set from the snapshot length. A buffer holds `buffer size ÷ slot size`
  packets, however small the packets are.
- libpcap reduces the slot to the interface MTU plus 18 bytes only on an
  Ethernet device (link type `EN10MB`) with NIC offloads off.
- `any`, sipnab's default device on Linux, has link type `LINUX_SLL2`. Its slot
  stays at the full snapshot length whatever the offload settings.
- Headless runs use a different ring. See
  "Which ring you get", below.

Slot size and capacity of the default 64 MiB buffer on the TUI's ring:

| Device | Link type | Offloads | Effective slot | 64 MiB ring holds |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **`any` (sipnab's default)** | `LINUX_SLL2` | no effect | ~65 KB | **~1,000 packets** |
| `eth0` | `EN10MB` | on (common default) | ~65 KB | **~1,000 packets** |
| `eth0` | `EN10MB` | off | MTU+18 ≈ 1518 B | **~41,000 packets** |

With the default device and default snaplen, a 64 MiB TUI ring holds about a
thousand packets.

### Fit more packets in the ring

Three changes raise the packet count. Each one helps alone, and they combine.

- **Cap the snaplen.** A 1600-byte snaplen gives slots a little over 1.6 KB,
  so 64 MiB holds tens of thousands of packets:

  ```bash
  sudo sipnab -d eth0 --snaplen 1600
  ```

- **Name the interface.** Only a named Ethernet interface can use the
  MTU-sized slot. Read
  [Which interfaces: `any` versus named](#which-interfaces-any-versus-named)
  before you make that change, because a named device can miss call legs that
  `any` sees.
- **Turn the offloads off** ([Interface and driver drops](#interface-and-driver-drops)).
  With offloads on, the kernel delivers merged frames that were not on the
  wire, and the Ethernet slot stays at 65 KB.

**`--capture-profile` picks the number for you.**

- `signaling` asks for a snaplen of 1500 — one MTU.
  - That keeps a whole INVITE carrying a long `Record-Route` set, ISUP
    encapsulation or a fat SDP offer.
  - It drops the bulk of every RTP packet.
- `full` is 65535, the default.
- An explicit `--snaplen` takes precedence over the profile.

A snaplen shorter than a SIP message cuts the message, and sipnab cannot parse
the cut message. A single INVITE with a long `Record-Route` set, a long
`Contact`, ISUP encapsulation or a large SDP offer often exceeds 400 bytes.
`sipnab_capture_snapped_frames_total` counts how many frames arrived truncated.

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --capture-profile signaling
```

> **Truncation is lossy, and not everything survives it.**
>
> - A small `--snaplen` breaks audio reconstruction.
>   - `--retain-audio`, Opus decode, the TUI's WAV save and the MCP
>     `export_audio` tool all need whole RTP payloads.
> - It degrades `-O` capture re-emit to truncated frames.
> - sipnab records the captured and original length of each packet, so the
>   metrics count the truncated frames.

To limit only how much sipnab *parses* without truncating what it *captures*,
use `-S`/`--limitlen` instead. That is a parser bound, not a capture bound.

---

### Which ring you get: TPACKET_V2 for the TUI, V3 for everything else

sipnab picks the capture mode from the run mode:

| Run mode | Immediate mode | Ring libpcap uses |
|---|---|---|
| TUI | on | TPACKET_V2: fixed-size slots, sized from `--snaplen` |
| Every run without the TUI (`-N`) | off | TPACKET_V3: blocks sized independently of `--snaplen` |

- In the TUI, each packet reaches the screen as soon as it arrives.
- A headless run lets libpcap batch packets into blocks. sipnab sets the block
  timeout to 5 ms, so libpcap delivers a block that does not fill after that
  timeout.
- libpcap uses TPACKET_V3 only when its build includes it. Check the second line
  of `sipnab --version`:

```bash
sipnab --version
```

```text
…
libpcap version 1.10.4 (with TPACKET_V3); alternate capture backends named: none
```

On a headless run, `--snaplen` and the offload settings still decide how many
bytes of each packet sipnab copies. The slot arithmetic in
[Snapshot length](#snapshot-length---snaplen--and-why-it-decides-your-ring-capacity)
applies to the TUI.

---

## Which interfaces: `any` versus named

**Default on Linux: `any` — every interface at once, loopback included.**

sipnab defaults to `any` so that it captures every call leg. SIP servers often send
signaling over loopback or a container bridge. Capture `eth0` alone and these
legs are absent:

- a B2BUA talking to a registrar over `127.0.0.1`;
- a containerized stack bridging SIP across `docker0`;
- a proxy handing calls to a media server over a veth pair.

A dialog missing one leg reconstructs wrong, in the same way as
[Are you dropping packets?](#are-you-dropping-packets) describes for dropped
packets.

`any` has four costs: three in performance and one in coverage.

### What `any` costs you

- **The TUI's ring holds about 40 times fewer packets.**
  - Every slot stays at the full snapshot length, 65535 bytes by default,
    whatever the interface MTU or `ethtool` settings.
  - At the 64 MiB default that is about 1,000 slots, against about 41,000 for
    a named Ethernet interface with offloads off.
  - [Snapshot length](#snapshot-length---snaplen--and-why-it-decides-your-ring-capacity) explains the slot size.
- **It cannot capture in promiscuous mode.**
  - sipnab does not request promiscuous mode on `any`, because the
    pseudo-device does not support it.
  - Promiscuous mode is on by default for a named device, and `--no-promisc`
    turns it off.
  - So **`any` misses traffic not addressed to the host**. On a SPAN port or
    tap that mirrors calls the capture host is not a party to, name the
    interface.
- **It runs one capture thread.**
  - Naming devices allows `--multi-device`.
  - That starts one coordinator thread plus **one capture thread per
    interface**.
  - Each has its own ring and its own drain loop.
  - `any` is one device. So it is one thread and one ring no matter how many
    interfaces the traffic actually arrives on.
  - `--cores N` ([On a live device it means capture sockets, not workers](#on-a-live-device-it-means-capture-sockets-not-workers))
    is the other way to get more than one socket. It works on a single device
    rather than on a list.
- **It sweeps interfaces you never wanted.**
  - `any` also picks up loopback, `docker0`, veth pairs, tunnels and
    management interfaces.
  - Every one of those packets costs a BPF evaluation.
  - Each packet the filter passes also takes a slot in the same ring as the
    traffic you want.

### Side by side

| | `any` (the default) | Named — `-d eth0` / `-d eth0,eth1 --multi-device` |
|---|---|---|
| **Loopback / container legs** | Captured | **Missed unless you name those interfaces too** |
| **Link type** | `LINUX_SLL2` | `EN10MB` |
| **MTU-sized TUI ring slot ([Snapshot length](#snapshot-length---snaplen--and-why-it-decides-your-ring-capacity))** | **Never** | Once offloads are off |
| **64 MiB ring holds** | ~1,000 packets | ~41,000 with offloads off (~1,000 with them on) |
| **Promiscuous mode** | **Unavailable** | On by default; `--no-promisc` to disable |
| **Capture threads** | 1 | 1 per named device under `--multi-device` |
| **Packets filtered and copied** | Every interface, `lo` and `docker0` included | Only the interfaces you named |

### Which one is right

**Stay on `any`** when any of these hold:

- You are diagnosing rather than monitoring.
- You do not yet know which interface carries the traffic.
- SIP genuinely crosses loopback or container bridges and you have not
  enumerated those interfaces.
- The drop counters from [Are you dropping packets?](#are-you-dropping-packets)
  read `no drops`.

**Name your interfaces** when any of these hold:

- [Are you dropping packets?](#are-you-dropping-packets) shows sustained
  `kernel buffer` drops.
- You are running a long-lived headless capture on a known topology.
- You need promiscuous mode, because the switch mirrors the traffic to you
  rather than addressing it to you.
- You have several busy interfaces and one thread cannot drain them all.

### The recommendation for a busy server

Name what you need, open them in parallel, and turn the offloads off so the
clamp can run:

First disable the offloads, once per interface you intend to capture:

```bash
sudo ethtool -K eth0 gro off lro off gso off tso off
```

Then name those interfaces and open them in parallel:

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d eth0,eth1 --multi-device -B 256 "port 5060 or port 5061"
```

Naming the devices addresses all four costs:

- The slots are now clamped to MTU+18. So the same 64 MiB holds tens of
  thousands of packets instead of ~1,000.
- Promiscuous mode is back.
- There is one capture thread per interface.
- Nothing goes to `docker0`.

The smaller slot needs both steps:

- On `any`, the slot stays at the full snapshot length whatever the `ethtool`
  settings.
- A named device with offloads on still has slots of about 65 KB
  ([Snapshot length](#snapshot-length---snaplen--and-why-it-decides-your-ring-capacity)).

**Check that no call leg is missing.** A leg on an interface you did not name
is not captured, and sipnab reports no error for it. List the interfaces and
their addresses:

```bash
ip -brief address
```

If any SIP endpoint answers on `127.0.0.1` or a container bridge, add `lo` or
`docker0` to the `-d` list rather than accepting the gap.

- `--multi-device` costs `-B` **per device** ([The kernel capture buffer](#the-kernel-capture-buffer--b----buffer)).
- So eight interfaces at the default reserve half a gigabyte.
- Name what you need and no more.

---

## Give sipnab less work

- `--no-rtp` — skip RTP/RTCP entirely when you only care about signaling.
  - A call with media carries far more RTP packets than SIP messages. In
    `sip-rtp-g711.pcap` from the test samples, 839 of the 852 packets are RTP.
  - So this is the largest single reduction available short of a BPF filter.
- `--no-dialog` — skip dialog reconstruction.
- `-N` / `--no-tui` — do not render a TUI you are not watching.
- `--quiet-bad-parse` — silence per-packet parse notices on dirty links.
- Avoid per-message output (`--json`, `--text-dump`) on a high-rate live
  capture unless you are consuming it.
  - Formatting and writing every message is real work on the capture path.

---

## Interface and driver drops

If `interface/driver` is non-zero, the packets never reached libpcap. `-B` is
irrelevant. Look outside sipnab:

- **NIC ring buffers**
  - `ethtool -g eth0` to inspect, `ethtool -G eth0 rx 4096` to raise.
  - This is the NIC's own ring, distinct from libpcap's.
- **Offloads**
  - GRO/LRO/GSO make the kernel hand you reassembled super-frames.
  - Those no longer match what was on the wire.
  - For accurate capture: `ethtool -K eth0 gro off lro off gso off tso off`.
- **IRQ affinity and RPS**
  - A single core servicing all NIC interrupts is a common ceiling on a busy
    server.
- **A tap or SPAN port that is already oversubscribed**
  - If the mirror source is dropping, nothing on the capture host can recover
    it.

### A different capture backend: `netmap:`

libpcap can read through netmap instead of the kernel's packet socket.

- The device name selects it: `--device netmap:eth0`.
- The libpcap behind a binary decides whether it can.
- That libpcap differs by artifact.

Where to check:

- [Which capture
  backends an artifact can
  reach](install.md#which-capture-backends-an-artifact-can-reach) has the
  table.
- The second line of `sipnab --version` names the libpcap your binary runs and
  the alternate backends its banner names.

That page also lists which sipnab versions support netmap on each artifact.

> **Warning:** use a `netmap:` device only on an interface dedicated to
> capture, such as a SPAN or mirror port. Never use it on one the host needs.
> netmap takes the interface's rings away from the kernel. So the host stops
> receiving that interface's traffic for as long as the capture runs. On the
> interface that carries your SIP service, that stops the service.

---

## Offline: `--cores`

`--cores N` names a different resource on each source. So read the one that
matches your run.

Reading files (`-I`), it is N parallel reconstruction workers.

- sipnab assigns packets to workers by host pair.
- Each worker has its own dialog and RTP-stream stores.

```bash
sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --cores 4 --report
```

```text
… INFO sipnab::parallel: Reading from 'capture.pcap'
… INFO sipnab::capture::file: Read 852 packets: 1 of 1 file(s) read in full
Call-ID                          From           To             State        Code   Duration   Msgs   PDD      Tags
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1-1966@10.0.2.20                 sipp           test           Completed    200    8s         6      -        -
1-1968@10.0.2.20                 sipp           test           InCall       200    0s         4      -        -
…
… INFO sipnab::app::batch: sipnab: 852 packets, 10 SIP messages, 839 RTP packets across 2 streams (4 cores)
```

The closing line names the worker count. On the reference corpus, throughput
stops rising beyond four workers. Extra workers add memory without adding
speed. [Benchmarks](benchmarks.md) has the measured figures.

### On a live device it means capture sockets, not workers

`--cores N` on `-d <device>` asks the kernel to spread that interface across N
`AF_PACKET` sockets through `PACKET_FANOUT`.

- Each socket gets its own ring and its own drain loop.
- A bigger `-B` gives a deeper ring that one thread still empties alone.
- Linux only. Elsewhere sipnab captures on one socket and logs the reason.

Before you use it:

- **It widens capture, not analysis.**
  - Every socket feeds the same channel and the same processing loop.
  - So `--cores 8` is not eight cores of reconstruction.
- **`-B` is per socket.**
  - N sockets ask the kernel for N rings of that size.
  - So `--cores 8` at the 64 MiB default reserves half a gigabyte.
  - sipnab states the total out loud when it opens the group.
- **A kernel that refuses `PACKET_FANOUT` gets one socket.**
  - sipnab tests `PACKET_FANOUT` on one socket first. If the kernel refuses it, sipnab
    logs a warning and captures on a single socket.

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 --cores 4 -B 32 "port 5060 or port 5061"
```

Reach for it when both of these hold:

- [Are you dropping packets?](#are-you-dropping-packets) shows sustained
  `kernel buffer` drops on ONE busy interface;
- [The kernel capture buffer](#the-kernel-capture-buffer--b----buffer) through [Which interfaces: `any` versus named](#which-interfaces-any-versus-named) have not cleared them.

Several interfaces is `--multi-device` ([Which interfaces: `any` versus named](#which-interfaces-any-versus-named)) instead.

---

## A worked starting point

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d eth0 \
  -B 256 \
  --snaplen 1600 \
  "port 5060 or port 5061 or (udp portrange 10000-20000)" \
  --report
```

Note that this already makes the interface choice from [Which interfaces: `any` versus named](#which-interfaces-any-versus-named).

- It names `eth0` rather than taking `any`.
- So confirm no SIP leg lives on loopback or a container bridge before adopting
  it.

Then read the drop line at the end.

- If it says `no drops`, stop there. You can then undo settings one at a
  time, for example the snaplen, while the line still says `no drops`.

- If it does not, work down these in that order:
  - [The kernel capture buffer](#the-kernel-capture-buffer--b----buffer)
  - [Capture less: BPF filters](#capture-less-bpf-filters)
  - [Which interfaces: `any` versus named](#which-interfaces-any-versus-named)
  - [Give sipnab less work](#give-sipnab-less-work)
  - [Interface and driver drops](#interface-and-driver-drops)
- Re-measure after each change rather than applying all of them at once.

---

# The vCon capture stack

OpenSIPS routes the call, rtpengine carries the media, sipnab watches both
without taking part, and a conserver keeps what comes out. This page is how to
build that, operate it, prove it works, and recognize the failure modes that
look like success.

Hostnames in the sample output below appear as `<proxy-host>` and
`<relay-host>`.

- Neither is a literal value. Both stand in for something taken out.
- `node` carries whatever hostname the container has.
  - On one side that is a private lab machine.
  - On the other side it is an ephemeral container ID.
- Everything else in those samples is verbatim.

It describes a test harness rather than a production deployment.

- Every command here ran against a real build.
- The addresses belong to a private lab bridge.
- The arrangement is deliberately more separated than a real one needs. So
  each half can prove itself on its own.

## Why two capture points

A proxy and a media relay see different halves of a call.

- `sipnab-proxy` shares the OpenSIPS network namespace.
  - It sees INVITE, 200 OK, ACK, BYE — and no media at all.
- `sipnab-relay` shares the rtpengine namespace.
  - It sees RTP — and never a SIP message.

Neither can answer *“was this call healthy?”* alone.

- Joining them is the thing under test.
- It only works because rtpengine mirrors its `ng` control plane where the
  relay can read it.

The harness gives rtpengine a network namespace of its own. Two sipnab
instances on one interface read the same packets, so they could not show that
a leg seen at the proxy is the leg seen at the relay. In separate namespaces
each instance captures only its own half.

## Choosing one node or two

Answer this before deploying. It decides four other things.

When OpenSIPS and rtpengine run on the same host, **one sipnab is enough and is the simpler build.**

- A single capture point sees the signaling and the media together.
- So it learns which streams belong to which call from the SDP.
- That is the way sipnab does it everywhere else.

Two nodes exist for the case that cannot cover: a relay on separate hardware.

- That relay never sees an INVITE.
- Attribution then has to come from the rtpengine `ng` control plane instead.
- That carries four requirements with it.

|  | Single node (co-located) | Two nodes (separate relay) |
|---|---|---|
| Stream attribution | SDP in the signaling | rtpengine ng control plane |
| `hep` build feature | Not needed | Required |
| HOMER mirroring | Not needed | Required |
| A sink to absorb the mirror | Not needed | Required |
| Control ports in the BPF | Not needed | Required |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  CALLER["caller"] --> OS
  subgraph H["one host, one namespace"]
    OS["OpenSIPS"]
    RE["rtpengine"]
    SN["sipnab · sees SIP and RTP"]
    OS -- "ng on loopback" --> RE
  end
  OS --> CALLEE["callee"]
  CALLER <-- "RTP" --> RE
  RE <-- "RTP" --> CALLEE
  SN --> CS["conserver"]
```

Two files. Compose merges them in order:

- The base defines every service.
- The overlay changes only what co-location makes different.

Open either to see exactly what it sets.

| Role | File | What it contains |
|---|---|---|
| Base · always | [`harness/docker-compose.yml`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/harness/docker-compose.yml) | Every service: OpenSIPS, rtpengine, both sipnabs, the SIPp endpoints and the HEP sink. On its own it stands up the two-node arrangement. |
| Overlay · co-located | [`harness/docker-compose.single.yml`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/harness/docker-compose.single.yml) | Puts rtpengine back in the proxy's namespace, moves the ng socket to loopback, turns mirroring off, and scales the relay-side sipnab and the HEP sink to zero. |

### MEDIA — rtpengine, co-located — the simple case

On the same host as OpenSIPS, the control socket stays on loopback. **Nothing needs mirroring**.

- sipnab reads the SDP that describes this media.
- So it can attribute streams without ever seeing an ng message.

Set `HOST_IP` to the address rtpengine offers media on:

```bash
HOST_IP=192.0.2.10
```

```bash
rtpengine \
  --interface="$HOST_IP" \
  --listen-ng=127.0.0.1:22222 \
  --port-min=30000 --port-max=30050
```

OpenSIPS then points at `udp:127.0.0.1:22222`. One sipnab watches the interface both use:

```bash
sipnab -N -d eth0 \
  --api 127.0.0.1:8080 \
  --mcp --mcp-transport http --mcp-bind 127.0.0.1:8731 \
  --retain-audio \
  --portrange 5060-5061 \
  "udp and (portrange 5060-5061 or portrange 30000-30050)"
```

This needs:

- no `hep` feature,
- no `--hep-parse`,
- no control ports in the filter.

Everything below this point applies only when the relay runs somewhere else.

### MEDIA — rtpengine on separate hardware — mirroring its control plane

Signaling cannot attribute a relay that never sees an INVITE.

- So the mirror becomes the only link.
- Without it every captured stream is media nobody can name.

Set `RELAY_IP` to the relay's own address. Set `COLLECTOR` to the host running the sipnab that receives the mirror:

- Set the relay's own address:

   ```bash
   RELAY_IP=192.0.2.20
   ```

- Set the address of the host running the sipnab that receives the mirror:

   ```bash
   COLLECTOR=192.0.2.30
   ```

Then start the relay:

```bash
rtpengine \
  --interface="$RELAY_IP" \
  --listen-ng="$RELAY_IP:22222" \
  --port-min=30000 --port-max=30050 \
  --homer="$COLLECTOR:9060" \
  --homer-protocol=udp \
  --homer-enable-ng
```

### SIGNAL — OpenSIPS, anchoring every call

Point the control socket at the relay.

- Co-located that is `udp:127.0.0.1:22222`.
- On separate hardware it is the relay's address.
  - Loopback fails to reach it without saying so.

```
loadmodule "rtpengine.so"
modparam("rtpengine", "rtpengine_sock", "udp:<relay-ip>:22222")

# in the INVITE route
rtpengine_offer();
# in the reply route
rtpengine_answer();
# on dialog teardown
rtpengine_delete();
```

### SIGNAL — sipnab on a separate relay

Only for the split arrangement. The co-located invocation is above.

Build with the features you need:

- `vcon` to produce containers,
- `audio` to carry media,
- `hep` to decode the control plane.

A build without `hep` refuses `--hep-parse` outright.

Build it:

```bash
cargo build --release --features "native,tls,api,mcp,mcp-http,audio,vcon,hep"
```

At the RELAY — media, plus the control plane that names it:

```bash
sipnab -N -d eth0 \
  --api 127.0.0.1:8081 \
  --mcp --mcp-transport http --mcp-bind 127.0.0.1:8732 \
  --hep-parse \
  --retain-audio \
  --portrange 5060-5061 \
  "udp and (portrange 5060-5061 or portrange 30000-30050 \
            or port 22222 or port 9060)"
```

At the PROXY — signaling only:

```bash
sipnab -N -d eth0 --api 127.0.0.1:8080 \
  --mcp --mcp-transport http --mcp-bind 127.0.0.1:8731 \
  --portrange 5060-5061
```

## Check the three settings relay naming needs

> **`--hep-parse` does not name relay media**
>
> It is for HEP-encapsulated *SIP*.
>
> - It unwraps each HEP datagram and reads the payload inside.
> - It neither helps nor stops relay naming.
> - sipnab recognizes mirrored rtpengine `ng` with or without it.
> - Either way, sipnab believes a sniffed mirror only when it went to the HEP port, 9060.
>
> What relay naming needs:
>
> - the `hep` build feature,
> - the control-plane ports in the capture filter.

> **The default filter excludes the control plane**
>
> Port 22222 and the HEP destination port are not in a SIP-and-media filter.
>
> - The kernel drops them where no counter reports it.
> - So the capture looks healthy and names nothing.

> **sipnab discards RTP payloads unless you ask for them**
>
> Without `--retain-audio` the container carries a Dialog Object typed `recording` with no `body` and zero bytes.
>
> - That is the placeholder of draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04 section 4.3.
> - It is a run that kept no audio, not a call that was silent.
> - The completeness caveat is the only thing that says which.
> - Read it before concluding anything about the media.

## Store a call

Post the container through an ingress list, then confirm that the durable
table holds it.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant OP as your job
  participant SN as sipnab
  participant CS as conserver
  participant PG as Postgres
  OP->>SN: GET /v1/dialogs/{call-id}/vcon
  SN-->>OP: vCon 0.4.0 + audio (base64url)
  OP->>CS: POST /vcon?ingress_lists=sipnab
  CS->>CS: chain sipnab_observer tags the role
  CS->>PG: write vcons_observed
  CS-->>OP: 201 Created
  OP->>PG: confirm the row exists
```

> **Posting without an ingress list stores nothing durable**
>
> `POST /vcon` with no `ingress_lists` writes the cache only.
>
> - It answers **201**.
> - It reads back correctly for about an hour.
> - Then it vanishes. Nothing ever wrote the durable tables.
>
> Name the ingress list, and confirm the row, every time.

Set these:

- `CONSERVER` to the conserver's host and port,
- `TOKEN` to the API token your conserver's configuration sets.

The later commands on this page read the same `TOKEN`:

- Set the conserver's host and port:

   ```bash
   CONSERVER=127.0.0.1:8000
   ```

- Set the API token:

   ```bash
   TOKEN='replace-with-your-conserver-api-token'
   ```

Then post the vCon:

```bash
curl -s -X POST "http://$CONSERVER/vcon?ingress_lists=sipnab" \
  -H "x-conserver-api-token: $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-binary @call.json
```

Query the table, not the API: `select count(*) from vcons_observed where uuid = '<uuid>'`.

- A 201 tells you the store accepted the request.
- Only the row tells you it kept the call.

Concretely, against a running harness:

Set up the variables.

- The Call-ID needs percent-encoding because it contains an `@`.
- A URL parser otherwise treats that as the start of a host.
- `jq -rR
  @uri` does it without a helper script:

```bash
KEY=$(cat secrets/api.key) ENC=$(jq -rR @uri <<<'1-133@172.28.0.21')
```

Ask the node that holds both the Call-ID and the audio for the container:

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:8081/v1/dialogs/$ENC/vcon" > call.json
```

Post it, naming the ingress list:

```bash
curl -s -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:8000/vcon?ingress_lists=sipnab" -H "x-conserver-api-token: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @call.json
```

Read it back with its audio. The container names itself in its `uuid` field:

```bash
VCON_UUID=$(jq -r .uuid call.json)
```

```bash
python3 ../clients/python/vcon_view.py "$VCON_UUID" --audio call.wav
```

## User guide

Day-to-day operation once the stack is up. Every task here reads and changes nothing, unless it says otherwise.

### Find the call you care about

The proxy node knows calls by Call-ID and knows nothing about their audio. Start there.

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \
  "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/dialogs?limit=50" | jq -r \
  '.dialogs[] | [.call_id, .state, .final_status_code] | @tsv'
```

### See whether sipnab captured its media

The relay node knows streams.

- Once it has decoded the control plane, it also knows which call each belongs to.
- A stream with a null `associated_dialog` is media the relay could not attribute.
  - Usually the control plane, not the media, is what went missing.

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \
  "http://127.0.0.1:8081/v1/streams?limit=50" | jq -r \
  '.streams[] | [.associated_dialog // "UNNAMED", .codec, .packets, .mos] | @tsv'
```

### Build and keep the container

Ask the node that holds both the Call-ID and the audio. On this topology, that is the relay.

Encode the Call-ID for the URL path. The `@` in it would otherwise read as a
host separator:

```bash
ENC=$(jq -rR @uri <<<'1-133@172.28.0.21')
```

Build the container:

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:8081/v1/dialogs/$ENC/vcon" > call.json
```

Store it, naming the ingress list so it reaches the durable tables:

```bash
curl -s -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:8000/vcon?ingress_lists=sipnab" -H "x-conserver-api-token: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @call.json
```

### Listen to a stored call

List the containers the store holds:

```bash
python3 ../clients/python/vcon_view.py
```

Show one container's parties, dialog and recording. First set `VCON_UUID` to a `uuid` from that list:

```bash
VCON_UUID=018f3a2b-4c5d-8e6f-9012-3456789abcde
```

```bash
python3 ../clients/python/vcon_view.py "$VCON_UUID"
```

Extract its audio to a WAV:

```bash
python3 ../clients/python/vcon_view.py "$VCON_UUID" --audio c.wav
```

### Answer "did we capture this call properly?"

Three checks, in the order that fails fastest.

| Question | Where to look | A bad answer means |
|---|---|---|
| Did the relay see the control plane? | `caveats.media_creating_commands` on `/v1/stats` | Zero means HEP decoding is off or a filter drops the ports, and no stream ever gets a name. |
| Is the media attributed? | `associated_dialog` on each stream | Null means the container describes a call with no audio. |
| Did the container survive? | A row in the durable table | Present in the API but absent from the table means the store cached it rather than keeping it. |

### Read the caveat before trusting the audio

Every container carries a completeness note built from that run's own counters.

- It states what the capture missed.
- It distinguishes what sipnab failed to see from what an operator chose not to keep.

A container that says `PARTIAL` is not broken. It is telling you which question it can answer.

## Manage what you have stored

| Task | How |
|---|---|
| List what persisted | Query `vcons_observed`. The cache-backed listing route also returns entries that expired and now answer 404. |
| Fetch one | `GET /vcon/{uuid}` |
| Play the audio | Base64url-decode `dialog[].body` where `type` is `recording` and `body` is present — it is a WAV. A `recording` with no `body` is a placeholder and carries no audio. |
| Verify integrity | Check the recording's `content_hash` against the body you hold. |
| Separate roles | Query the role view. An observation and a recording of one call are two UUIDs and stay that way. |

> **Stereo means two sources, or it means nothing**
>
> A relay sees each direction twice, arriving and leaving.
>
> - So a two-party call yields four stream records carrying two SSRCs.
> - A container whose two channels are byte-identical is one leg duplicated.
> - sipnab selects one stream per SSRC to avoid exactly that.
> - If you build containers another way, do the same.

## Topology

Four containers on one bridge. Plus two sipnab sidecars. The sidecars join existing namespaces rather than getting their own.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  UAC["sipp-uac · 172.28.0.21"]
  UAS["sipp-uas · 172.28.0.20"]
  subgraph PX["proxy namespace · 172.28.0.10"]
    OS["opensips-proxy"]
    SNP["sipnab-proxy · MCP 8731 · REST 8080"]
  end
  subgraph RL["relay namespace · 172.28.0.11"]
    RE["rtpengine"]
    SNR["sipnab-relay · MCP 8732 · REST 8081"]
  end
  HEP["hep-sink · 172.28.0.30:9060"]
  UAC -- "INVITE" --> OS
  OS -- "INVITE" --> UAS
  OS -- "ng control :22222" --> RE
  UAC <-- "RTP" --> RE
  RE <-- "RTP" --> UAS
  RE -. "ng mirrored as HEP" .-> HEP
  SNR -. "reads HEP off the wire" .-> HEP
```

| Service | Role | Namespace |
|---|---|---|
| `opensips-proxy` | Registrar and stateful proxy; anchors all media through rtpengine | own |
| `rtpengine` | Media relay in userspace; mirrors its ng control plane as HEP | own |
| `sipnab-proxy` | Signaling capture point | joins `opensips-proxy` |
| `sipnab-relay` | Media capture point; decodes HEP to name streams | joins `rtpengine` |
| `sipp-uac` | Places calls, plays caller audio | own |
| `sipp-uas` | Answers, plays *different* callee audio back | own |
| `hep-sink` | Absorbs the HEP mirror so rtpengine keeps sending it | own |

> **hep-sink is not optional**
>
> rtpengine *connects* its Homer socket.
>
> - A destination that answers ICMP port-unreachable makes it give up and send nothing.
> - That looks exactly like the feature not working.
> - Something must absorb the datagrams.
> - That holds even though sipnab reads them passively off the wire rather than receiving them.

## One call, end to end

What each node observes, and the moment the two halves become one call.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant UAC as sipp-uac
  participant OS as opensips-proxy
  participant RE as rtpengine
  participant UAS as sipp-uas
  participant SNP as sipnab-proxy
  participant SNR as sipnab-relay

  UAC->>OS: INVITE (SDP: PCMA, port 6000)
  SNP-->>SNP: dialog created
  OS->>RE: ng offer
  RE-->>SNR: HEP mirror of ng offer
  SNR-->>SNR: learns Call-ID + media ports
  RE-->>OS: allocated ports 30000-30050
  OS->>UAS: INVITE (SDP rewritten to relay)
  UAS-->>OS: 200 OK (PCMA)
  OS->>RE: ng answer
  OS-->>UAC: 200 OK
  SNP-->>SNP: dialog Completed / 200
  UAC->>RE: RTP ssrc=0x0e330af3
  RE->>UAS: RTP (relayed)
  UAS->>RE: RTP ssrc=0x5afe1234
  RE->>UAC: RTP (relayed)
  SNR-->>SNR: 4 streams, named by Call-ID
  UAC->>OS: BYE
  OS->>UAS: BYE
```

> **Read the step "learns Call-ID + media ports" twice**
>
> That is the only step linking the two nodes.
>
> - Signaling never transits rtpengine.
> - So without the HEP mirror every relay stream carries `associated_dialog: null`.
> - No downstream correlation can recover a Call-ID it was never told.

## Setup

From a clone to a running stack.

- Docker and Docker Compose are the only prerequisites.
- The repository builds everything else.

Every command below runs from the `harness` directory.

```bash
cd harness
```

### Mint the credentials

Two secrets:

- a long-lived HMAC key that mints rotating MCP bearer tokens,
- a REST API key.

Both land in the harness `secrets/` directory. The repository ignores it by
pattern. Both targets are idempotent.

```bash
make signing-key
```

```bash
make api-key
```

### Generate the two voices

The caller and callee must play *different* media. Otherwise the two legs are
indistinguishable.

- Use real speech rather than a tone, so a listener can judge the captured
  audio. A male caller counting up and a female callee counting down make
  each leg recognizable.
- The script defaults to:
  - `en_US-ryan-medium` with SSRC `0x0CA11E12` for the caller,
  - `en_US-amy-medium` with SSRC `0x5AFE1234` for the callee.

```bash
./scripts/make-speech-pcaps.sh
```

### Build and start

The sipnab image must carry `vcon`, `audio` and `hep`. Without `hep` the relay
cannot decode the control plane at all.

```bash
docker compose build
```

```bash
docker compose up -d
```

```bash
docker compose ps
```

### Confirm both nodes answer

Different `capture_identity.node` values are the proof. They show two capture
points, not one reached twice.

```bash
KEY=$(cat secrets/api.key)
```

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/stats | jq .capture_identity
```

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" http://127.0.0.1:8081/v1/stats | jq .capture_identity
```

### Run the test

The test:

- places calls,
- waits for the relay to name the media,
- queries both nodes over REST and MCP,
- writes a timestamped report to `results/e2e-<UTC>.md`.

`CALLS` sets how many calls to place. It defaults to 3.

```bash
CALLS=3 ./scripts/run-e2e.sh
```

## What a good run looks like

The same call, the same audio, measured on both arrangements. One node or two changes where the evidence lives. It does not change what the evidence says.

### Co-located — one sipnab

```
Successful call: 1        Failed call: 0

node=<proxy-host>  dialogs=1  streams=4
streams=4 named=4 ssrcs=['0x0ca11e12', '0x5afe1234']
  1-13@172.28.0.21   172.28.0.20:6000  -> 172.28.0.10:30034   4500p  mos=4.36
  1-13@172.28.0.21   172.28.0.10:30012 -> 172.28.0.21:6000    4500p  mos=4.36
  1-13@172.28.0.21   172.28.0.21:6000  -> 172.28.0.10:30012   4500p  mos=4.36
  1-13@172.28.0.21   172.28.0.10:30034 -> 172.28.0.20:6000    4500p  mos=4.36
```

One node holds the whole call. Nothing needs correlating, because nothing split it apart.

### Separate relay — two sipnabs

```
Successful call: 1        Failed call: 0

proxy: node=<proxy-host>      dialogs=1  streams=0
relay: node=<relay-host>    dialogs=0  streams=4

Call-ID                  State       Code  Strm  Pkts    Codec   MOS   2-way
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
1-13@172.28.0.21         Completed   200   4     18000   PCMA    4.36  yes

  1 call(s) correlated across both nodes
```

The proxy reports **zero streams** and the relay **zero dialogs**. That asymmetry is the arrangement working.

- Neither node holds the other's half.
- The join is what puts the call back together.

| Measured | What it is |
|---|---|
| **4** | stream records |
| **4 / 4** | named by Call-ID |
| **2** | distinct SSRCs |
| **4.36** | MOS, both arrangements |

Four stream records for two audio streams is correct, not duplication.

- A relay sees each direction arriving and leaving.
- Two SSRCs is the number of voices.

## The three clients

Both run on the host, outside the containers. Read-only.

| Client | Door | What it proves |
|---|---|---|
| [`../clients/python/leg_correlate.py`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/clients/python/leg_correlate.py) | REST 8080 / 8081 | Joins proxy dialogs to relay streams on `associated_dialog`; reports unnamed media rather than dropping it |
| [`../clients/python/mcp_probe.py`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/clients/python/mcp_probe.py) | MCP 8731 / 8732 | Drives the door an agent uses; compares both nodes' answers |
| [`../clients/python/vcon_view.py`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/clients/python/vcon_view.py) | conserver 8000 | Lists stored vCons, renders one, extracts its audio as WAV |

The two capture clients refuse to report on one node reached twice.

- `leg_correlate.py` compares capture instances.
- `mcp_probe.py` compares `capture_identity.instance`.
- Point them both at the same URL and they exit. They do not present a node
  agreeing with itself as corroboration.
- `vcon_view.py` reads the conserver instead. So the check does not apply to it.

## Troubleshoot the harness

Each of these fails without an error in a log, or reports something misleading.

**HEP support requires --features hep**

The build omitted the `hep` feature.

- So the relay could never decode the control plane.
- Every stream stayed orphaned.

**`media_creating_commands: 0`**

Control traffic is on the wire and in the filter, yet nothing decodes. Check the port the mirror goes to:

- sipnab believes a sniffed mirror only on UDP port 9060.
- It logs one refusal naming any other port it saw.

**associated_dialog: null on every stream**

The default capture filter admits SIP and the media range only. The kernel drops the ng port and its HEP mirror where no counter reports it.

**Everything correct, still nothing named**

The symptoms:

- feature built in,
- ports in the filter,
- datagrams on the wire,
- no stream ever gets a Call-ID.

A sipnab older than 0.5.128 with `--hep-parse` on does not name relay media.
Run a current release.

**Correlation empty after a container restart**

A sidecar shares the namespace of the service it watches.

- Recreating that service kills the sidecar.
- A join over the surviving node then reads as "no calls matched".

**Build says "Built", version unchanged**

Three layers set the OpenSIPS ref:

- the Dockerfile ARG,
- the compose `args:` block,
- a git-ignored `.env`.

The last wins. So editing the first two produces a full cache hit.

**Unsupported link-type 12**

SIPp refuses a pcap written with `DLT_RAW` and plays nothing.

**<recv> before <nop> without a mandatory message**

SIPp rejects a `<nop>` that follows an `optional="true"` `<recv>`.

**GET /vcons → 500**

The plural path is in the conserver's OpenAPI schema but fails. That reads as a broken store rather than as a caller using the wrong path.

**Both WAV channels identical**

Both ends replayed the same pcap, SSRC included. So the legs carried byte-identical audio.

**Counts far higher than the calls placed**

A background call loop keeps dialing during a measurement. So every figure is the calls under test plus whatever the loop fit in the same window.

## Reference

Everything the rest of the page refers to, in one place.

### Ports

| Port | Service | Bind |
|---|---|---|
| 5060/udp | SIP — OpenSIPS | loopback unless deliberately exposed |
| 22222/udp | rtpengine ng control | reachable from the proxy only |
| 30000-30050/udp | rtpengine media | reachable from endpoints |
| 9060/udp | HEP mirror destination | a collector, or any UDP sink |
| 8080 / 8081 | sipnab REST — proxy / relay | loopback |
| 8731 / 8732 | sipnab MCP — proxy / relay | loopback |
| 8000 | conserver API | loopback |

### sipnab flags that decide whether this works

| Flag | Default | Without it |
|---|---|---|
| `--hep-parse` | off | For HEP-encapsulated SIP. Not needed for relay naming. sipnab believes mirrored ng on port 9060 only, with or without it |
| `--retain-audio` | off | Containers carry a `recording` placeholder with no bytes |
| `--api <addr>` | off | No REST surface. A non-loopback bind requires an API key |
| `--portrange` | 5060-5061 | Names which ports carry SIP, separate from the capture filter |

### Endpoints

| Endpoint | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `GET /v1/stats` | Node identity, counts, capture quality |
| `GET /v1/dialogs` | Calls this node observed |
| `GET /v1/streams` | Media, with the call it belongs to |
| `GET /v1/dialogs/{call-id}/vcon` | Build a container for one call |
| `POST /vcon?ingress_lists=<list>` | Store durably through a chain |
| `GET /vcon/{uuid}` | Fetch a stored container |

### Real output

A running harness answered `/v1/stats` with this.

```json
{
  "capture_identity": {
    "instance": "118cfa82b3c2df7bc-1",
    "node": "<proxy-host>",
    "dialog_generation": 1089,
    "stream_generation": 0
  },
  "capture_name": "eth0",
  "capture_quality": {
    "degraded": false,
    "kernel_dropped_packets": 0,
    "interface_dropped_packets": 0,
    "undecodable_frames": 0,
    "snapped_frames": 0
  },
  "source": "live"
}
```

`instance` is what tells two nodes apart.

- Compare it before trusting any answer that claims to join them.
- Two clients pointed at one sipnab otherwise agree with each other perfectly.

The `capture_quality` block above shows the keys this page uses. The block
also carries `invalid_timestamps`, `unanswered_nat_requests`,
`lapsed_turn_allocations`, `lapsed_turn_allocation_streams` and
`ice_role_conflicts`. The [REST API reference](rest-api.md) describes each.

```
1-141@172.28.0.21  172.28.0.20:6000  -> 172.28.0.11:30006  PCMA  4500p  jitter=0.00ms  mos=4.36
1-141@172.28.0.21  172.28.0.11:30036 -> 172.28.0.21:6000   PCMA  4500p  jitter=0.01ms  mos=4.36
1-141@172.28.0.21  172.28.0.21:6000  -> 172.28.0.11:30036  PCMA  4500p  jitter=0.34ms  mos=4.36
1-141@172.28.0.21  172.28.0.11:30006 -> 172.28.0.20:6000   PCMA  4500p  jitter=0.34ms  mos=4.36
```

Four rows, two audio streams.

- Each direction appears twice because the relay sees it arrive and sees it leave.
- All four carry a Call-ID. That is what the mirrored control plane bought.
- Without it every row reads `associated_dialog: null`.

A container, trimmed to its parties and its recording. sipnab exported this
one from [`tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/raw/main/tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap) with `--retain-audio`. The
call's audio flowed one way. `<host>` stands for the capturing host's name:

```json
{
  "vcon": "0.4.0",
  "uuid": "0158a120-0392-864f-994e-dce45c3575ca",
  "parties": [
    {
      "sip": "sip:sipp@10.0.2.20:5060",
      "validation": "none",
      "name": "PCMU/8000",
      "sip_display_name": "PCMU/8000",
      "sip_contact": "sip:sipp@10.0.2.20:5060"
    },
    {
      "sip": "sip:test@10.0.2.15:5060",
      "validation": "none",
      "name": "test",
      "sip_display_name": "test",
      "sip_contact": "<sip:test@10.0.2.15:5060;transport=udp>",
      "sip_user_agent": "FreeSWITCH-mod_sofia/1.6.12-20-b91a0a6~64bit"
    },
    {
      "validation": "none",
      "role": "observer",
      "sip_user_agent": "sipnab/0.5.222 (observer; node <host>)"
    }
  ],
  "dialog": [
    {
      "type": "recording",
      "sip_call_id": "1-1966@10.0.2.20",
      "duration": 8.5,
      "parties": [1],
      "mediatype": "audio/x-wav",
      "encoding": "base64url",
      "content_hash": "sha512-GVphUEyrsE9TSwxDIUBOUWDh1xEmmbHbpT5SqrtTVVVOQWy9JUPWgvOtxlFy1Rr-p8gcpy8pRosgohjHBa6uQg",
      "body": "<182022 base64url chars>"
    }
  ]
}
```

Three things to read here:

- Every party carries `validation: "none"`.
  - The wire carried these names, and sipnab identified nobody.
- The third party is sipnab itself, declared as an `observer`.
  - So a consumer can see that something which never took part produced the container.
- The recording's `parties` is `[1]`: its one channel came from the media
  address party 1 advertised in its SDP.
  - On a relay capture, where the audio comes from the relay's addresses,
    the recording has no `parties`.

### Build features

```bash
cargo build --release \
  --features "native,tls,api,mcp,mcp-http,audio,vcon,hep"
```

Drop `hep` and the relay cannot decode the control plane at all. sipnab refuses `--hep-parse` outright.

## What a stereo recording and a 201 do not prove

Both of these produce output that passes inspection and means something other
than it appears to.

### A stereo recording is not proof of two speakers

A relay observes each direction of a call **twice** — once arriving, once leaving.

- So a two-party call reaches an exporter as four stream records carrying two SSRCs.
- The two records of one leg can precede either record of the other.

An exporter that takes the first two streams it finds therefore selects the same voice twice.

- The result is a stereo file whose channels are byte-identical.
- It claims a conversation and carries one side of it.
- Nothing in the file marks the difference.

sipnab selects one stream per SSRC. It falls back to mono when only one source is present.

- If you build containers by another route, apply the same rule.
- To check an existing file, compare the channels.
  - Identical RMS across a whole recording means one leg, not a quiet line.

The same reasoning governs the omission caveat. It counts *sources*, not records.

- Counting records would report two of four streams missing on a call where sipnab captured both parties.

### A 201 from the conserver does not prove it kept the container

A conserver can do all of these while never having written a container to durable storage:

- accept the container,
- answer **201**,
- return it byte-identical on the next request.

Cache-backed writes behave this way by design. The cache commonly expires in about an hour.

A round-trip performed immediately after the write proves acceptance. It says nothing about retention.

- Every check a careful reader runs passes against a container that vanishes overnight:
  - matching UUID,
  - matching content hash,
  - a WAV that decodes and plays.

Two habits close the gap:

- Post through an ingress chain, naming the list explicitly.
  - So the container enters a pipeline that writes durably rather than landing in a cache.
- Then confirm by querying the durable table for the UUID.
  - That asks a different question than the API does and takes no longer.

The listing route deserves the same suspicion.

- An index that only ever grows commonly backs it.
- So it offers UUIDs that expired hours ago and now answer 404.

## Before this carries real calls

- **Check the recording law that applies.**
  - Consent requirements differ by jurisdiction and by who is on the call.
  - Decide what the law lets you keep before building something that keeps it.
- **Give each producer its own scoped key.**
  - The key decides the role.
  - So a shared key is a producer that can claim any role.
- **Audio is the payload, so size the retention.**
  - Ninety seconds of stereo G.711 is roughly a megabyte of base64 per call.
  - Set a retention policy before the first busy day.
- **Bind to loopback unless you mean otherwise.**
  - A SIP service on `0.0.0.0` answers calls from anyone who can route to the host.
  - Scanners find it.
- **The file store's permissions are part of the design.** `0600` files in `0700` directories. Call audio is not world-readable.
- **Never commit the secrets directory.**
  - It holds the signing key, the per-node tokens and the REST API key.
  - Match by pattern. Then a token for a node nobody has added yet is still covered.
- **Captures and results are local artifacts.** A pcap from a shared network may hold traffic that was never yours to publish.

Harness lives in `harness/`. Run `make help` for the full target list.

---

<!-- source: docs/vcon.md -->

# Export one observed call as a vCon

Something downstream wants the call rather than the packets.

- Examples are a conversation archive, a compliance store, or an agent that reasons over calls.
- Hand any of them a pcap, and you have made the decoding their problem.
- vCon is the interchange container those systems already read.
- sipnab writes one per observed dialog.

**The short version.** A vCon is a JSON object about one conversation. It holds:

- the parties,
- what passed between them,
- what some tool concluded about it.

sipnab fills that shape from signaling it watched go past a tap. Each container carries:

- the SIP ladder,
- the parties the `From` and `To` headers named,
- a diagnosis of the call,
- a statement of what the capture missed, in two places.

When the run retained the RTP payload, the container also carries the audio, inline.

- sipnab decodes PCMU, PCMA, G.722 and Opus, and G.729 on a host where `sipnab g729 install` has installed its tables (see [G.729 decoding](g729.md)).
- sipnab leaves a stream in any other codec out, and the container's caveat names its codec. For a G.729 stream without the tables, the caveat says `G.729 not decoded: codebook tables not installed; run sipnab g729 install`.

- It is the whole call, from its first frame, unless a retention limit cut it.
- If a limit cut it, the container says so (see [Audio retention budget](config-reference.md#audio-retention-budget)).
- sipnab writes no claim that somebody consented to anything.
- A lawful basis appears only when an enrichment service you allow supplies one.
  - The container names that service as its source.
- None carries a signature unless you configure a rule to sign:
  - a rule with `encrypt_to` signs each container and then encrypts it (see [Encrypt what a rule writes](#encrypt-what-a-rule-writes));
  - a rule with `sign_only = true` writes the signed form alone, with no encryption (see [Sign without encrypting](#sign-without-encrypting)).

<!-- vale Google.Passive = NO -->

The lawful basis is in
[Enrich a call before it is written](#enrich-a-call-before-it-is-written).

<!-- vale Google.Passive = YES -->

**A sipnab vCon records what an instrument
saw, not what the parties said.** Read [What may you conclude](#someone-handed-you-a-sipnab-vcon-what-may-you-conclude),
below, before you trust a container. It is the one part of this page to read first.

## What a vCon is, and what sipnab is to it

vCon means "Conversation Data Container". It travels between systems as four arrays:

- `parties`: who took part.
- `dialog`: what passed between them, and when.
- `analysis`: what a machine concluded about that.
- `attachments`: documents riding alongside.

The ecosystem around the format assumes a **recorder**.

- A recorder is something inside the conversation.
- It took the media from a party, and it can say what that party agreed to.
- A recorder can write *"I received this audio from the caller."*

sipnab was never inside the conversation. It reads a mirror port.

- So the strongest sentence it can write is *"I saw packets claiming to be this
  call go past this tap."*
- Those two sentences look alike in JSON. They mean entirely different things.

So sipnab emits **observer** vCons.

- The container names sipnab as a passive party.
- That party contributes to a record somebody else owns. The format itself defines this role.
- The container stops there. It never claims to **be** the conversation.
- [The vCon design decision](design/vcon.md) records the reasoning for that position,
  including every refusal summarized further down this page.

## Produce one

### Check that the binary carries the export

The export needs a binary built with the `vcon` Cargo feature. A default build
does not carry it, and the `full` feature includes it. `sipnab --version` lists the
features a binary carries:

```sh
sipnab --version
```

```text
sipnab 0.5.222 (7f9ffaa7) features: native,tui,audio,tls,hep,api,mcp,mcp-http,metrics,wasm,plugins,bpf,vcon,opus,archive,g729
libpcap version 1.10.4 (with TPACKET_V3); alternate capture backends named: none
```

A binary without `vcon` refuses the export, with exit code 2:

```text
2026-10-16T11:46:58.806503Z ERROR sipnab: --export-vcon needs the 'vcon' Cargo feature, which this build does not carry. Rebuild with --features vcon (or --features full); `sipnab --version` lists the features a binary was built with
```

To build one that carries it from a source checkout:

```sh
cargo build --release --features vcon
```

### Choose how to ask for a container

sipnab builds a container from one dialog. Every surface that offers the
export writes the same bytes. Pick the one that suits you:

| You are | Ask this way | Answers with |
|---|---|---|
| At a shell, reading a capture file | `sipnab -N -I call.pcap --export-vcon 'CALL-ID' --vcon-out out.json` | the container in `out.json` |
| At a shell, wanting it on stdout | `sipnab -N -I call.pcap --export-vcon 'CALL-ID'` | the container on stdout |
| An agent holding an MCP session, one call | the `export_vcon` tool, with `call_id` | one container, its SHA-256, and what the capture missed |
| An agent holding an MCP session, a set | the `export_vcon` tool, with `filter` | one entry per matching dialog, bounded by `--mcp-max-rows` |
| An agent checking a container before sending it | the `validate_vcon` tool | a verdict against the working group's draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04 schema, with every finding named |
| A program over HTTP | `GET /v1/dialogs/{call_id}/vcon` | `200` and the container, or `404` |
| Rust, in-process | `sipnab::output::vcon::export_dialog` | a `Vcon` value |

Two refusals of the CLI pair, each with exit code 2:

- `--vcon-out` requires `--export-vcon`. Without it, sipnab prints
  `error: the following required arguments were not provided:` and
  `--export-vcon <CALL-ID>`. Add `--export-vcon` with the Call-ID.
- sipnab refuses a `--vcon-out` that names the capture it is reading, and
  writes nothing:

  ```text
  2026-10-16T11:50:20.726302Z ERROR sipnab::app::bootstrap: --vcon-out 'sip-rtp-g711.pcap' would overwrite the capture being read ('…/sip-rtp-g711.pcap'). They are the same file. Writing it would destroy the input — choose a different output path.
  ```

  Choose another output path.

On a live capture (`-d` or `--hep-listen`), `--export-vcon` writes the call's
container when that call ends.

- It uses the same timing the spool below follows:
  - the call has ended,
  - it has been quiet for five seconds,
  - sipnab keeps capturing meanwhile.
- sipnab writes a call that has not ended once it has carried no SIP
  and no RTP for 120 seconds.
  - It writes it again if it changes later (see
    [When the call had not ended](#when-the-call-had-not-ended)).
- A live capture that you stop writes nothing.
  - So a call that had not ended and settled leaves no
    `--vcon-out` file behind.
- A live run can end on its own (`--duration`, `--autostop`).
  - It then writes the call, if it was not already written.
  - It still fails if that Call-ID never appeared.
- With `-I`, sipnab writes the container at the end of the run, as before.

The TUI has no export key. Its help screen names the REST route and the
feature flag: use one of the ways in the table above.

Read on for what the container means once you hold one.

## Write calls by rule

A `[[vcon.rule]]` in the config file pairs a filter with two things:

- the directory its containers go to,
- what they carry.

A run can hold several rules. sipnab writes a call that matches several rules once per rule, into each rule's directory.

```toml
[filters]
support = "to.user == '7000' OR header.X-Queue == 'support'"

[[vcon.rule]]
name  = "support-with-audio"
when  = "@support"
dir   = "/var/spool/sipnab-vcon/support"
audio = "inline"

[[vcon.rule]]
name  = "all-calls"
when  = "method == 'INVITE'"
dir   = "/var/spool/sipnab-vcon/all"
```

| Key | Meaning |
|-----|---------|
| `name` | The rule's name, used in the run's report and to pick its spool over REST and MCP. 1 to 64 ASCII letters, digits, `-` or `_` |
| `when` | The filter a call must match. [Named filters](filter-dsl.md#named-filters) work here as `@name` |
| `dir` | The directory the rule writes to. sipnab creates it if it is missing |
| `audio` | `inline`: the audio the run retained travels inside the container, within `--vcon-max-inline-media`. `omit` (the default): no audio, and the container records `media: "not-considered"`. A rule with `inline` turns audio retention on for the run, as `--retain-audio` does |
| `audio` = `url` | sipnab writes the audio to a file beside the container. The file has the container's name with `.wav` in place of `.vcon.json` (`.ogg` with `audio_format = "opus"`): `1-1966_10.0.2.20-1cc03f180ff8a774.vcon.json` gets `1-1966_10.0.2.20-1cc03f180ff8a774.wav`. An encrypting rule names the file by its hash instead (see [Encrypt what a rule writes](#encrypt-what-a-rule-writes)). The container's recording names `audio_url_base` followed by that file name, with the `content_hash` of the file and no body; the completeness block records `media: "referenced"`. sipnab writes the file and serves nothing: the operator's storage serves the URL. Turns audio retention on, as `inline` does |
| `audio_url_base` | For `audio = "url"`: the HTTPS base URL that serves the audio files. Required with `url`; core-04 section 2.4.1 requires HTTPS for a reference |
| `audio_format` | `wav` (the default): the recording is a WAV, `audio/x-wav`. `opus`: Ogg Opus, `audio/ogg`, about a fifth of the size. Needs `audio = "inline"` or `"url"`. See [Audio as Ogg Opus](#audio-as-ogg-opus) |
| `max_inline_media_mib` | The largest audio this rule's containers inline, in MiB. sipnab writes a call above it without its audio and the container records `media: "refused-over-budget"`. Unset: `--vcon-max-inline-media` |
| `live_audio` | `true`: serve each matching call's audio while it is in progress, over the REST API. See [Hear a call while it is in progress](#hear-a-call-while-it-is-in-progress) |
| `live_rtp` | A UDP `host:port`: send each matching call's audio there as RTP while it is in progress. See [Send a call's audio as RTP](#send-a-calls-audio-as-rtp) |
| `live_rtp_allow_remote` | `true`: let `live_rtp` name an address other than loopback. See [Send a call's audio as RTP](#send-a-calls-audio-as-rtp) |
| `live` | `true`: on a live capture, write each matching call's container as the call starts and rewrite it in place each time the call changes. See [Follow a call while it is in progress](#follow-a-call-while-it-is-in-progress) |
| `encrypt_to` | A PEM certificate, or a list of them. Set, the rule writes only the encrypted form, once, to every certificate's key. Needs `sign_key` and `sign_cert`. See [Encrypt what a rule writes](#encrypt-what-a-rule-writes) |
| `sign_key`, `sign_cert` | The PEM RSA or EC P-256 private key an encrypting or `sign_only` rule signs with, and its certificate chain, leaf first |
| `sign_only` | `true`: write the signed form alone, with no encryption. See [Sign without encrypting](#sign-without-encrypting) |
| `compress` | For an encrypting rule: `none` (the default) or `gzip`, which signs the gzip of the vCon instead of the vCon. See [Encrypt what a rule writes](#encrypt-what-a-rule-writes) |
| `sealed_updates` | What an encrypting rule writes when a call it already wrote changes: `new-uuid` (the default), `same-uuid` or `final-only`. No effect without `encrypt_to`. See [When an encrypted call changes](#when-an-encrypted-call-changes) |
| `grouping` | `leg` (the default): one container per dialog. `call`: one container per call, holding every leg the rule selects. See [Calls through a PBX or a B2BUA](#calls-through-a-pbx-or-a-b2bua) |

Other options work with rules:

- `--export-vcon-when` with `--export-vcon-dir` still works. It is one more
  rule beside the configured ones.
- `--since` and `--until` narrow every rule.
- `--content-deny-header` applies before every rule.
- Each rule's directory is a spool the forwarder can deliver. Run one `--vcon-forward` per directory.

A rule runs the same way as `--export-vcon-when`.

- With `-I`, sipnab writes every matching call at the end of the run.
- On a live capture, sipnab writes each call on the timing described under
  [When a container appears](#the-spool-contract-for-a-bridge-that-consumes-it).
  - It uses each rule's own record of what it has written.
- On a live capture, sipnab gives back a call's retained audio only once every `inline` rule that matches
  the call has written it.

sipnab checks every rule when it starts. It refuses to start, with exit code 1, and names the rule, when:

- a name is unusable or used twice,
- a rule has no `dir`,
- `audio` is not `inline`, `url` or `omit`,
- `audio_format` is not `wav` or `opus`,
- a rule whose `audio` is `omit` sets `audio_format`,
- `audio_format` is `opus` and the build has no `opus` feature,
- `grouping` is not `leg` or `call`,
- `when` does not resolve.

sipnab also refuses a rule with any other key. So a misspelled key cannot leave a rule that
writes nowhere.

A live capture with a rule refuses `--redact`, `--redact-map`
and `--content-deny-tombstone`. It does the same with `--export-vcon-when`.

The end of a run reports each rule on its own line, for example
`[[vcon.rule]] 'all-calls': Wrote 2 vCon container(s) to '/var/spool/sipnab-vcon/all'.`

### Audio as Ogg Opus

`audio_format = "opus"` writes a rule's recordings in Ogg Opus instead of WAV:

```toml
[[vcon.rule]]
name         = "support-with-audio"
when         = "@support"
dir          = "/var/spool/sipnab-vcon/support"
audio        = "inline"
audio_format = "opus"
```

What the recording is:

- The Opus codec ([RFC 6716](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6716.html)) in an Ogg stream ([RFC 7845](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7845.html)).
- Its `mediatype` is `audio/ogg`.
  - [core-04 section 4.3.8](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-4.3.8) lists `audio/ogg` among the media types a Dialog Object SHOULD use.
  - It carries no `codecs` parameter. [Section 2.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-2.2) defines a media type as `type "/" subtype` alone.
- Its `content_hash` is over the Ogg bytes.
- It holds the same audio the WAV would. sipnab encodes the PCM it decoded for the WAV.
- The provenance note the WAV carries travels as the stream's `DESCRIPTION` comment.

The bitrate is 24 kbit/s per channel, constant.

- [RFC 7587 section 3.1.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7587.html#section-3.1.1) recommends 8 to 12 kbit/s for narrowband speech and 16 to 20 kbit/s for wideband speech. 24 kbit/s is above both.
- Constant, because [RFC 7587 section 3.1.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7587.html#section-3.1.2) names an encrypted stream as the reason to choose a constant bitrate. A rule with `encrypt_to` encrypts the recording.
- A two-way call is two channels: 6,000 bytes of audio a second.
- Each Opus packet is at most 1275 bytes, the largest [RFC 6716 section 3.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6716.html#section-3.4) allows.

The inline budget applies to the encoded size. For the two-way G.711 call
`12013223@200.57.7.195` in
[`tests/pcap-samples/SIP_CALL_RTP_G711`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/tests/pcap-samples/SIP_CALL_RTP_G711),
26.45 seconds exported as 8 kHz stereo by an `inline` rule of each format:

| Format | Audio | base64url in the container | Seconds that fit in the 5 MiB default |
|--------|-------|----------------------------|---------------------------------------|
| `wav` | 846,832 bytes | 1,129,110 bytes | 122 |
| `opus` | 161,304 bytes | 215,072 bytes | about 644 |

Which builds carry it:

- `opus` is its own Cargo feature, in `full`. It compiles libopus from source, which needs `cmake` and a C compiler.
- The gnu tarballs and packages, the macOS tarballs and the Docker image carry it.
- The static musl tarballs and the `-noaudio` packages do not. They have no vCon export.
- `sipnab --version` lists `opus` when the binary carries it.
- A build without it refuses `audio_format = "opus"` at startup and names the feature.

### Calls through a PBX or a B2BUA

A call through a PBX or a B2BUA is two dialogs or more. There is one per leg, and each has
its own Call-ID.

sipnab ties the legs with the same correlation strategies that
`get_call_tree` and `GET /v1/dialogs/{call_id}/tree` report:

- an identifier both legs carry. This is one of:
  - [RFC 7989](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7989.html) `Session-ID`,
  - a header listed in [`[sip] xcid_headers`](config-reference.md#sip),
  - the SDP origin,
  - a charging vector,
  - a Via branch.
- when the legs share none, a timing guess from shared
  addresses and close start times.

With `grouping = "leg"`, the default, each leg is its own container.

- Every export adds a `sipnab-related-legs` attachment to a leg that has others. The exports are:
  - a rule,
  - `--export-vcon-when`,
  - `--export-vcon`,
  - REST `/v1/dialogs/{call_id}/vcon`,
  - MCP `export_vcon`.
- Its body lists each other leg, strongest tie first:

```json
{"legs": [{"uuid": "018bcfe5-6800-88c0-b9c0-24e4c93555ff",
           "strategy": "x_call_id", "identifier_match": true, "score": 100}]}
```

- `uuid` is the other leg's container uuid. It stays the same under
  `--redact`.
- `identifier_match` is `false` for a timing guess. A busy
  server can get a timing guess wrong.

With `grouping = "call"`, the rule writes one container per call. It holds
every leg the rule selects:

- the parties of each leg in leg order, then the sipnab observer, last;
- each leg's Dialog Objects in leg order;
- each leg's message trace, completeness attachment and analysis. These point at that leg's objects;
- with `audio = "inline"` or `"url"`, each leg's own two-channel recording.
  - Its `parties` maps each channel to a party of that leg. So every party of
    the call has a channel.
  - sipnab does not mix the legs into one file. They
    start at different times and can use different sample rates.
  - Each recording keeps the timing sipnab captured it with;
- a `sipnab-call-legs` attachment. It names:
  - each leg's signaling object,
  - every tie, with its strategy, `identifier_match` and score,
  - `truncated: true` when the call had more than 16 legs and the rest went into further
    containers.

More about the per-call container:

- The container has its own uuid, derived from every leg's Call-ID.
  - So it is the same each time sipnab exports the capture.
  - It differs from every leg container's uuid.
- sipnab names it after the earliest leg.
- A PBX can be the callee on one leg and the caller on the next.
  - It appears once in each leg's parties.
  - Nothing in the signaling proves the two are one party.
- Some legs are not in the container:
  - a leg the rule's `when` does not match,
  - a leg that a `--content-deny-header` withheld.
  - So write `when` to match every leg of the calls you want.
- On a live capture, sipnab writes a call once every leg the rule selects has ended or gone idle.
  - It writes it again when a leg changes.

Before you set `grouping = "call"`, check what ties your PBX's legs together:

- A PBX that copies no identifier between legs leaves one tie, the timing
  guess, and a wrong guess puts two unrelated calls in one container.
- Read the call tree of a sample of calls, with
  `GET /v1/dialogs/{call_id}/tree` or the MCP `get_call_tree` tool. A leg with
  `identifier_match: true` shares an identifier with the other leg.
- A container written with `call` lists every tie in its
  `sipnab-call-legs` attachment, so a reader can see which ones were timing
  guesses.

<!-- The heading keeps its wording because its anchor,
#enrich-a-call-before-it-is-written, is linked from vcon.md, config-reference.md
and errors.md. Rewording it would change the anchor. -->
<!-- vale Google.Passive = NO -->

### Enrich a call before it is written

<!-- vale Google.Passive = YES -->

A `[[vcon.enrich]]` names a service of yours, such as a transcriber or a summarizer.
