## Reading a toll-fraud probe line by line

**Situation:** `--analyze` reports an authentication loop from an address you
do not recognize. The whole probe fits on one screen. Every line of it is a
signature.

**Command:**

```bash
sipnab -N -I pbx.pcap4 --portrange 1-65535 --quiet \
       -e '9f4c2a71-3e08-4b6d-a520-71c0d9e4f832'
```

**Output** (numbers, addresses and the Call-ID replaced, everything else
verbatim):

```text
17:40:41.924 203.0.113.66:53168 -> 192.0.2.30:5060 INVITE UDP
INVITE sip:<redacted-e164>@192.0.2.30 SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 0.0.0.0:53168;branch=z9hG4bK704192338
Max-Forwards: 70
From: <sip:<redacted-e164>@192.0.2.30>;tag=51720483
To: <sip:<redacted-e164>@192.0.2.30>
Call-ID: 9f4c2a71-3e08-4b6d-a520-71c0d9e4f832
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:<redacted-e164>@203.0.113.77:53168>
User-Agent: pplsip
Content-Type: application/sdp
Content-Length: 206

v=0
o=<redacted-e164> 16264 18299 IN IP4 0.0.0.0
s=pplsip
c=IN IP4 0.0.0.0
t=0 0
m=audio 25282 RTP/AVP 100 6 0 8 3 18 5 101
a=rtpmap:0 pcmu/8000
a=rtpmap:101 telephone-event/8000
a=fmtp:101 0-11
17:40:41.968 192.0.2.30:5060 -> 203.0.113.66:53168 401 Unauthorized UDP
17:40:42.467 192.0.2.30:5060 -> 203.0.113.66:53168 401 Unauthorized UDP
17:40:43.468 192.0.2.30:5060 -> 203.0.113.66:53168 401 Unauthorized UDP
17:40:45.468 192.0.2.30:5060 -> 203.0.113.66:53168 401 Unauthorized UDP
```

**What it means.** Six things in that message identify it. None of them needs a
threat feed:

- **`c=IN IP4 0.0.0.0` and `o=` on 0.0.0.0.**
  - The sender wants no audio.
  - It is asking one question: does this PBX route the call?
  - A real media address would cost it a socket it has no use for.
- **`Via` on 0.0.0.0 as well.**
  - So no response can ever route back by the Via.
  - A tool that has given up on receiving replies is not placing a call.
- **`Contact` names 203.0.113.77 while the packet came from 203.0.113.66.**
  - Two different hosts.
  - The generator hardcodes a Contact and sprays from whatever address it
    happens to hold.
- **`a=rtpmap:0 pcmu/8000` in lowercase.**
  - Every real stack writes `PCMU`.
  - The codec list also declares eight payload types and provides an `rtpmap`
    for two.
- **`User-Agent: pplsip`, echoed in `s=pplsip`.**
  - A session name matching the User-Agent is a template, not a session.
- **The dialed digits.**
  - Both `From` and `To` carry a long digit string.
  - It opens with the same fixed prefix and ends in an international
    destination.
  - That is the shape of a prefix probe looking for a route that bills
    somewhere expensive.

Now read the four 401s, because sipnab's own summary needs the correction:

```bash
sipnab -N -I pbx.pcap4 --portrange 1-65535 --json-dialogs --no-cli-print --quiet \
  | jq -c 'select(.call_id == "9f4c2a71-3e08-4b6d-a520-71c0d9e4f832")
           | {auth_loop: .signaling_diagnosis.auth_loop,
              hints: .signaling_diagnosis.hints, timing}'
```

```json
{"auth_loop":{"challenges":4,"evidence":[1,2,3,4],"kind":"silent_drop"},"hints":["Authentication loop: 4 challenges and no Authorization header ever sent — the client is not attempting the challenge, or a proxy is stripping it."],"timing":{"retransmits":3}}
```

Four challenges, and the attacker sent **one** INVITE.

- The intervals between the 401s are 0.499 s, 1.001 s and 2.000 s.
- That is the INVITE server transaction's Timer G ladder from
  [RFC 3261 section 17.2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3261.html#section-17.2.1),
  doubling from T1 up to T2.
- The PBX retransmitted its own final response because nothing ever
  acknowledged it.
- `timing.retransmits: 3` says so in the same record. 4 challenges minus 3
  retransmissions is one challenge.

**What to do next.** Match on the properties, not the address. A single source
address is one rented host.

- `c=IN IP4 0.0.0.0` on an INVITE from outside your network has no legitimate
  reading.
- Neither does a Contact whose host differs from the source.
- Both survive the attacker changing address, User-Agent and prefix.

Block the destination prefix at the trunk as well as the source. The source is
disposable, and the prefix is what pays.
[Cookbook recipe "Detect toll fraud and wangiri call-back bait"](examples.md#detect-toll-fraud-and-wangiri-call-back-bait)
covers the fraud heuristics that run over this pattern live.

---

## One call, two carrier edge nodes

**Situation:** a wholesale carrier's inbound call rings and gets no answer.
Then a duplicate INVITE for the same call arrives almost three minutes later
from a different address. `--analyze` calls the capture clean.

**Command:**

```bash
sipnab -N -I inbound.pcap --portrange 1-65535 --analyze --no-cli-print
```

```text
No problems found in 1 dialog(s) and 0 stream(s) across 60 frame(s). Every frame
decoded, no port gate discarded SIP, and no retention cap was reached — so this
is a statement about the capture, not only about what sipnab could read of it.
```

One dialog, and the ladder shows two sources:

```bash
sipnab -N -I inbound.pcap --portrange 1-65535 --quiet \
       -e '708134922_51772608@203.0.113.53' \
  | grep -E '^[0-9]{2}:|^(Via|Call-ID|CSeq):'
```

`-e` prints each matching message in full. So the `grep` keeps the timestamp
line and the three header fields that carry the finding. Header lines belong to
the message above them:

```text
15:27:14.693 203.0.113.41:5060 -> 192.0.2.10:5060 INVITE UDP
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.41:5060;branch=z9hG4bK4f3e.b7e94c1052d8a3f6417c02be95d3ff81.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.51:5060;branch=z9hG4bK4f3e.9c0a44b7e1d2650fa839cb7f21e408d6.2
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.52:5060;branch=z9hG4bK4f3e.2fb18e05c3947da6b0e572139c4a86ef.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.53:5060;branch=z9hG4bK00B1a97f38e6dc410b2
Call-ID: 708134922_51772608@203.0.113.53
CSeq: 543439 INVITE
15:27:14.698 192.0.2.10:5060 -> 203.0.113.41:5060 100 trying UDP
15:27:15.614 192.0.2.10:5060 -> 203.0.113.41:5060 180 Ringing UDP
15:27:49.170 192.0.2.10:5060 -> 203.0.113.41:5060 BYE UDP
15:27:49.327 203.0.113.41:5060 -> 192.0.2.10:5060 200 OK UDP
15:30:14.459 203.0.113.41:5060 -> 192.0.2.10:5060 CANCEL UDP
15:30:14.460 203.0.113.42:5060 -> 192.0.2.10:5060 INVITE UDP
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.42:5060;branch=z9hG4bK4f3e.5d3ab8146fc70e29d5b1938ae0c6274b.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.51:5060;branch=z9hG4bK4f3e.9c0a44b7e1d2650fa839cb7f21e408d6.3
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.52:5060;branch=z9hG4bK4f3e.2fb18e05c3947da6b0e572139c4a86ef.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.53:5060;branch=z9hG4bK00B1a97f38e6dc410b2
Call-ID: 708134922_51772608@203.0.113.53
CSeq: 543439 INVITE
15:30:14.465 192.0.2.10:5060 -> 203.0.113.42:5060 100 trying UDP
15:30:14.490 203.0.113.42:5060 -> 192.0.2.10:5060 CANCEL UDP
15:30:14.493 192.0.2.10:5060 -> 203.0.113.42:5060 200 canceling UDP
15:30:14.612 192.0.2.10:5060 -> 203.0.113.42:5060 487 Request Terminated UDP
15:30:14.619 203.0.113.42:5060 -> 192.0.2.10:5060 ACK UDP
```

**What it means.** Same Call-ID, same CSeq (`543439 INVITE`), same bottom three
Via entries, three minutes apart, from two different carrier edge nodes.

- Read the Via stack from the bottom up. It names every hop the carrier put the
  call through.
- The branch on the second-from-top entry moves from
  `z9hG4bK4f3e.9c0a44b7e1d2650fa839cb7f21e408d6.2` to
  `z9hG4bK4f3e.9c0a44b7e1d2650fa839cb7f21e408d6.3`.
- That suffix is the carrier's own retry counter.
- Its core re-fired the same call through a second edge node.
- Neither the Call-ID nor the CSeq changed to say so.

Everything downstream of that reads badly without it.

- The edge sent `BYE` at 15:27:49 after 34.5 s of ringing.
- The carrier's `CANCEL` for the first attempt arrived at 15:30:14. That is two
  minutes and twenty-five seconds after the edge had already given up.
- The second node's attempt lasted 30 ms before its own CANCEL.

`--lint` names the fork mechanically. Two findings follow. This page elides the
Call-ID and the rule's own RFC explanation to leave the evidence:

```bash
sipnab -N -I inbound.pcap --portrange 1-65535 --lint --no-cli-print
```

```text
error: SIP-3261-12.1.1-RECORD-ROUTE-NOT-COPIED [...] observed=request recorded
["sip:203.0.113.41;lr", "sip:203.0.113.52;lr"], the 2xx returned [] expected=the
2xx ending with ["sip:203.0.113.41;lr", "sip:203.0.113.52;lr"], in that order
error: SIP-3261-17.1.1.3-ACK-BRANCH-MISMATCH [...] observed=ACK
branch=z9hG4bK4f3e.5d3ab8146fc70e29d5b1938ae0c6274b.0, INVITE branch=z9hG4bK4f3e.b7e94c1052d8a3f6417c02be95d3ff81.0
```

The ACK carries the **second** node's branch. The recorded INVITE branch is the
**first** node's.

- This is the same cross-hop shape as
  [the example "Conformance findings move with the vantage point"](#conformance-findings-move-with-the-vantage-point).
- Except here the two branches come from two boxes rather than two hops.
- That makes it the finding rather than an artifact.

The Record-Route error is separate and real.

- A `2xx` returns an empty Record-Route set when the request recorded two
  entries.
- That leaves the caller with no route set.
- So any in-dialog request afterwards has nowhere to go.

**What to do next.** A duplicate INVITE may arrive on an established Call-ID.
Before treating it as a retransmission, compare the top Via host and its branch
suffix against the first attempt.

- A retransmission repeats the branch exactly.
- A re-fork increments a suffix and changes the sending node.

Take the pair to the carrier with both timestamps. The gap between your `BYE`
and their `CANCEL` is the number that identifies whose timer is wrong.

  when you have a complaint rather than a capture.

  apply, including the fail2ban wiring, the audio export and the MCP surface.
- [Tuning capture](tuning-capture.md#capture-less-bpf-filters) — the BPF
  expressions that scope a capture to one hop, as
  [the example "Conformance findings move with the vantage point"](#conformance-findings-move-with-the-vantage-point) needs.
- [Output formats](output-formats.md#one-object-per-dialog) — every field these
  examples read out of `--json-dialogs`, with its type and meaning.
- [Attribute media on an rtpengine relay](rtpengine.md#the-problem-on-a-relay-capture)
  — what to do when the media in a capture like these arrives with no call
  attached to it.

# Triage a capture from the command line

Your first analysis without the TUI, one command at a time. You list the calls
in a capture and find the ones that went wrong. You explain one of them and
hand the answer to another tool as JSON.

Every command reads a file, so none of them needs root.

- Each step shows the output it prints.
- sipnab also writes progress lines, such as `Reading from 'sample-call.pcap'`,
  to stderr. The outputs below leave those out.
- The [Glossary](glossary.md) defines any term you do not recognize.

## Download a capture

Download the sample call the website uses. It holds:

- one phone call between Alice and Bob,
- the registrations, subscriptions and keepalives around it.

```bash
curl -LO https://sipnab.com/demos/sample-call.pcap
```

## List the calls

Ask for one line per [dialog](glossary.md#dialog). A dialog is every SIP
message that shares a Call-ID.

- `-N` skips the TUI.
- `--report` prints the per-call table.
- `--no-cli-print` leaves out the per-message lines. Without it, they would
  come first.

```bash
sipnab -N -I sample-call.pcap --report --no-cli-print
```

The table comes first, then the RTP streams:

```text
Call-ID                          From           To             State        Code   Duration   Msgs   PDD      Tags
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
reg-alice-4f2a19@192.0.2.10      alice          alice          Registered   200    0s         4      -        -
reg-bob-7c3d02@192.0.2.30        bob            bob            Expired      200    14s        8      -        -
sub-alice-mwi-2b81@192.0.2.10    alice          alice          Active       200    0s         3      -        -
sub-bob-blf-9e42@192.0.2.30      bob            bob            Pending      202    0s         3      -        -
sub-alice-pres-5c07@192.0.2.10   alice          alice          Terminated   200    14s        6      -        -
opt-8b7c02@192.0.2.20            pbx            alice          Completed    200    0s         2      -        -
call-2c9d47@192.0.2.10           alice          bob            Completed    200    8s         7      0.2s     -

RTP Streams:
SSRC         PT   Codec    Clock  Source                Destination           Pkts    Lost   Loss%   Jitter   Dur    Kbps
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0x1a2b3c4d   0    PCMU     8000   192.0.2.10:10000      192.0.2.20:10002      300     0      0.0%    0ms      6s     64
0x5e6f7a8b   0    PCMU     8000   192.0.2.20:10002      192.0.2.10:10000      300     0      0.0%    0ms      6s     64
```

Read it left to right. The last row is the phone call. It is an INVITE that:

- got a `200` answer,
- lasted 8 seconds,
- waited 0.2 seconds for the first ringing response. That wait is the
  [PDD](glossary.md#pdd) (post-dial delay).

The two streams below it are the call's audio. There is one per direction,
with no loss.

The rows above it are not calls. sipnab tracks these as dialogs too:

- registrations (`reg-`),
- subscriptions (`sub-`),
- an OPTIONS keepalive (`opt-`).

The `Code` column is the final response to the request that opened each
dialog. For these rows that is the REGISTER, SUBSCRIBE or OPTIONS answer:
`200`, or `202` for the subscription Bob's phone opened.

## Find the calls that went wrong

`--problems` keeps only the dialogs that failed, or that show:

- one-way audio,
- high loss or jitter,
- a NAT mismatch,
- retransmits,
- slow setup,
- a media asymmetry.

Combined with `--report`, it prints the same table, filtered to those calls:

```bash
sipnab -N -I sample-call.pcap --problems --report --no-cli-print
```

On the sample, the table is empty apart from its header. Nothing in it went
wrong. **An empty answer is a result:** sipnab looked at every call and found
no problem.

To see what a problem looks like, download a second sample from the
repository. It holds five calls. Four of them failed:

```bash
curl -LO https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/raw/main/tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap
```

```bash
sipnab -N -I sip-problem-call.pcap --problems --report --no-cli-print
```

```text
Call-ID                          From           To             State        Code   Duration   Msgs   PDD      Tags
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
busy-3a2b1c@192.0.2.30           carol          dave           Failed       486    1s         4      -        -
decline-7c6d5e@198.51.100.30     erin           frank          Failed       603    1s         4      -        -
notfound-1b2c3d@203.0.113.30     grace          heidi          Failed       404    1s         4      -        -
unavail-4e5f60@192.0.2.50        ivan           judy           Failed       503    1s         4      -        -
```

The completed call drops out. The four failures remain, each with the
response code that ended it:

- busy,
- declined,
- not found,
- unavailable.

## Explain one call

Pick a Call-ID from the table and ask for its report. Set it in a shell
variable first:

- Most Call-IDs contain an `@`.
- Some contain characters the shell would otherwise interpret.

```bash
CALL_ID='call-2c9d47@192.0.2.10'
```

```bash
sipnab -N -I sample-call.pcap --call-report "$CALL_ID" --no-cli-print
```

```text
Call Report: call-2c9d47@192.0.2.10
════════════════════════════════════════
Time:       2023-11-14 22:13:25 -> 22:13:33 (8s)
From:       "Alice" <sip:alice@...>
To:         <sip:bob@...>
Result:     Completed (BYE)
Frame:      sample-call.pcap#19@db3d2ea0ae5df067

Timing:
  PDD:        0.18s
  Setup:      2.42s
  Ring:       2.24s
  Teardown:   0.01s
  Retransmits: 0

SIP Transactions:
  INVITE -> 100 (6ms) -> 180 (180ms) -> 200 (2420ms)
  ACK
  BYE -> 200 (8468ms)

Media Streams:
  RTP 192.0.2.10->192.0.2.20 PCMU SSRC=0x1a2b3c4d pkts=300 jitter=0ms loss=0.0% mos=4.36 R=90.8
  RTP 192.0.2.20->192.0.2.10 PCMU SSRC=0x5e6f7a8b pkts=300 jitter=0ms loss=0.0% mos=4.36 R=90.8

Issues Detected: None
```

The `SIP Transactions` line is the call in one row. The INVITE got:

- `100 Trying` after 6 ms,
- `180 Ringing` after 180 ms,
- `200 OK` after 2.4 seconds, when Bob answered.

`Frame` names the packet the report starts from. You can find the same bytes
in Wireshark. `Issues Detected: None` is the verdict.

Try the same command on `sip-problem-call.pcap` with
`CALL_ID='busy-3a2b1c@192.0.2.30'`.

- Its report ends with `Final failure: 486 Busy Here` under `Signaling Issues`.
- It names the message that says so.

## Hand the answer to another tool

`--json` prints one JSON object per SIP message. `jq` can slice it. This
lists the call's messages in order, with the time of each:

```bash
sipnab -N -I sample-call.pcap --json | jq -r --arg id "$CALL_ID" 'select(.call_id == $id) | [.timestamp, .method // (.status_code | tostring)] | @tsv'
```

```text
2023-11-14T22:13:25+00:00	INVITE
2023-11-14T22:13:25.006+00:00	100
2023-11-14T22:13:25.180+00:00	180
2023-11-14T22:13:27.420+00:00	200
2023-11-14T22:13:27.430+00:00	ACK
2023-11-14T22:13:33.460+00:00	BYE
2023-11-14T22:13:33.468+00:00	200
```

`--json-dialogs` prints one JSON object per call instead.

- It needs `--no-cli-print`, so the per-message lines stay out of the JSON.
- Its `timing` object carries the numbers from the report, in milliseconds:

```bash
sipnab -N -I sample-call.pcap --json-dialogs --no-cli-print | jq --arg id "$CALL_ID" 'select(.call_id == $id) | .timing'
```

```json
{
  "pdd_ms": 180,
  "retransmits": 0,
  "ring_ms": 2240,
  "setup_ms": 2420,
  "teardown_ms": 8,
  "trying_delay_ms": 6
}
```

  one-way audio or a call that drops after 30 seconds. It says which command

  capture to scanner blocking.

<!-- source: docs/glossary.md -->

# Glossary

The VoIP and sipnab terms the rest of these pages use, one short definition
each. Every definition says what the term means **in sipnab's output**. That
sometimes differs from a textbook.

## ACD

Average call duration. The mean talk time, in seconds, of the calls that were
both answered and hung up inside the capture.

- A call still up when the capture ended does not count.

## ASR

Answer-seizure ratio. Of the INVITEs that reached a final response, the
percentage answered with a 2xx.

- An INVITE still ringing when the capture ended is not counted.
- A REGISTER is never a call attempt.

## B2BUA

Back-to-back user agent. A SIP element that ends a call on one side and starts
a new call on the other.

- Each side (a **leg**) carries its own Call-ID.
- The TUI's extended flow (`x` or `F4` in the call flow) draws the legs sipnab
  matched as one ladder.

## BPF

Berkeley Packet Filter. The kernel filter, written in `tcpdump` syntax, that
decides which packets reach sipnab during a live capture.

- sipnab builds one from `--portrange` unless you pass your own.
- The eBPF uprobe backend reads TLS without keys. It uses the same kernel
  machinery for a different job.

## Call-ID

The SIP header that names one call. Every message in a dialog carries the same
value. sipnab keys each dialog on it. So `--call-report` and the REST and
MCP lookups all take a Call-ID.

## Dialog

One SIP conversation: every message that shares a Call-ID. The call list shows
one row per dialog. That includes registrations and other exchanges that
are not calls.

## HEP

Homer Encapsulation Protocol. A proxy such as Kamailio, OpenSIPS or Asterisk
copies each SIP message into a HEP packet. It sends that packet to a collector.

- sipnab can be that collector (`-L`) or a sender (`-H`).
- It works over UDP, TCP or TLS.

## Jitter

How much the spacing between RTP packets varies, in milliseconds. sipnab
computes it with the interarrival algorithm of
[RFC 3550](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3550.html#appendix-A.8).

## MCP

Model Context Protocol. The protocol an AI agent uses to call tools. With
`--mcp`, sipnab offers its analysis as MCP tools. An agent then asks the capture
questions instead of parsing text output. See [MCP server](mcp.md).

## MOS

Mean opinion score. An estimate of how the audio sounded, on a scale from 1.0
(bad) to 4.5 (excellent).

- sipnab derives it from loss, jitter, delay and the codec with the
  ITU-T G.107 E-model.
- sipnab gives an AMR-WB stream a second, wideband score on its own scale.
- Some codecs have no published basis for the score. For those, sipnab
  reports a flagged placeholder. [MOS and codecs](mos-and-codecs.md) lists
  which.

## NER

Network effectiveness ratio (ITU-T E.411). Of the INVITEs that reached a final
response, the percentage the network delivered to the far end. That is:

- answered calls,
- plus those the callee refused with 480, 486, 487, 600 or 603.

A low NER points at the network. A low ASR with a normal NER means the network
reached the called phones. People then chose not to answer.

## Orphan stream

An RTP stream sipnab could not match to any dialog's SDP. It has no Call-ID.
Only SDP in an offer or an answer can match a stream.
SDP in a 3xx to 6xx response matches none.
SDP in an OPTIONS response, or in any method other than INVITE, ACK, PRACK and UPDATE, matches none.
Common causes:

- NAT rewriting the media address,
- SIP that happened somewhere the capture did not see.

## PDD

Post-dial delay. The time from the INVITE to the first 180 Ringing or 183
Session Progress. It is how long the caller waited before hearing anything.

## R-factor

The E-model's transmission rating, from 0 to 100. sipnab computes the MOS
from it.

- sipnab reports its own R-factor beside the MOS.
- sipnab separately shows the far end's R-factor when that endpoint sends it
  in RTCP XR.

## RTP and RTCP

RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) carries the audio or video. RTCP is its
control channel: each end reports the loss and delay it sees. sipnab measures
RTP itself. It reads RTCP as the far end's own account.

## SBC

Session border controller. The SIP element at the edge of a network, between a
carrier and a PBX for example. Most SBCs act as a B2BUA. So a call crossing one
shows up as two dialogs.

## SDP

Session Description Protocol. The body of an INVITE or its answer. It names
the codecs and the address and port each side expects media on. sipnab reads
it to match RTP streams to dialogs.

## SIPREC, SRC and SRS

SIPREC ([RFC 7866](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7866.html)) is how a call gets
recorded.

- The session recording client (SRC) sends the call's media and a metadata
  document to a session recording server (SRS).
- sipnab reads that metadata, meaning who was on the call and which stream
  belongs to whom.
- sipnab is neither an SRC nor an SRS.

## SSRC

Synchronization source. The 32-bit number in every RTP header that names one
media stream. Two streams on the same address and port stay apart in sipnab's
output. Their SSRCs differ.

## TFPS

A toll-fraud prevention system. It is optional separate software. It decides
which sources to ban and enforces that in the firewall.

- sipnab can ask it what it decided (the `tfps_*` MCP tools and the
  `/v1/tfps/` routes).
- sipnab never decides a ban itself. It asks TFPS to ban only:
  - when an operator asks,
  - and only where `--allow-action` enables it.

## TUI

Text user interface. The interactive full-screen view sipnab opens when you run
it without `-N`.

## vCon

A JSON container for one conversation: parties, dialog, and optionally the
audio.

- sipnab writes one observed dialog as a vCon with `--export-vcon`.
- It writes it unsigned, and as an observer rather than a party.
- See [Export a call as a vCon](vcon.md).

# Bearer-token authentication

Two servers authenticate clients with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`:

- the REST API (`--api`),
- the HTTP MCP server (`--mcp --mcp-transport http`, see [mcp.md](mcp.md)).

[cli-reference.md](cli-reference.md#network-listeners) lists every related flag.
sipnab supports two token kinds, checked with a constant-time comparison:

- **Static secrets** — `--api-key` / `--mcp-token` (or `--mcp-token-file`,
  `$SIPNAB_API_KEY` / `$SIPNAB_MCP_TOKEN` env).
  - A fixed shared secret with **no expiry**.
  - Simple, but nothing expires or revokes it short of a restart.
- **Signed self-describing tokens** — HMAC-signed tokens that carry their own
  expiry and id.
  - They enable **expiry, rotation, and revocation** without a server-side session store.
  - This page documents those.

> On a non-loopback bind, sipnab **requires** a token (static or signed).
> The server refuses to start otherwise.
>
> On loopback with no token configured, requests pass without a credential,
> as long as their `Host` header names this server.
> A web page that rebinds its own name to `127.0.0.1` is
> refused with `403`. See
> [Which `Host` names the API answers](rest-api.md#which-host-names-the-api-answers).

The steps below set up signed tokens from scratch. After the steps, this page covers:

- what a token contains,
- how its audience binds it to one server.

## Configure a signing key

Give the server one or more HMAC signing keys (use a long, random secret).
Each surface reads its own flag. So configure the one you are actually exposing.

The REST API takes `--api-signing-key`:

```bash
sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --api 127.0.0.1:8080 \
  --api-signing-key "$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
```

The HTTP MCP server takes `--mcp-signing-key`. Running both of these mints two
unrelated keys. That is deliberate, since a token binds to one audience anyway:

```bash
sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-transport http --mcp-bind 127.0.0.1:8731 \
  --mcp-signing-key "$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
```

You can also pass keys through:

- `--api-signing-key-file` / `--mcp-signing-key-file` (file contents, trimmed),
- the `$SIPNAB_API_SIGNING_KEY` / `$SIPNAB_MCP_SIGNING_KEY` environment variables.

`--api-signing-key` / `--mcp-signing-key` are **repeatable** (see *Rotation*).

## Mint (issue) a token

`--mint-token` signs a token with the **first** configured signing key.
It prints the token and exits. It does not start any capture or server.

An API token at the default one-hour TTL needs nothing but the signing key:

```bash
sipnab --mint-token --api-signing-key "$KEY"
```

An MCP token for a CI runner gets a 24-hour life and an explicit id that a
denylist can name later:

```bash
sipnab --mint-token --mcp-signing-key "$KEY" --mcp-token-ttl 86400 --token-id ci-runner-1
```

- `--api-token-ttl` / `--mcp-token-ttl` (default `3600`) set the lifetime.
- `--token-id` sets the `jti` (defaults to a generated id).

Distribute the printed token to clients.

### Scope: what a token may reach

`--token-scope` sets what a token may reach. It takes `full` (the default),
`metrics`, `read`, `actions` or `audio`:

| Scope | Surface | What it reaches |
|---|---|---|
| `full` | either | Every read route or tool on the token's audience. Not the actions, and not the live-audio routes. |
| `metrics` | REST API | `GET /metrics`, and nothing else. Every `/v1/` route answers `401`. |
| `read` | MCP | Only the tools `tools/list` marks read-only. Calling any other tool gets a JSON-RPC error refusal, not a `401`. |
| `actions` | either | Everything `full` reaches, plus the actions that change another system, such as a TFPS ban, where the server enables them with `--allow-action`. |
| `audio` | REST API | The live-audio routes under `/v1/calls/`, and nothing else. No other scope reaches them. |

Give each client the narrowest scope that does its job:

- A `full` REST token reads call content, including SIP messages that sipnab
  decrypted from TLS. A metrics scrape needs only `metrics`.
- On MCP, a `full` token can also stop the server, export files, and point
  the capture elsewhere. A diagnostic agent needs only `read`.

`metrics` and `audio` exist only on the REST API, and `read` only on MCP. A
mint that pairs one with the other surface's signing key fails and prints no
token:

```bash
sipnab --mint-token --token-scope metrics --mcp-signing-key "$KEY"
```

```text
2026-10-16T12:00:16.370935Z ERROR sipnab::app::bootstrap: --token-scope metrics applies to the REST API only; the MCP surface has no /metrics endpoint
```

It exits with status `2`.

Mint a scrape-only token for the REST API:

```bash
TOKEN="$(sipnab --mint-token --token-scope metrics --api-signing-key "$KEY")"
```

Then confirm the scope took effect. A `full` token and a `metrics` token look
alike until you decode the payload, the part between the two dots:

```bash
python3 - "$TOKEN" <<'PY'
import base64, sys
p = sys.argv[1].split(".")[1]
print(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(p + "=" * (-len(p) % 4)).decode())
PY
```

```json
{"id":"tok-1792151388671087","exp":1792154988,"aud":"api","scope":"metrics"}
```

- `"scope":"metrics"` is the claim that narrows the token.
- A decoded payload with **no** `scope` field is a `full` credential. If you
  meant to mint a narrower one, mint it again.

The signature covers the claim.

- So a holder cannot widen a token by editing or stripping `scope`.
  The signature stops matching.
- Static `--api-key` / `--mcp-token` secrets carry no claims at all.
  They are therefore always `full`.
- Scoping needs a signed token.

## Use a token

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/dialogs
```

That returns `200` when both of these hold:

- the token is valid, unexpired, non-revoked, and wide enough for the route,
- *and* the request asks for something that exists.

A failure is not automatically a `401`:

| Status | What happened |
|---|---|
| `403` | The `Host` header names a host that is not on the allowlist (`--api-allowed-host` / `--mcp-allowed-host`). sipnab checks it before the rate limiter and authentication, so the credential was never read. |
| `503` | The client is over its per-IP rate budget (100 requests/second) or the in-flight cap (`--api-max-conn`). **The rate limiter runs before authentication**, so this answer arrives whether the credential is good, bad, or missing — see [rest-api.md](rest-api.md#bind-address--connection-limits). |
| `401` | Missing, non-Bearer, malformed, expired, revoked, wrong-audience, or wrong-key credential — **or a good credential scoped too narrowly for the route**. A `metrics` token verifies fine and still gets `401` on `/v1/dialogs`, because that route demands `full`. |
| `404` | The credential passed, but nothing matches: no dialog carries that Call-ID on `/v1/dialogs/{call_id}`, or no stream carries that SSRC on `/v1/streams/{id}`. |
| `400` | The credential passed, but the request does not parse: `/v1/streams/{id}` got an id that is not hexadecimal. |
| `408` | The handler exceeded the request timeout. |

Reading a `401` as "bad token" is safe. Reading a `503` that way is not.
A `503` says nothing about the credential, because nothing looked at it yet.

On the HTTP MCP surface a `401` also carries a `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`
challenge:

- `error="invalid_token"` when the client presented a credential that failed,
- no error code at all when it presented none.

So the two read differently in a log. The REST API answers with the status alone. See
[the MCP security model](mcp-protocol.md#security-model).

`/health` needs no credential and skips the rate limiter entirely.

## Expiry

A token stops verifying (`401`) once `exp <= now`. It needs no server action.

- Mint short-lived tokens for CI/automation.
- Mint longer-lived ones sparingly.

## Rotation

Two independent mechanisms:

- **Token rotation:**
  - Mint a new token before the old one expires.
  - Switch clients over.
  - Let the old token lapse.
  - Multiple tokens are valid simultaneously.
- **Signing-key rotation:** pass `--api-signing-key`/`--mcp-signing-key` more
  than once.
  - The **first** key mints. **All** keys verify.
  - To roll a key:
    - add the new key alongside the old,
    - mint with the new key,
    - migrate clients,
    - then drop the old key on the next restart.

## Revocation

To kill a still-valid token before its `exp`:

- add its `id` to a denylist file,
- point the server at it.

Both steps matter. An id in a file no server reads revokes nothing:

- Add the token's `id` to the denylist file:

   ```bash
   echo "ci-runner-1" >> /etc/sipnab/revoked.txt
   ```

- Start the server with the denylist file:

   ```bash
   sipnab ... --api-signing-key "$KEY" --api-revoked-file /etc/sipnab/revoked.txt
   ```

The file is one token `id` per line (blank lines and `#` comments ignored).

It is **re-read when its mtime changes**.

- So appending an id revokes that token within the next request.
- It needs no restart.
- (Signed tokens are otherwise valid until `exp`. So a denylist is the revocation mechanism for the
  stateless model.)

## Token format

```text
s2.<base64url(payload)>.<base64url(HMAC-SHA256)>
```

- `payload` is compact JSON
  `{"id":"<jti>","exp":<unix_seconds>,"aud":"<api|mcp>","scope":"<metrics|read|actions|audio>"}`.
- The signature is `HMAC-SHA256(signing_key, "s2." + base64url(payload))`.
- base64url is URL-safe, no padding.

`scope` appears **only when it narrows something**.

- A `full` token — the default — omits the claim.
  So its payload is the three-field `{"id":...,"exp":...,"aud":...}` form.
- A payload carrying no `scope` means `full`.
- Seeing `scope` in a decoded payload therefore always means
  "restricted". See [Scope: what a token may reach](#scope-what-a-token-may-reach) above.

Verification is **stateless**. The server:

- recomputes the HMAC,
- compares it in constant time against every configured signing key,
- then checks:
  - the audience,
  - `exp > now`,
  - the scope the route demands,
  - that `id` is not revoked.

A malformed token loses (fail-closed).

## Audience binding

`aud` names the surface a token belongs to.

- The HTTP MCP endpoint turns away a token minted from `--api-signing-key`.
- The REST API turns away one minted from `--mcp-signing-key`.
- This holds **even when both surfaces carry the same signing
  key**.

The version prefix is part of the signed input. So an `s2` token cannot be
rewritten as another version to remove its audience.

### Replace an `s1` token

sipnab accepts only `s2` tokens. A token that begins `s1.` carries no
audience and gets `401` on both surfaces. Mint a replacement with
`--mint-token` against the signing key of the surface the client uses.

## Security notes

- Signing keys and tokens are secrets.
  Prefer `*-signing-key-file` or env over argv (argv is visible in `ps`).
- Signature and static-secret comparison runs in **constant time**.
- Do not choose a static `--api-key`/`--mcp-token` shaped like `s2.x.y`.
  - It would parse as a (failing) signed token rather than matching a static secret.
  - (An `s1.x.y` shape is no longer a recognized version.
    So sipnab treats it as an ordinary opaque secret.)
- Static secrets carry no audience.
  - If you set the same static `--api-key` and `--mcp-token`, that one secret opens both surfaces.
  - Audience binding applies to signed tokens only.
- Anyone on the path can read a bearer credential sent over plain HTTP.
  For a non-loopback deployment, do one of these:
  - serve the REST API over HTTPS with `--api-tls-cert` and `--api-tls-key`,
    and HTTP MCP with `--mcp-tls-cert` and `--mcp-tls-key`,
  - or terminate TLS at a reverse proxy in front of a loopback bind.
  - Passing only one of a pair stops sipnab at startup.
    It does not serve plain HTTP on a port meant for HTTPS.
  - See [API TLS](rest-api.md#api-tls) and [MCP TLS](mcp-deploy.md#mcp-tls).
