<!-- source: docs/opensips.md -->

# Use OpenSIPS as your voice stack's SIP server

[OpenSIPS](https://opensips.org) is an open-source SIP server. With Kamailio,
it is one of the two most common SIP proxies in front of phones, PBXes and
carriers. The other voice-stack guides add a component beside it:

- a vCon server,
- TFPS,
- rtpengine,
- Homer,
- Prometheus.

This guide does three things:

- It installs OpenSIPS.
- It sets OpenSIPS up as a proxy that routes each call and stays in its
  signaling path.
- It proves the setup with a test call.

This guide does not use sipnab. When you have this working, [Run sipnab beside
OpenSIPS](opensips-sipnab.md) adds sipnab. If you use Kamailio instead, see
[Use Kamailio as your voice stack's SIP server](kamailio.md).

## Tested on

Every block on this page ran as written, in order, on 2026-10-01.

- The machines were clean x86_64 virtual machines with 2 cores and 3 GB of
  memory:
  - Debian 13 (kernel 6.12.63),
  - Ubuntu 24.04 (kernel 6.8.0).
- On each machine:
  - The source build ran on a machine with nothing installed.
  - The 4.0 packages ran on the same machine after its uninstall removed the
    source build. Kamailio was already running on 5062.
- [OpenSIPS and Kamailio on one machine](#opensips-and-kamailio-on-one-machine)
  and the uninstall ran on both.
- Every test call carried audio both ways, counted on the wire.
- Causing each fault under [When something does not
  work](#when-something-does-not-work) produced the message it quotes, on both.

| Software | Version or commit |
|---|---|
| OpenSIPS, from packages | 4.0.2, the current stable release, from the OpenSIPS project's own package repository |
| OpenSIPS, from source | [`f46ef9337b`](https://github.com/OpenSIPS/opensips/commit/f46ef9337b), master, 4.1.0-dev |
| SIPp (for the test call) | the distribution's `sip-tester`: 3.7.3 on Debian 13, 3.7.2 on Ubuntu 24.04 |

The examples use `192.0.2.10` as the machine's address. Replace it with yours
everywhere it appears.

## Install OpenSIPS

Choose one of the two installs.

- The packages are the stable release, and what most people run.
- The source build is OpenSIPS's development branch. The other voice-stack
  guides build it when they install OpenSIPS for you.

The steps after this one work with either.

Both add the OpenSIPS project's package repository:

- the packages come from it,
- the source build takes `opensips-cli`, OpenSIPS's command-line tool, from it.

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y ca-certificates curl
sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo curl -fsSL https://apt.opensips.org/opensips-org.gpg -o /etc/apt/keyrings/opensips-org.gpg
. /etc/os-release
echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/opensips-org.gpg] https://apt.opensips.org $VERSION_CODENAME 4.0-releases" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/opensips.list >/dev/null
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y opensips-cli
```

### Install the 4.0 packages

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo apt-get install -y opensips
sudo opensips -V | head -1
```

The package installs OpenSIPS under `/usr`. Its configuration is in
`/etc/opensips/opensips.cfg`. It adds a systemd unit that runs it as the
`opensips` user. It enables the unit but does not start it.

### Or build master from source

OpenSIPS master builds with compiler optimizations turned off. That is right
for OpenSIPS's own developers and wrong for a proxy carrying calls. Turn them
back on before you build:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git build-essential bison flex uuid-dev pkg-config libncurses-dev libssl-dev
sudo mkdir -p /usr/local/src/voice && sudo chown "$USER": /usr/local/src/voice
cd /usr/local/src/voice
git clone https://github.com/OpenSIPS/opensips.git
cd opensips
git checkout f46ef9337b
make Makefile.conf
sed -i 's/^DEFS+= -DCC_O0/#DEFS+= -DCC_O0/' Makefile.conf
make -j2 all
sudo make install
/usr/local/sbin/opensips -V | head -1
```

Leave `DBG_MALLOC` as it is. With both it and `CC_O0` switched off, this commit
of master does not compile:

- `net/tcp_conn_defs.h` calls `get_ticks()` without including the header that
  declares it.
- Only `DBG_MALLOC`'s headers happen to supply it.

The build installs OpenSIPS under `/usr/local`. Its configuration is in
`/usr/local/etc/opensips/opensips.cfg`. Give it its own user and a systemd
unit, as the package would:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo useradd --system --home-dir /run/opensips --shell /usr/sbin/nologin opensips
sudo chown root:opensips /usr/local/etc/opensips
sudo chmod 750 /usr/local/etc/opensips
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/opensips.service >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[Unit]
Description=OpenSIPS SIP server
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=forking
User=opensips
Group=opensips
RuntimeDirectory=opensips
RuntimeDirectoryMode=775
PIDFile=/run/opensips/opensips.pid
ExecStart=/usr/local/sbin/opensips -P /run/opensips/opensips.pid -f /usr/local/etc/opensips/opensips.cfg -m 64 -M 8
Restart=always
TimeoutStopSec=30s
LimitNOFILE=262144

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable opensips
```

## Configure OpenSIPS as a proxy

This configuration is a minimal proxy:

- it routes every call to one destination,
- it stays in the path of the call's later requests.

Your own script does much more (registration, authentication, routing to
carriers).

If Kamailio already runs on this machine on 5060, move it to 5062 first. [OpenSIPS
and Kamailio on one machine](#opensips-and-kamailio-on-one-machine) explains
how. Two SIP servers on one UDP port do not refuse each other. The one that
starts last silently receives all of that port's traffic.

The two installs keep their configuration and their modules in different
places. The first two lines find them:

- `C` is your configuration file.
- `M` is the directory your install loads modules from. The script's `mpath`
  names it.

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
for f in /etc/opensips/opensips.cfg /usr/local/etc/opensips/opensips.cfg; do sudo test -f "$f" && C=$f && break; done
for d in /usr/lib/*/opensips/modules /usr/local/lib64/opensips/modules; do [ -f "$d/tm.so" ] && M=$d && break; done
echo "configuration: $C   modules: $M"
sudo tee "$C" >/dev/null <<'EOF'
# OpenSIPS as a SIP proxy that stays in the path of every call.
log_level=3
stderror_enabled=no
syslog_enabled=yes
syslog_facility=LOG_LOCAL0
udp_workers=2
open_files_limit=4096

socket=udp:192.0.2.10:5060   # the address your phones and carriers reach

mpath="MODULES/"

loadmodule "proto_udp.so"   # built into the core, but still loaded by name
loadmodule "signaling.so"
loadmodule "sl.so"
loadmodule "tm.so"
loadmodule "rr.so"
loadmodule "maxfwd.so"
loadmodule "sipmsgops.so"

loadmodule "mi_fifo.so"
modparam("mi_fifo", "fifo_name", "/run/opensips/opensips_fifo")

route {
	if (!mf_process_maxfwd_header(10)) {
		send_reply(483, "Too Many Hops");
		exit;
	}

	if (has_totag()) {
		if (is_method("ACK") && t_check_trans()) {
			t_relay();
			exit;
		}
		if (!loose_route()) {
			send_reply(404, "Not here");
			exit;
		}
		t_relay();
		exit;
	}

	if (is_method("CANCEL")) {
		if (t_check_trans())
			t_relay();
		exit;
	}
	t_check_trans();

	if (!is_method("INVITE")) {
		send_reply(405, "Method Not Allowed");
		exit;
	}

	record_route();

	# Where the call goes. Here, a test callee on this machine; in your
	# stack, lookup("location"), dispatcher or a carrier.
	$du = "sip:127.0.0.1:5070";
	t_relay();
}
EOF
sudo sed -i "s|^mpath=\"MODULES/\"|mpath=\"$M/\"|" "$C"
sudo chown root:opensips "$C"
sudo chmod 640 "$C"
sudo opensips -C -f "$C"
sudo systemctl restart opensips
systemctl is-active opensips
```

What the parts do:

- `record_route()` adds a `Record-Route` header naming OpenSIPS. So the call's
  later requests, the `ACK` and the `BYE`, come back through it.
- `loose_route()` routes those later requests along the recorded route.
- `t_relay()` forwards the request and handles retransmissions and replies.
- `mi_fifo` is what lets `opensips-cli` talk to the running OpenSIPS.

`opensips -C` checks the configuration and prints `config file ok` before
anything starts.

## Place a test call

SIPp plays both ends:

- a callee on this machine that echoes audio back,
- a caller that dials through OpenSIPS and plays a recorded G.711 sample.

So the call carries real audio both ways.

- SIPp's built-in caller ignores the `Record-Route` header. So its `BYE` would
  miss the proxy and draw `404 Not here`.
- The two route `sed` lines make it honor the route set, the way a real phone
  does.
- The callee writes what it receives to `uas.msg`:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo apt-get install -y sip-tester
mkdir -p ~/sipp/pcap && cd ~/sipp
ln -sf /usr/share/sip-tester/*.pcap pcap/
sipp -sd uac_pcap > uac_rr.xml
sed -i 's|<recv response="200" rtd="true" crlf="true">|<recv response="200" rtd="true" crlf="true" rrs="true">|' uac_rr.xml
sed -i -E 's#^( *)(ACK|BYE) sip:\[service\]@\[remote_ip\]:\[remote_port\] SIP/2.0#\1\2 [next_url] SIP/2.0\n\1[routes]#' uac_rr.xml
sipp -sn uas -i 127.0.0.1 -p 5070 -rtp_echo -m 1 -trace_msg -message_file uas.msg -bg
sudo sipp -sf uac_rr.xml 192.0.2.10:5060 -i 192.0.2.10 -p 5080 -s echo -m 1 -timeout 90s
awk '/INVITE sip:/{f=1} f' uas.msg | grep -m1 -i '^Record-Route:'
```

The caller needs `sudo` because it plays the audio sample through a raw socket.

- It sends about 7 seconds of audio, then a short DTMF clip, and hangs up.
- At the end, SIPp's statistics screen shows `Successful call` at 1.
- The last line prints the `Record-Route` OpenSIPS added.

OpenSIPS carries the signaling only. The audio goes straight between the two
ends, at the addresses and ports their SDP names. So this proxy never touches
it.

- [Run sipnab beside OpenSIPS](opensips-sipnab.md) shows both directions of it.
- [rtpengine](rtpengine-relay.md) puts a media relay in its path.

## Operate it

**See what OpenSIPS has handled.** `opensips-cli` asks the running OpenSIPS
through its management interface. OpenSIPS 4 groups the management commands
by namespace. So `statistics:get` is what OpenSIPS 3 called `get_statistics`:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo opensips-cli -x mi statistics:get rcv_requests
sudo opensips-cli -x mi statistics:get tm:
```

After the test call, `core:rcv_requests` is 3:

- the `INVITE`,
- the `ACK`,
- the `BYE`.

**Check health and read the logs.**

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
systemctl is-active opensips
sudo opensips-cli -x mi core:uptime
sudo journalctl -u opensips -n 30
```

**Apply a configuration change.** Check it first, then restart:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
for f in /etc/opensips/opensips.cfg /usr/local/etc/opensips/opensips.cfg; do sudo test -f "$f" && C=$f && break; done
sudo opensips -C -f "$C"
sudo systemctl restart opensips
```

**Uninstall.**

- For the packages, purge them.
- For the source build, remove what it installed under `/usr/local`:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo systemctl disable --now opensips
if dpkg -s opensips >/dev/null 2>&1; then sudo apt-get purge -y opensips; fi
sudo rm -rf /usr/local/sbin/opensips* /usr/local/lib64/opensips /usr/local/etc/opensips /etc/systemd/system/opensips.service
sudo apt-get purge -y opensips-cli
sudo rm /etc/apt/sources.list.d/opensips.list /etc/apt/keyrings/opensips-org.gpg
```

## OpenSIPS and Kamailio on one machine

Developers often run both, to compare them or to test against each. They can
share a machine as long as they do not share a port.

- Keep OpenSIPS on 5060.
- Move Kamailio to 5062, as [the Kamailio guide's
  section](kamailio.md#opensips-and-kamailio-on-one-machine) describes.
- Give sipnab both ports with `--portrange 5060-5062`.

## When something does not work

- **`apt-get` says `Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend. It is held
  by process ...`.**
  - Another package tool holds the lock. On a machine that has just booted,
    this is usually the system's own scheduled update.
  - Wait for it to finish, then run the block again.
- **`opensips -C` reports `could not open module <signaling.so>`.**
  - The `mpath` line is missing or names the wrong directory.
  - OpenSIPS does not fall back to its own module directory without it.
- **`opensips-cli` says `FIFO file /var/run/opensips/opensips_fifo does not
  exist`.** One of these is true:
  - OpenSIPS is not running.
  - `mi_fifo` is not loaded.
  - Its `fifo_name` is not `/run/opensips/opensips_fifo`, where `opensips-cli`
    looks.
- **`opensips-cli` says `no command 'get_statistics' in module 'mi'`.** That
  is the OpenSIPS 3 name. OpenSIPS 4 calls it `statistics:get`.
- **The test call's `BYE` gets `404 Not here`.** The caller ignored the route
  set. Use the edited `uac_rr.xml`, not SIPp's built-in `uac_pcap`.

# Run sipnab beside OpenSIPS

sipnab reads the SIP that passes through OpenSIPS off the wire. So it needs
nothing from OpenSIPS: no module, no configuration change.

On the OpenSIPS machine, sipnab sees both legs of every call:

- the caller's side into OpenSIPS,
- OpenSIPS's side out to the callee.

It puts them together into one call.

This guide adds sipnab to the OpenSIPS proxy from
[Use OpenSIPS as your voice stack's SIP server](opensips.md), installed from
the packages or built from source.

## Tested on

Every block on this page ran as written, in order, on 2026-10-01, with sipnab
0.5.198 from its release package.

- It ran on the Debian 13 (kernel 6.12.63) and Ubuntu 24.04 (kernel 6.8.0)
  machines that [the OpenSIPS guide](opensips.md) had set up:
  - the Watch a call through OpenSIPS step with OpenSIPS from source,
  - [With Kamailio on the same machine](#with-kamailio-on-the-same-machine)
    with the OpenSIPS packages.
- The test calls carried audio.
- The terminal interface showed each call on one row.
- On both machines, causing the fault under [When something does not
  work](#when-something-does-not-work) produced the message it quotes.

The examples use `192.0.2.10` as the machine's address.

## Install sipnab

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
V=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/NormB/sipnab/releases/latest \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["tag_name"].lstrip("v"))')
curl -fsSLO https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/releases/download/v$V/sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb
curl -fsSL https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/releases/download/v$V/SHA256SUMS.txt \
  | grep " sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb$" | sha256sum -c -
sudo apt-get install -y ./sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb
sipnab --version
```

## Watch a call through OpenSIPS

Start sipnab on every interface for 30 seconds. It prints each SIP message as
it passes, and a report of the calls at the end:

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d any --duration 30 --report
```

While it runs, place a test call from a second terminal. Do it as in
[the Place a test call step of the OpenSIPS guide](opensips.md#place-a-test-call):

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
cd ~/sipp
sipp -sn uas -i 127.0.0.1 -p 5070 -rtp_echo -m 1 -bg
sudo sipp -sf uac_rr.xml 192.0.2.10:5060 -i 192.0.2.10 -p 5080 -s echo -m 1 -timeout 90s
```

sipnab prints every message OpenSIPS relays twice, once on each leg:

- the caller's `INVITE` to OpenSIPS at `192.0.2.10:5060`,
- then OpenSIPS's copy of it to the callee at `127.0.0.1:5070`,
- and the same for the replies and the `BYE`.

OpenSIPS's own `100 Giving it a try` goes to the caller alone.

When the 30 seconds are up, the report lists the call once:

- It shows the call as `Completed`, with 13 messages from both legs.
- Below it, an `RTP Streams:` table holds the call's audio.
  - The audio goes straight between the caller and the callee. It never goes
    through OpenSIPS.
  - The table shows the caller's 236 `PCMA` packets and 10 `telephone-event`
    (DTMF) packets.
  - It shows the same again coming back from the callee's echo.
  - That is four streams in all.

You can get the same view in a terminal interface, which updates as calls
happen. Run `sudo sipnab -d any` without `-N` and without `--duration`. It
lists the call on one row, `Completed`, with the same 13 messages.

## With Kamailio on the same machine

[OpenSIPS and Kamailio on one
machine](opensips.md#opensips-and-kamailio-on-one-machine) sets up OpenSIPS on
5060 and Kamailio on 5062. With that setup, give sipnab both ports:

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d any --duration 30 --report --portrange 5060-5062
```

A call through each proxy then appears in the report, one row per call.

- The two test calls send their audio from the same ports with the same RTP
  SSRC.
- sipnab starts a new stream when the second call's SDP renegotiates those
  ports.
- So the `RTP Streams:` table lists each call's streams on rows of their own:
  - 236 `PCMA` packets each way for each call,
  - not one stream of 472 across both.

## When something does not work

- **sipnab reports `No SIP signaling found, but ... RTP packets across ...
  stream(s) were parsed`.**
  - It saw the call's audio, which uses other ports, but none of its SIP.
  - OpenSIPS listens on a port outside 5060-5061, the range sipnab watches by
    default.
  - Give sipnab OpenSIPS's ports with `--portrange`.

# Use Kamailio as your voice stack's SIP server

[Kamailio](https://www.kamailio.org) is an open-source SIP server. With
OpenSIPS, it is one of the two most common SIP proxies in front of phones,
PBXes and carriers. The two share their origins. A routing script written for
one reads much like one written for the other.

The other voice-stack guides use OpenSIPS. This guide sets up Kamailio in the
same role:

- as a proxy that routes each call and stays in its signaling path,
- proved with a test call.

This guide does not use sipnab. When you have this working, [Run sipnab beside
Kamailio](kamailio-sipnab.md) adds sipnab.

## Tested on

Every block on this page ran as written on 2026-10-01.

- The machines were clean x86_64 virtual machines with 2 cores and 3 GB of
  memory:
  - Debian 13 (kernel 6.12.63),
  - Ubuntu 24.04 (kernel 6.8.0).
- On each, the install ran on the machine the OpenSIPS guide had used for its
  source build and then its uninstall. No SIP server was running.
- [OpenSIPS and Kamailio on one
  machine](#opensips-and-kamailio-on-one-machine) ran on both, with OpenSIPS
  from the packages on 5060. Then the uninstall ran on both.
- Every test call carried audio both ways, counted on the wire.
- Causing each fault under [When
  something does not work](#when-something-does-not-work) produced what it
  describes, on both.

| Software | Version |
|---|---|
| Kamailio | 6.1.4, from the Kamailio project's own package repository |
| SIPp (for the test call) | the distribution's `sip-tester`: 3.7.3 on Debian 13, 3.7.2 on Ubuntu 24.04 |

The examples use `192.0.2.10` as the machine's address. Replace it with yours
everywhere it appears.

## Install Kamailio

The distributions carry older Kamailio releases. The Kamailio project publishes
current ones for Debian and Ubuntu, one repository per release series. Add the
6.1 series and install:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y ca-certificates curl gpg
sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://deb.kamailio.org/kamailiodebkey.gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/kamailio.gpg
gpg --show-keys /etc/apt/keyrings/kamailio.gpg | grep -A1 '^pub'
. /etc/os-release
echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/kamailio.gpg] https://deb.kamailio.org/kamailio61 $VERSION_CODENAME main" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kamailio.list >/dev/null
sudo apt-get update
printf '#!/bin/sh\nexit 101\n' | sudo tee /usr/sbin/policy-rc.d >/dev/null
sudo chmod 755 /usr/sbin/policy-rc.d
sudo apt-get install -y kamailio
sudo rm /usr/sbin/policy-rc.d
/usr/sbin/kamailio -v | head -1
```

`gpg --show-keys` prints the key's fingerprint. It is
`E79ACECB87D8DCD23A20AD2FFB40D3E6508EA4C8`, the Kamailio Package Team's.

The Kamailio package starts Kamailio the moment it installs. It uses its sample
configuration, which listens on port 5060 of every address.

- The `policy-rc.d` file around the install is Debian's way to tell a package
  not to start its service.
- The block removes it straight after.
- Kamailio stays stopped until the next step has given it your configuration.

That matters most on a machine already running a SIP server on 5060, such as
OpenSIPS.

- Two SIP servers on one UDP port do not refuse each other. The one that
  starts last silently receives all of that port's traffic.
- A measurement with OpenSIPS running showed this. Kamailio's sample
  configuration answered every request sent to 5060 the moment the package
  started it.

## Configure Kamailio as a proxy

This configuration is a minimal proxy:

- it routes every call to one destination,
- it stays in the path of the call's later requests.

Your own script does much more (registration, authentication, routing to
carriers).

If OpenSIPS already runs on this machine, change `5060` to `5062` in two
places, as
[OpenSIPS and Kamailio on one machine](#opensips-and-kamailio-on-one-machine)
explains:

- in the `listen` line, before you run this block,
- in the caller's `192.0.2.10:5060` in the Place a test call step.

Otherwise the Place a test call step's call reaches OpenSIPS, and tests it
instead.

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo tee /etc/kamailio/kamailio.cfg >/dev/null <<'EOF'
#!KAMAILIO
# Kamailio as a SIP proxy that stays in the path of every call.
debug=2
log_stderror=no
log_facility=LOG_LOCAL0
children=2

listen=udp:192.0.2.10:5060   # the address your phones and carriers reach

loadmodule "tm.so"
loadmodule "sl.so"
loadmodule "rr.so"
loadmodule "maxfwd.so"
loadmodule "siputils.so"
loadmodule "textops.so"
loadmodule "pv.so"
loadmodule "kex.so"
loadmodule "corex.so"
loadmodule "ctl.so"

request_route {
	if (!mf_process_maxfwd_header("10")) {
		sl_send_reply("483", "Too Many Hops");
		exit;
	}

	if (has_totag()) {
		if (loose_route()) {
			t_relay();
			exit;
		}
		if (is_method("ACK") && t_check_trans()) {
			t_relay();
		}
		exit;
	}

	if (is_method("CANCEL")) {
		if (t_check_trans()) {
			t_relay();
		}
		exit;
	}
	t_check_trans();

	if (!is_method("INVITE")) {
		sl_send_reply("405", "Method Not Allowed");
		exit;
	}

	record_route();

	# Where the call goes. Here, a test callee on this machine; in your
	# stack, lookup("location"), dispatcher or a carrier.
	$du = "sip:127.0.0.1:5070";
	t_relay();
}
EOF
sudo kamailio -c -f /etc/kamailio/kamailio.cfg
sudo systemctl enable kamailio
sudo systemctl restart kamailio
systemctl is-active kamailio
```

What the parts do:

- `record_route()` adds a `Record-Route` header naming Kamailio. So the call's
  later requests, the `ACK` and the `BYE`, come back through it.
- `loose_route()` routes those later requests along the recorded route.
- `t_relay()` forwards the request and handles retransmissions and replies.
- `ctl.so` is what lets `kamcmd` talk to the running Kamailio.

`kamailio -c` checks the configuration before anything starts.

## Place a test call

SIPp plays both ends:

- a callee on this machine that echoes audio back,
- a caller that dials through Kamailio and plays a recorded G.711 sample.

So the call carries real audio both ways.

- SIPp's built-in caller ignores the `Record-Route` header. So Kamailio cannot
  route its `ACK` and `BYE`.
- The two route `sed` lines make it honor the route set, the way a real phone
  does.
- The callee writes what it receives to `uas.msg`:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo apt-get install -y sip-tester
mkdir -p ~/sipp/pcap && cd ~/sipp
ln -sf /usr/share/sip-tester/*.pcap pcap/
sipp -sd uac_pcap > uac_rr.xml
sed -i 's|<recv response="200" rtd="true" crlf="true">|<recv response="200" rtd="true" crlf="true" rrs="true">|' uac_rr.xml
sed -i -E 's#^( *)(ACK|BYE) sip:\[service\]@\[remote_ip\]:\[remote_port\] SIP/2.0#\1\2 [next_url] SIP/2.0\n\1[routes]#' uac_rr.xml
sipp -sn uas -i 127.0.0.1 -p 5070 -rtp_echo -m 1 -trace_msg -message_file uas.msg -bg
sudo sipp -sf uac_rr.xml 192.0.2.10:5060 -i 192.0.2.10 -p 5080 -s echo -m 1 -timeout 90s
awk '/INVITE sip:/{f=1} f' uas.msg | grep -m1 -i '^Record-Route:'
```

The caller needs `sudo` because it plays the audio sample through a raw socket.

- It sends about 7 seconds of audio, then a short DTMF clip, and hangs up.
- At the end, SIPp's statistics screen shows `Successful call` at 1.
- The last line prints the `Record-Route` Kamailio added, such as
  `<sip:192.0.2.10;lr;ftag=52680SIPpTag091>`. It holds:
  - Kamailio's address,
  - `lr` for loose routing,
  - the caller's `From` tag.

Kamailio carries the signaling only. The audio goes straight between the two
ends, at the addresses and ports their SDP names. So this proxy never touches
it.

- [Run sipnab beside Kamailio](kamailio-sipnab.md) shows both directions of it.
- [rtpengine](rtpengine-relay.md#with-kamailio) puts a media relay in its path.

## Operate it

**See what Kamailio has handled.** `kamcmd` asks the running Kamailio. Name a
statistic, or a group with a trailing colon. The `core:` group holds the
counts of requests received and replies relayed:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo kamcmd stats.get_statistics rcv_requests_invite
sudo kamcmd stats.get_statistics core: | grep -E 'rcv_(requests|replies_2xx)_invite'
```

After the test call, `rcv_requests_invite` is 1. So is
`rcv_replies_2xx_invite`, the callee's `200 OK`.

**Check health and read the logs.**

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
systemctl is-active kamailio
sudo kamcmd core.uptime
sudo journalctl -u kamailio -n 30
```

**Apply a configuration change.** Check it first, then restart:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo kamailio -c -f /etc/kamailio/kamailio.cfg
sudo systemctl restart kamailio
```

**Uninstall.**

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo systemctl disable --now kamailio
sudo apt-get purge -y kamailio
sudo rm /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kamailio.list /etc/apt/keyrings/kamailio.gpg
```

## OpenSIPS and Kamailio on one machine

Developers often run both, to compare them or to test against each. They can
share a machine as long as they do not share a port.

- A shared port does not fail loudly. Whichever server starts last silently
  takes all of its traffic.
- Keep OpenSIPS on 5060, as [the OpenSIPS guide](opensips.md) sets it up.
- Keep Kamailio on 5062.
- If you set Kamailio up on 5060 first, move it before OpenSIPS starts:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo sed -i 's|^listen=udp:192.0.2.10:5060 |listen=udp:192.0.2.10:5062 |' /etc/kamailio/kamailio.cfg
grep '^listen=' /etc/kamailio/kamailio.cfg
sudo kamailio -c -f /etc/kamailio/kamailio.cfg
sudo systemctl restart kamailio
```

A test call now reaches Kamailio on 5062 and OpenSIPS on 5060. Place one
through each, from `~/sipp`, with the callee from the Place a test call step
running:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
cd ~/sipp
sipp -sn uas -i 127.0.0.1 -p 5070 -rtp_echo -m 2 -bg
sudo sipp -sf uac_rr.xml 192.0.2.10:5062 -i 192.0.2.10 -p 5080 -s echo -m 1 -timeout 90s
sudo sipp -sf uac_rr.xml 192.0.2.10:5060 -i 192.0.2.10 -p 5080 -s echo -m 1 -timeout 90s
```

Each shows `Successful call` at 1. sipnab watches ports 5060-5061 by default.
So give it both proxies' ports: `--portrange 5060-5062`.

## Kamailio in the other voice-stack guides

The other guides use OpenSIPS. Each has a section that says what changes with
Kamailio:

- [rtpengine](rtpengine-relay.md#with-kamailio): Kamailio's `rtpengine` module.
- [rtpproxy](rtpproxy-relay.md#with-kamailio): Kamailio's `rtpproxy` module.
- [Homer](homer.md#with-kamailio): Kamailio's `siptrace` module sends HEP.
- [Prometheus](prometheus.md#with-kamailio): Kamailio's `xhttp_prom` module.
- [TFPS](tfps.md): nothing changes. TFPS needs nothing from the SIP server.
- [vCon server](vcon-server.md#with-kamailio-a-gap): a gap. Kamailio has no
  SIPREC module, so it cannot record calls for the vCon server.
  [sipnab's own vCons](vcon-sipnab.md#with-kamailio) are what a Kamailio stack
  can send it.

## When something does not work

- **`apt-get` says `Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend. It is held
  by process ...`.**
  - Another package tool holds the lock. On a machine that has just booted,
    this is usually the system's own scheduled update.
  - Wait for it to finish, then run the block again.
- **`kamailio -c` reports `parse error in config file` and `unknown command,
  missing loadmodule?`.**
  - The script calls a function whose module is not loaded.
  - The error names the line and column.
  - The line before it names the function, such as
    `failed to find command is_method`.
  - Load the module that provides it.
- **`kamcmd` says `connect(//var/run/kamailio/kamailio_ctl): No such file or
  directory`.** Kamailio is not running, or `ctl.so` is not loaded.
- **The test call's `BYE` gets no answer.**
  - The caller ignored the route set. So Kamailio dropped its `ACK` and `BYE`.
  - SIPp can still report the call as successful:
    - the callee, which never got the `ACK`, sends its `200 OK` again,
    - SIPp takes one of those for the `BYE`'s answer.
  - Use the edited `uac_rr.xml`, not SIPp's built-in `uac_pcap`.

<!-- source: docs/kamailio-sipnab.md -->

# Run sipnab beside Kamailio

sipnab reads the SIP that passes through Kamailio off the wire. So it needs
nothing from Kamailio: no module, no configuration change.

On the Kamailio machine, sipnab sees both legs of every call:

- the caller's side into Kamailio,
- Kamailio's side out to the callee.

It puts them together into one call.

This guide adds sipnab to the Kamailio proxy from
[Use Kamailio as your voice stack's SIP server](kamailio.md).

## Tested on

Every block on this page ran as written, in order, on 2026-10-01, with sipnab
0.5.198 from its release package.

- It ran on the Debian 13 (kernel 6.12.63) and Ubuntu 24.04 (kernel 6.8.0)
  machines that [the Kamailio guide](kamailio.md) had set up.
- Kamailio ran alone and beside OpenSIPS.
- The test calls carried audio.
- The terminal interface showed each call on one row.
- On both machines, causing the fault under [When
  something does not work](#when-something-does-not-work) produced the message
  it quotes.

The examples use `192.0.2.10` as the machine's address.

## Install sipnab

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
V=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/NormB/sipnab/releases/latest \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["tag_name"].lstrip("v"))')
curl -fsSLO https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/releases/download/v$V/sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb
curl -fsSL https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/releases/download/v$V/SHA256SUMS.txt \
  | grep " sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb$" | sha256sum -c -
sudo apt-get install -y ./sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb
sipnab --version
```

## Watch a call through Kamailio

Start sipnab on every interface for 30 seconds. It prints each SIP message as
it passes, and a report of the calls at the end:

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d any --duration 30 --report
```

While it runs, place a test call from a second terminal. Do it as in
[the Place a test call step of the Kamailio guide](kamailio.md#place-a-test-call):

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
cd ~/sipp
sipp -sn uas -i 127.0.0.1 -p 5070 -rtp_echo -m 1 -bg
sudo sipp -sf uac_rr.xml 192.0.2.10:5060 -i 192.0.2.10 -p 5080 -s echo -m 1 -timeout 90s
```

sipnab prints every message Kamailio relays twice, once on each leg:

- the caller's `INVITE` to Kamailio at `192.0.2.10:5060`,
- then Kamailio's copy of it to the callee at `127.0.0.1:5070`,
- and the same for the replies and the `BYE`.

Kamailio's own `100 trying -- your call is important to us` goes to the caller
alone.

When the 30 seconds are up, the report lists the call once:

- It shows the call as `Completed`, with 13 messages from both legs.
- Below it, an `RTP Streams:` table holds the call's audio.
  - The audio goes straight between the caller and the callee. It never goes
    through Kamailio.
  - The table shows the caller's 236 `PCMA` packets and 10 `telephone-event`
    (DTMF) packets.
  - It shows the same again coming back from the callee's echo.
  - That is four streams in all.

You can get the same view in a terminal interface, which updates as calls
happen. Run `sudo sipnab -d any` without `-N` and without `--duration`. It
lists the call on one row, `Completed`, with the same 13 messages.

## With OpenSIPS on the same machine

[OpenSIPS and Kamailio on one
machine](kamailio.md#opensips-and-kamailio-on-one-machine) sets up OpenSIPS on
5060 and Kamailio on 5062. With that setup, give sipnab both ports:

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d any --duration 30 --report --portrange 5060-5062
```

A call through each proxy then appears in the report, one row per call.

- The two test calls send their audio from the same ports with the same RTP
  SSRC.
- sipnab starts a new stream when the second call's SDP renegotiates those
  ports.
- So the `RTP Streams:` table lists each call's streams on rows of their own:
  - 236 `PCMA` packets each way for each call,
  - not one stream of 472 across both.

## When something does not work

- **sipnab reports `No SIP signaling found, but ... RTP packets across ...
  stream(s) were parsed`.**
  - It saw the call's audio, which uses other ports, but none of its SIP.
  - Kamailio listens on a port outside 5060-5061, the range sipnab watches by
    default.
  - Give sipnab Kamailio's ports with `--portrange`.

<!-- source: docs/asterisk.md -->

# Use Asterisk as your voice stack's PBX

[Asterisk](https://www.asterisk.org) is an open-source PBX. It does three
things:

- It answers calls.
- It runs a dialplan that decides what happens to each one.
- It places calls to phones and carriers.

OpenSIPS and Kamailio are proxies. They pass a call's SIP messages along.
Asterisk is a [B2BUA](glossary.md#b2bua) (back-to-back user agent) instead:

- It answers the caller's call itself.
- It places a second call to the callee.
- It connects the two.

Each call through Asterisk is therefore two SIP calls, called legs. Each leg
has its own Call-ID.

This guide does the following:

- It builds Asterisk from source.
- It sets up two endpoints and a dialplan that connects them.
- It proves it with a test call that carries audio both ways through Asterisk.

This guide does not use sipnab. When you have this working,
[Run sipnab beside Asterisk](asterisk-sipnab.md) adds sipnab.

## Tested on

Every block on this page ran as written on 2026-10-12.

- The machines were clean x86_64 virtual machines with 2 cores and 3 GB of
  memory.
- They ran Debian 13 (kernel 6.12.63) and Ubuntu 24.04 (kernel 6.8.0).
- The machines had nothing installed before the build.
- On Ubuntu 24.04, the install, configuration, test call and uninstall then ran
  a second time on the same machine, after its first uninstall.
- Every test call carried audio both ways through Asterisk, counted on the
  wire.
- Causing each fault under
  [When something does not work](#when-something-does-not-work) produced what
  it describes, on both.

| Software | Version |
|---|---|
| Asterisk | 22.11.0, the Asterisk project's source release. 22 is a long-term support series, which the project lists as fully supported until 2028-10-16 |
| SIPp (for the test call) | the distribution's `sip-tester`: 3.7.3 on Debian 13, 3.7.2 on Ubuntu 24.04 |

The examples use `192.0.2.10` as the machine's address. Replace it with yours
everywhere it appears.

## Install Asterisk

Debian 13 has no Asterisk package. Ubuntu 24.04 carries the older 20.6.0.
The Asterisk project publishes source releases. They build the same way on
both. This block does the following:

- It installs the build tools and libraries.
- It downloads 22.11.0.
- It checks it against the project's published SHA-256 checksum.
- It builds it.

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends build-essential curl ca-certificates pkg-config bzip2 patch \
  libedit-dev libjansson-dev libxml2-dev uuid-dev libsqlite3-dev libssl-dev
sudo mkdir -p /usr/local/src/voice && sudo chown "$USER": /usr/local/src/voice
cd /usr/local/src/voice
curl -fsSLO https://downloads.asterisk.org/pub/telephony/asterisk/asterisk-22.11.0.tar.gz
curl -fsSL https://downloads.asterisk.org/pub/telephony/asterisk/asterisk-22.11.0.sha256 | sha256sum -c -
tar xzf asterisk-22.11.0.tar.gz
cd asterisk-22.11.0
./configure
make -j2
sudo make install
sudo asterisk -V
```

- `sha256sum -c` prints `asterisk-22.11.0.tar.gz: OK`.
  - The checksum file comes from the same server as the source.
  - So it detects a damaged download, not a replaced one.
- `./configure` also downloads PJSIP from `raw.githubusercontent.com`.
  - PJSIP is the SIP library that Asterisk's `chan_pjsip` uses.
  - That step checks PJSIP before the build uses it.
- The last line prints `Asterisk 22.11.0`.

`make install` does three things:

- It puts the program in `/usr/sbin/asterisk`.
- It puts its modules in `/usr/lib/asterisk/modules`.
- It creates an empty `/etc/asterisk` for the configuration.

Give Asterisk its own user and a systemd unit that runs it as that user:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo useradd --system --home-dir /var/lib/asterisk --shell /usr/sbin/nologin asterisk
sudo chown -R asterisk:asterisk /var/lib/asterisk /var/log/asterisk /var/spool/asterisk
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/asterisk.service >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[Unit]
Description=Asterisk PBX
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=asterisk
Group=asterisk
RuntimeDirectory=asterisk
WorkingDirectory=/var/lib/asterisk
ExecStart=/usr/sbin/asterisk -f -C /etc/asterisk/asterisk.conf
ExecReload=/usr/sbin/asterisk -rx 'core reload'
Restart=always
RestartSec=4

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable asterisk
```

- `-f` keeps Asterisk in the foreground, where systemd can watch it.
- `RuntimeDirectory` creates `/run/asterisk` for the `asterisk` user at every
  start.
  - Asterisk puts its control socket there.
  - The `asterisk -rx` commands below use that socket to talk to the running
    Asterisk.

## Configure Asterisk

This configuration has two endpoints, a caller and a callee. It also has a
dialplan. The dialplan connects a call to extension `100` from the caller to
the callee. Your own configuration does much more (phones that register with a
password, voicemail, carriers).

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
printf '[options]\n' | sudo tee /etc/asterisk/asterisk.conf >/dev/null
sudo tee /etc/asterisk/modules.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[modules]
autoload = yes
EOF
sudo tee /etc/asterisk/logger.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[logfiles]
messages.log => notice,warning,error
EOF
sudo tee /etc/asterisk/rtp.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[general]
rtpstart = 10000
rtpend = 20000
EOF
sudo tee /etc/asterisk/pjsip.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[transport-udp]
type = transport
protocol = udp
bind = 0.0.0.0:5060

[caller]
type = endpoint
context = from-caller
disallow = all
allow = alaw,ulaw
direct_media = no

[caller-ip]
type = identify
endpoint = caller
match = 192.0.2.10

[callee]
type = endpoint
context = from-callee
disallow = all
allow = ulaw
direct_media = no
dtmf_mode = auto
aors = callee

[callee]
type = aor
contact = sip:192.0.2.10:5070
EOF
sudo tee /etc/asterisk/extensions.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[from-caller]
exten => 100,1,Dial(PJSIP/callee,30)
 same => n,Hangup()
EOF
sudo systemctl restart asterisk
until sudo asterisk -rx 'core waitfullybooted' 2>/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
sudo asterisk -rx 'pjsip show endpoints'
```

What the files do:

- `asterisk.conf` is the first file Asterisk reads.
  - An empty `[options]` section keeps Asterisk's built-in settings.
  - Without the file, every `asterisk -rx` command prints `Unable to open
    specified master config file`.
- `modules.conf` loads every module the build installed.
  - Some modules decline to load without a configuration file of their own.
  - Each of them logs a line such as `app_queue declined to load.` to
    `/var/log/asterisk/messages.log`.
- `logger.conf` writes notices, warnings and errors to
  `/var/log/asterisk/messages.log`.
- `rtp.conf` sets the UDP ports Asterisk takes for each call's audio.
- `pjsip.conf` sets up SIP:
  - The `transport` listens on UDP port 5060 on every address.
  - An `endpoint` is a phone or a carrier Asterisk talks to.
    - `context` names the dialplan section that handles calls from it.
  - The `identify` section tells Asterisk that requests from `192.0.2.10` come
    from the `caller` endpoint.
    - Requests from any other address get `401
      Unauthorized`.
  - `allow` lists the codecs each end may use.
    - The caller sends G.711 A-law (`alaw`, called PCMA in SDP).
    - The callee takes only G.711 u-law (`ulaw`, PCMU).
    - So Asterisk converts the audio between the two codecs.
  - `direct_media = no` keeps the audio flowing through Asterisk.
    - The sample configuration that ships with Asterisk describes the setting
      as `Determines whether media may flow directly between endpoints`.
    - Its default is `yes`.
  - `dtmf_mode = auto` sets how Asterisk passes key presses (DTMF) to the
    callee.
    - Asterisk's own description of `auto` is `DTMF is sent as RFC 4733
      if the other side supports it or as INBAND if not`.
    - That means as [RFC 4733](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4733.html) event packets, or as tones inside the audio.
    - This test callee supports no events.
    - With the default, `rfc4733`, Asterisk sent the test caller's key press
      to this callee as events anyway.
    - The echoing callee returned them. The two then exchanged more than
      6,000 event packets each way within 0.15 seconds.
  - The `aor` (address of record) gives the address Asterisk calls the
    callee at.
- `extensions.conf` is the dialplan.
  - A call from the caller to `100` rings the callee for up to 30 seconds.
  - It hangs up when either side does.

systemd counts Asterisk as started as soon as the process runs. That is before
Asterisk has opened its control socket. So an `asterisk -rx` straight after a
restart can fail.

- The `until` line waits until `core waitfullybooted` answers
  `Asterisk has fully booted.`.
- `pjsip show endpoints` then lists both endpoints:
  - `caller` with `Match: 192.0.2.10/32`,
  - `callee` with its contact `sip:192.0.2.10:5070`.

## Place a test call

SIPp plays both ends:

- a callee on this machine at port 5070 that echoes audio back,
- a caller that dials extension `100` and plays a recorded G.711 sample.

So the call carries real audio both ways. Both SIPp ends write the same SDP
origin line (`o=user1 53655765 2353687637`) by default. The `sed` line gives
the callee its own, as two separate phones would have:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo apt-get install -y sip-tester
mkdir -p ~/sipp/pcap && cd ~/sipp
ln -sf /usr/share/sip-tester/*.pcap pcap/
sipp -sd uas > uas.xml
sed -i 's/o=user1 53655765 2353687637/o=callee 1 1/' uas.xml
sipp -sf uas.xml -i 192.0.2.10 -p 5070 -min_rtp_port 7000 -max_rtp_port 7100 -rtp_echo -m 1 -bg
sudo sipp -sn uac_pcap 192.0.2.10:5060 -i 192.0.2.10 -p 5080 -s 100 -m 1 -timeout 90s
```

- The callee takes its audio ports from 7000-7100. That way it does not
  collide with the caller's port 6000 on the same address.
- The caller needs `sudo` because it plays the audio sample through a raw
  socket.
- The caller sends about 7 seconds of audio, then a short DTMF clip, and hangs
  up.
- At the end SIPp's statistics screen shows `Successful call` at 1.

Unlike a proxy, Asterisk carries the audio as well as the signaling.

- The caller sends its audio to Asterisk, at the port Asterisk's answer names.
- Asterisk sends it on to the callee from a second port, converted to PCMU.
- The callee's echo comes back the same way.

[Run sipnab beside Asterisk](asterisk-sipnab.md) shows both legs and all of
their audio.

## Operate it

**See what Asterisk has handled.**

- `asterisk -rx` runs one command in the running Asterisk.
- It needs `sudo`, because the control socket belongs to the `asterisk` user.
- `core show calls` prints the calls in progress.
  - It prints `0 active
    calls` once the test call has ended.
  - It also prints a `calls processed` count.
- `pjsip show endpoints` lists the endpoints again:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo asterisk -rx 'core show calls'
sudo asterisk -rx 'pjsip show endpoints'
```

**Check health and read the logs.**

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
systemctl is-active asterisk
sudo asterisk -rx 'core show uptime'
sudo tail -n 20 /var/log/asterisk/messages.log
```

**Apply a configuration change.** `core reload` makes Asterisk reread its
configuration files. `pjsip.conf` and `extensions.conf` are among them:

```bash
sudo asterisk -rx 'core reload'
```

A configuration file that did not exist when Asterisk started can need a
restart instead.

- [Run sipnab beside Asterisk](asterisk-sipnab.md) has you create a
  `hep.conf`.
- After you create it, `core reload` leaves the modules that read it
  `Not Running`.
- A restart starts them:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo systemctl restart asterisk
systemctl is-active asterisk
```

**Uninstall.** `make uninstall-all` removes:

- the program,
- its modules,
- the configuration, logs and data under `/etc/asterisk`, `/var/log/asterisk`,
  `/var/lib/asterisk` and `/var/spool/asterisk`.

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo systemctl disable --now asterisk
cd /usr/local/src/voice/asterisk-22.11.0
sudo make uninstall-all
sudo rmdir /usr/lib/asterisk
sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/asterisk.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo userdel asterisk
cd /usr/local/src/voice && rm -rf asterisk-22.11.0 asterisk-22.11.0.tar.gz
```

`make uninstall-all` leaves the empty `/usr/lib/asterisk` directory behind.
`rmdir` removes it.

## When something does not work

- **`apt-get` says `Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend. It is held
  by process ...`.**
  - Another package tool holds the lock.
  - On a machine that has just booted, it is usually the system's own
    scheduled update.
  - Wait for it to finish, then run the block again.
- **`asterisk -rx` says `Unable to connect to remote asterisk (does
  /var/run/asterisk/asterisk.ctl exist?)`.** One of these is true:
  - Asterisk is not running.
  - It has not finished starting.
  - You ran the command without `sudo`.
    - On Debian 13, `/usr/sbin` is not in an ordinary user's `PATH`.
    - There the command without `sudo` answers `asterisk: command not found`
      instead.
- **`asterisk -rx 'pjsip reload'` says `No such command 'pjsip reload'`.** Use
  `core reload`, which rereads `pjsip.conf` with the rest.
- **The caller gets `404 Not Found`.**
  - The dialplan has no such extension.
  - `messages.log` names it: `Call (UDP:192.0.2.10:5080) to extension '999'
    rejected because extension not found in context 'from-caller'.`
- **The caller gets `401 Unauthorized`.**
  - Asterisk matched the request to no endpoint.
  - `messages.log` says `No matching endpoint found`. It names the address the
    request came from.
  - Add that address to the `identify` section's `match`.
- **The caller gets `603 Decline`.**
  - Asterisk could not reach the callee at the `aor`'s `contact`.
  - Check that the callee runs and listens there.

---

<!-- source: docs/asterisk-sipnab.md -->

# Run sipnab beside Asterisk

sipnab reads the SIP and the audio that pass through Asterisk off the wire.
So it needs nothing from Asterisk: no module, no configuration change.

Asterisk is a [B2BUA](glossary.md#b2bua). Every call through it is two SIP
calls, called legs:

- the caller's leg into Asterisk,
- Asterisk's leg out to the callee.

Each leg has its own Call-ID. sipnab does three things with the two legs:

- It lists them as two [dialogs](glossary.md#dialog).
- It shows them together as one call flow.
- It measures the audio on each.

This guide adds sipnab to the Asterisk machine from
[Use Asterisk as your voice stack's PBX](asterisk.md). It does the following:

- It watches a test call.
- It shows its two legs in the terminal interface.
- It explains it from a saved capture.
- It answers about it over MCP and the REST API.
- Finally, it receives Asterisk's own copies of its SIP over HEP.

**What works without Asterisk.** sipnab does not depend on Asterisk.

- The sections from "Watch a call through Asterisk"
  to "Keep sipnab running, and query it over REST"
  use sipnab's own capture.
  - They work the same way beside any SIP server.
- The section "Receive Asterisk's HEP" is the one that uses an
  Asterisk module.
  - You can leave it out.

## Tested on

Every block on this page ran as written, in order, on 2026-10-12.

- It ran with sipnab 0.5.211 from its release package.
- It ran on the Debian 13 (kernel 6.12.63) and Ubuntu 24.04 (kernel 6.8.0)
  machines that [the Asterisk guide](asterisk.md) had set up.
- The terminal interface ran in a terminal 160 columns wide and 40 lines high.
  - The test call took place while it ran.
  - The keys in "See both legs as one call flow"
    showed what that section describes.
- Every test call carried audio both ways.
- On both, causing each fault under [When something does not
  work](#when-something-does-not-work) produced the message it quotes.

The examples use `192.0.2.10` as the machine's address. Replace it with yours
everywhere it appears.

## Install sipnab

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
V=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/NormB/sipnab/releases/latest \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["tag_name"].lstrip("v"))')
curl -fsSLO https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/releases/download/v$V/sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb
curl -fsSL https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/releases/download/v$V/SHA256SUMS.txt \
  | grep " sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb$" | sha256sum -c -
sudo apt-get install -y ./sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb jq
sipnab --version
```

The commands in the sections from
"Explain the call from the saved capture"
to "Keep sipnab running, and query it over REST"
use `jq` to pick fields out of sipnab's JSON. So the block installs it too.

## Watch a call through Asterisk

Start sipnab on every interface for 30 seconds.

- It prints each SIP message as it passes.
- It prints a report of the calls at the end.
- `-O` saves every packet it captured to `/tmp/asterisk-call.pcap`.
  - The sections "Explain the call from the saved capture"
    and "Ask about the call over MCP" use that
    file.

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d any --duration 30 --report -O /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap
```

While it runs, place a test call from a second terminal. Do it as in
[Place a test call in the Asterisk guide](asterisk.md#place-a-test-call):

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
cd ~/sipp
sipp -sf uas.xml -i 192.0.2.10 -p 5070 -min_rtp_port 7000 -max_rtp_port 7100 -rtp_echo -m 1 -bg
sudo sipp -sn uac_pcap 192.0.2.10:5060 -i 192.0.2.10 -p 5080 -s 100 -m 1 -timeout 90s
```

sipnab prints, in order:

- the caller's `INVITE` to Asterisk at `192.0.2.10:5060`,
- then Asterisk's own `INVITE` to the callee at `192.0.2.10:5070`.
  - It has a Call-ID Asterisk generated.
  - It has an SDP offer of its own.

When the 30 seconds are up, the report lists the two legs as two calls. Both
are `Completed` with code `200`:

```text
Call-ID                          From           To             State        Code   Duration   Msgs   PDD      Tags
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1-50232@192.0.2.10               sipp           100            Completed    200    9s         7      0.0s     -
37e58306-c14d-4a0f-9fa1-41a...   sipp           -              Completed    200    9s         6      0.0s     -
```

- The first is the caller's leg, to extension `100`, with 7 messages.
  - Asterisk's `100 Trying` to the caller is among them.
- The second is Asterisk's leg to the callee, with 6.
  - Its `To` column shows `-`.
  - That is because Asterisk addressed the callee as `<sip:192.0.2.10>`, with
    no user name.

Below them, the `RTP Streams:` table shows that the audio goes through
Asterisk. Each leg has a different codec:

- On the caller's leg:
  - 236 `PCMA` packets from the caller to Asterisk,
  - 236 `PCMA` packets back, the callee's echo.
- On the callee's leg, 236 `PCMU` packets each way between Asterisk and the
  callee.
  - Asterisk converts the caller's PCMA to PCMU.
  - PCMU is the only codec the callee takes.
- The caller's key press: 10 `telephone-event` (DTMF) packets to Asterisk.
  - Asterisk passes it to the callee as a tone inside the audio.
  - So the callee's leg carries no `telephone-event` stream.
  - After the key press, both legs show short PCMU and PCMA streams under new
    SSRCs:
    - 6 `PCMU` packets each way on the callee's leg,
    - 10 `PCMA` packets toward the caller.

## See both legs as one call flow

The terminal interface shows the same calls, and updates as they happen:

```bash
sudo sipnab -d any
```

Place the test call from a second terminal, as in
"Watch a call through Asterisk". The call list
shows two rows, one per leg. Both are `Completed`, with 7 and 6 messages. Then,
in the terminal interface:

- **Press `F4`** with the first row selected.
  - The extended flow draws both legs in one ladder with three columns:
    - the caller at `192.0.2.10:5080`,
    - Asterisk at `192.0.2.10:5060`,
    - the callee at `192.0.2.10:5070`.
  - The ladder shows these messages, in the order they happened:
    - the caller's `INVITE` to Asterisk,
    - Asterisk's `INVITE` to the callee,
    - the callee's answer,
    - Asterisk's answer to the caller.
  - Press `Esc` to go back to the list.
- **Press `Space`, `↓` (the down arrow), `Space` again, then `Enter`.**
  - `Space` stars the selected row, so this stars both legs.
  - With two rows starred, `Enter` opens one flow of both, in time order.
    It is the same three-column ladder.
  - Press `Esc` to go back to the list.
- **Press `Tab`** for the RTP streams.
  - Each stream names the leg it belongs to in the `Dialog` column.

Press `q`, then `y`, to quit.

## Explain the call from the saved capture

`--call-report` explains one call:

- its SIP transactions with their timings,
- for each audio stream, its packets, jitter, loss and estimated
  [MOS](glossary.md#mos) (call quality on a scale from 1 to 5).

Reading a file needs no root. The first line finds the caller's leg in the
capture from "Watch a call through Asterisk":

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
CALL=$(sipnab -N -I /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap --json-dialogs --no-cli-print | jq -r 'select(.to == "100") | .call_id')
sipnab -N -I /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap --call-report "$CALL" --no-cli-print
```

The report covers the caller's leg. Its `SIP Transactions` show:

- the `INVITE` answered in a few milliseconds,
- then the `ACK`,
- the `BYE` 9 seconds later:

```text
SIP Transactions:
  INVITE -> 100 -> 180 (1ms) -> 200 (3ms)
  ACK
  BYE -> 200 (9008ms)
```

Under `Media Streams`:

- The two PCMA streams of 236 packets, one each way, show no loss and
  `mos=4.36 R=90.8`.
- The `telephone-event` stream shows `mos=unknown (unpublished)`.
  - sipnab gives no quality estimate for DTMF events.
- The last stream is the 10 PCMA packets toward the caller.

The report ends with `Issues Detected: None`.

## Ask about the call over MCP

sipnab's MCP server lets an AI agent ask about a capture. The [MCP
guide](mcp.md) sets it up for a client. This block does the following:

- It sends the three messages a client would, straight from the shell.
- It asks `find_correlated` which other leg belongs to the caller's call.
- Its first line takes the caller's Call-ID from the report. It uses the row
  whose `To` is `100`:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
CALL=$(sipnab -N -I /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap --report --no-cli-print | awk '$3 == "100" {print $1}')
printf '%s\n' \
  '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"shell","version":"0"}}}' \
  '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}' \
  "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":2,\"method\":\"tools/call\",\"params\":{\"name\":\"find_correlated\",\"arguments\":{\"call_id\":\"$CALL\"}}}" \
  | sipnab --mcp -N -I /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap --quiet \
  | jq 'select(.id == 2) | .result.content[0].text | fromjson | {total_matched, heuristic_only, legs}'
```

The answer names Asterisk's leg:

```json
{
  "total_matched": 1,
  "heuristic_only": true,
  "legs": [
    {
      "call_id": "37e58306-c14d-4a0f-9fa1-41a2b3c05f96",
      "identifier_match": false,
      "observed_gap_ms": 1,
      "score": 50,
      "strategy": "timing_heuristic"
    }
  ]
}
```

`timing_heuristic` means that sipnab matched the legs for two reasons:

- They share an address.
- They started within 2 seconds of each other. Here they were 1 millisecond
  apart (`observed_gap_ms`).

That is a guess, and the answer says so:

- `identifier_match` is false.
- `heuristic_only` is true.

Asterisk puts no header on its leg that names the caller's leg. So sipnab has
no identifier to match on.

## Keep sipnab running, and query it over REST

The sipnab package installs a systemd service, `sipnab`. It captures on every
interface without the terminal interface. Turn on its REST API.

- sipnab reads the API key from the environment.
- Keep the key in a file only root can read. That keeps it out of the command
  line, where every user on the machine could read it:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo sh -c 'umask 077; printf "SIPNAB_API_KEY=%s\n" "$(openssl rand -hex 32)" > /etc/sipnab/api.env'
sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/sipnab.service.d
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/sipnab.service.d/api.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[Service]
EnvironmentFile=/etc/sipnab/api.env
ExecStart=
ExecStart=/usr/bin/sipnab -N -d any --no-cli-print --syslog --metrics 127.0.0.1:9090 --api 127.0.0.1:8080
EOF
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now sipnab
systemctl is-active sipnab
```

The `ExecStart` line keeps the package's own arguments and adds `--api`. The
API listens on `127.0.0.1` only.

Place the test call again, as in
"Watch a call through Asterisk". Then ask
sipnab for:

- its calls,
- the leg that goes with the caller's,
- the audio streams:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
KEY=$(sudo sed -n 's/^SIPNAB_API_KEY=//p' /etc/sipnab/api.env)
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" 127.0.0.1:8080/v1/dialogs \
  | jq -r '.dialogs[] | [.call_id, .to_user // "-", .state, .msg_count] | @tsv'
CALL=$(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" 127.0.0.1:8080/v1/dialogs | jq -r '.dialogs[] | select(.to_user == "100") | .call_id')
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "127.0.0.1:8080/v1/dialogs/$CALL/correlated" | jq -c '.legs[]'
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" 127.0.0.1:8080/v1/streams \
  | jq -r '.streams[] | [.associated_dialog, .codec, .packets, .loss_pct] | @tsv'
```

- The first answer lists the two legs, `Completed` with 7 and 6 messages.
- The second names Asterisk's leg with `"strategy":"timing_heuristic"`.
  - MCP did the same in "Ask about the call over MCP".
- The third lists each stream with:
  - the leg it belongs to,
  - its codec,
  - its packets,
  - its loss.

The [REST API reference](rest-api.md) gives every route.

## Receive Asterisk's HEP

[HEP](glossary.md#hep) is the protocol SIP servers use to send a copy of their
traffic to a collector such as Homer.

- Asterisk sends HEP with its `res_hep` module.
  - The build in the Asterisk guide includes it.
- sipnab can receive it.
  - sipnab then sees the SIP as Asterisk handled it, with no capture on the
    wire.

Point Asterisk at sipnab's HEP listener, on port 9060 of the loopback address.
Then restart it:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo tee /etc/asterisk/hep.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[general]
enabled = yes
capture_address = 127.0.0.1:9060
capture_id = 1234
uuid_type = call-id
EOF
sudo systemctl restart asterisk
until sudo asterisk -rx 'core waitfullybooted' 2>/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
sudo asterisk -rx 'module show like hep'
```

- The `until` line waits for Asterisk to finish starting. It works as in
  [Configure Asterisk in the Asterisk guide](asterisk.md#configure-asterisk).
- `module show like hep` lists `res_hep.so`, `res_hep_pjsip.so` and
  `res_hep_rtcp.so` as `Running`.
- `capture_id` is the number Asterisk stamps on every copy it sends.
  - A collector uses it to tell its senders apart.
- `uuid_type
  = call-id` labels each copy with the SIP Call-ID.

Start sipnab's HEP listener for 30 seconds:

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -L 127.0.0.1:9060 --duration 30 --report --hep-senders
```

While it runs, place the test call from a second terminal, as in
"Watch a call through Asterisk".

- sipnab prints each message as it arrives, marked `origin=hep`.
- When the 30 seconds are up, the report lists the same two legs, and who sent
  them:

```text
  SOURCE                                PACKETS  LAST SEEN                    IDLE  STATE
  hep:1234@127.0.0.1                         15  2026-10-12T07:52:29.691Z      14s  sending
```

- `hep:1234` is Asterisk's `capture_id`.
- The last line counts `15 packets
  captured, 13 SIP messages`.
- The other two packets are RTCP summaries from `res_hep_rtcp`.
  - Asterisk sends them as JSON.
  - sipnab's report shows nothing from them.
- HEP carries no audio, so this report has no `RTP Streams:` table.
  - For the audio, capture on the wire as in
    "Watch a call through Asterisk".

HEP over UDP carries no authentication of its own. The capture id is what the
sender claims. Listening on `127.0.0.1` keeps every sender but this machine
out.

## Remove what this guide added

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo systemctl disable --now sipnab
sudo apt-get purge -y sipnab
sudo rm -rf /etc/systemd/system/sipnab.service.d /etc/sipnab
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo rm -f /etc/asterisk/hep.conf /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap
sudo systemctl restart asterisk
```

- `apt-get purge` removes the package and its own configuration.
- The API key file and the drop-in are yours, so the block removes them.
- The package leaves the `sipnab` user in place.

## When something does not work

- **sipnab says `sipnab: the terminal UI could not start: No such device or
  address (os error 6). It needs a terminal; add -N for a run without one.`**
  - The terminal interface needs an interactive terminal.
  - This session has none, as with a command passed to `ssh` without `-t`.
  - Run it from an interactive login, or use `-N` as in
    "Watch a call through Asterisk".
- **sipnab's HEP listener ends with `HEP listener on 127.0.0.1:9060 finished: 0
  packets received`.**
  - Asterisk sent nothing.
  - Run `sudo asterisk -rx 'module
    show like hep'`.
  - If the three modules show `Not Running`, Asterisk has not read
    `hep.conf`.
  - `core reload` does not start them. Restart Asterisk.
- **The REST API answers
  `{"status":401,"title":"Unauthorized","type":"https://sipnab.com/problems/unauthorized"}`.**
  - The request carried no API key, or the wrong one.
  - Read it from `/etc/sipnab/api.env`, as in
    "Keep sipnab running, and query it over REST".
