# Use FreeSWITCH in your voice stack

[FreeSWITCH](https://signalwire.com/freeswitch) is an open-source softswitch.

- It answers calls and bridges them.
- It plays and records audio.
- It runs conferences and voicemail.

It works as a back-to-back user agent (B2BUA).

- A proxy such as OpenSIPS or Kamailio passes the caller's request on to the
  callee.
- A B2BUA instead answers the caller's call itself.
  - It places a second, separate call to the callee, with its own Call-ID.
  - It carries the audio of both calls through itself.

One call through FreeSWITCH is therefore two SIP dialogs, one per leg. Its
audio is four streams:

- caller to FreeSWITCH,
- FreeSWITCH to caller,
- the same pair on the callee's side.

This guide does the following:

- It builds FreeSWITCH from source.
- It sets it up to bridge a test call to a callee on the same machine.
- It proves it with a call that carries audio.

This guide does not use sipnab. When you have this working, [Run sipnab beside
FreeSWITCH](freeswitch-sipnab.md) adds sipnab.

## Tested on

Every block on this page ran as written, in order, on 2026-10-12.

- The machines were clean x86_64 virtual machines with 2 cores and 3 GB of
  memory.
- They ran Debian 13 (kernel 6.12.63) and Ubuntu 24.04 (kernel 6.8.0).
- On each:
  - The build ran on a machine with nothing installed.
  - [Run sipnab beside FreeSWITCH](freeswitch-sipnab.md) ran between the
    operate blocks in "Operate it" and the uninstall.
  - The uninstall ran last.
- Every test call carried audio both ways on both legs, counted on the wire.
- Causing each fault under [When something does not
  work](#when-something-does-not-work) produced the message it quotes, on both.

| Software | Version |
|---|---|
| FreeSWITCH | 1.11.3, the current release, built from the release archive on `files.freeswitch.org` |
| sofia-sip (FreeSWITCH's SIP stack) | 1.13.18, built from the `v1.13.18` tag of `github.com/freeswitch/sofia-sip` |
| spandsp (FreeSWITCH's signal-processing library) | 3.1.1, built from the `v3.1.1` tag of `github.com/freeswitch/spandsp` |
| SIPp (for the test call) | the distribution's `sip-tester`: 3.7.3 on Debian 13, 3.7.2 on Ubuntu 24.04 |

The examples use `192.0.2.10` as the machine's address. Replace it with yours
everywhere it appears.

## Install FreeSWITCH

### What each distribution offers

FreeSWITCH's own packages come from SignalWire's package repository. That
repository answers only with a SignalWire account's access token.

- Neither distribution carries a `freeswitch` package.
- The versions of sofia-sip and spandsp they carry are older than FreeSWITCH
  1.11.3 accepts. It needs:
  - sofia-sip 1.13.18 or later,
  - spandsp 3.1.1 or later.

This block shows all three on your machine:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y ca-certificates curl
apt-cache policy freeswitch libsofia-sip-ua-dev libspandsp-dev
. /etc/os-release
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "https://freeswitch.signalwire.com/repo/deb/debian-release/dists/$VERSION_CODENAME/Release"
```

- `apt-cache policy` prints nothing for `freeswitch`.
- It prints a `Candidate` of:
  - 1.12.11 for `libsofia-sip-ua-dev`,
  - 0.0.6 for `libspandsp-dev`.
- The last line prints `401`. That is the HTTP status for a request that needs
  credentials.

| | Debian 13 | Ubuntu 24.04 |
|---|---|---|
| A `freeswitch` package from the distribution | none | none |
| SignalWire's FreeSWITCH packages | need a SignalWire access token | need a SignalWire access token |
| Build from source, as below | no account needed | no account needed |

This guide builds from source.

- That needs no account.
- The same steps work on both distributions.
- The build installs everything under `/usr/local/freeswitch`.
  - sofia-sip and spandsp are the exception. They go under `/usr/local`.

### Build sofia-sip and spandsp

First the compiler, the build tools, and the libraries FreeSWITCH's core and
its default modules use:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git build-essential automake autoconf libtool libtool-bin pkg-config xz-utils \
  libssl-dev zlib1g-dev libjpeg-dev libtiff-dev libsqlite3-dev libcurl4-openssl-dev libpcre2-dev \
  libspeex-dev libspeexdsp-dev libldns-dev libedit-dev uuid-dev libopus-dev libsndfile1-dev liblua5.4-dev yasm nasm
```

Then the two libraries. They come from the FreeSWITCH project's own
repositories, at the versions FreeSWITCH 1.11.3 asks for:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo mkdir -p /usr/local/src/voice && sudo chown "$USER": /usr/local/src/voice
cd /usr/local/src/voice
git -c advice.detachedHead=false clone --depth 1 -b v1.13.18 https://github.com/freeswitch/sofia-sip.git
git -c advice.detachedHead=false clone --depth 1 -b v3.1.1 https://github.com/freeswitch/spandsp.git
for d in sofia-sip spandsp; do (cd "$d" && ./bootstrap.sh && ./configure && make -j2 && sudo make install); done
sudo ldconfig
pkg-config --modversion sofia-sip-ua spandsp
```

The last line prints `1.13.18` and `3.1.1`.

### Build FreeSWITCH

`modules.conf` lists the modules the build compiles. Four of the default ones
need libraries this guide does not install:

- `mod_signalwire` and `mod_verto` need SignalWire's `libks`.
- `mod_av` needs the FFmpeg development libraries.
- `mod_pgsql` needs the PostgreSQL client library.

The `sed` line leaves those four out:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
cd /usr/local/src/voice
curl -fsSLO https://files.freeswitch.org/releases/freeswitch/freeswitch-1.11.3.-release.tar.xz
curl -fsSL https://files.freeswitch.org/releases/freeswitch/freeswitch-1.11.3.-release.tar.xz.sha256 | sha256sum -c -
tar xf freeswitch-1.11.3.-release.tar.xz
cd freeswitch-1.11.3.-release
sed -i -E 's#^(applications/mod_av|applications/mod_signalwire|endpoints/mod_verto|databases/mod_pgsql)$#\#\1#' modules.conf
./configure
make -j2
sudo make install
sudo ln -sf /usr/local/freeswitch/bin/freeswitch /usr/local/freeswitch/bin/fs_cli /usr/local/bin/
freeswitch -version
```

- `sha256sum -c` prints `freeswitch-1.11.3.-release.tar.xz: OK`.
  - The checksum comes from the same server as the archive.
  - So it detects a damaged download, not a changed one.
- The last line prints `FreeSWITCH version:
  1.11.3-release~64bit (-release 64bit)`.

The release archive's name has a dot before `-release`. That is the name on the
server.

### Run it as a service

FreeSWITCH runs as its own user.

- This unit is the one in the FreeSWITCH source tree,
  `debian/freeswitch-systemd.freeswitch.service`, with the paths of this
  build.
- FreeSWITCH starts as root.
  - It raises its own scheduling priority.
  - Then it drops to the `freeswitch` user.
- `-ncwait` makes `systemctl start` wait until FreeSWITCH is ready to take
  commands:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo useradd --system --home-dir /usr/local/freeswitch --shell /usr/sbin/nologin freeswitch
sudo chown -R freeswitch:freeswitch /usr/local/freeswitch
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/freeswitch.service >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[Unit]
Description=FreeSWITCH
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=forking
PIDFile=/usr/local/freeswitch/run/freeswitch.pid
ExecStart=/usr/local/freeswitch/bin/freeswitch -u freeswitch -g freeswitch -ncwait -nonat
TimeoutSec=45s
Restart=always
LimitCORE=infinity
LimitNOFILE=100000
LimitNPROC=60000
LimitSTACK=250000
LimitRTPRIO=infinity
LimitRTTIME=infinity
IOSchedulingClass=realtime
IOSchedulingPriority=2
CPUSchedulingPolicy=rr
CPUSchedulingPriority=89
UMask=0007

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable freeswitch
```

`-nonat` stops FreeSWITCH from asking the local router to forward ports to it
(UPnP and NAT-PMP).

## Configure FreeSWITCH

`make install` put FreeSWITCH's example configuration in
`/usr/local/freeswitch/conf`. The FreeSWITCH project calls it "vanilla". It
runs two SIP profiles. Each profile is a SIP listener with its own settings:

- `internal`, on port 5060, for your own phones.
  - It asks every caller for a user name and password.
- `external`, on port 5080, for carriers and other servers.
  - It asks for no password.
  - It sends each call to the dialplan's `public` context.

The test call in "Place a test call" goes to `external`.
This block changes five things:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
cd /usr/local/freeswitch/conf
sudo sed -i 's|=stun:stun.freeswitch.org"|=192.0.2.10"|' vars.xml
P=$(od -An -tx1 -N12 /dev/urandom | tr -d ' \n')
sudo sed -i "s|data=\"default_password=1234\"|data=\"default_password=$P\"|" vars.xml
sudo sed -i 's|<param name="listen-ip" value="::"/>|<param name="listen-ip" value="127.0.0.1"/>|' autoload_configs/event_socket.conf.xml
sudo sed -i -E 's#^( *)(<load module="mod_(verto|signalwire|av)"/>)#\1<!-- \2 -->#' autoload_configs/modules.conf.xml
sudo tee dialplan/public/01_echo.xml >/dev/null <<'EOF'
<include>
  <!-- A call to "echo" goes to the test callee on this machine, in PCMU. -->
  <extension name="test_callee">
    <condition field="destination_number" expression="^echo$">
      <action application="bridge" data="{absolute_codec_string=PCMU}sofia/external/echo@127.0.0.1:5070"/>
    </condition>
  </extension>
</include>
EOF
sudo chown -R freeswitch:freeswitch /usr/local/freeswitch/conf
grep 'stun-set' vars.xml
sudo systemctl restart freeswitch
fs_cli -x 'sofia status'
```

What the changes do:

- **The machine's address.**
  - `external_rtp_ip` and `external_sip_ip` are the addresses FreeSWITCH puts
    in its SIP and SDP for the `external` profile.
  - The example configuration asks the public STUN server
    `stun.freeswitch.org` for them at startup.
  - That gives the address of your internet connection, not of this machine.
  - With that default, the `Contact` header of FreeSWITCH's replies to the
    test call named the public address.
  - On a machine with its own public address, put that address here.
- **The SIP password.**
  - `default_password` is the password of the 20 example users, `1000` to
    `1019`, that the `internal` profile accepts.
  - The example configuration sets it to `1234`.
  - The block replaces it with a random one.
- **The event socket.**
  - `fs_cli` is FreeSWITCH's command-line client.
  - It talks to FreeSWITCH over its event socket, TCP port 8021, with the
    password `ClueCon`.
  - The example configuration listens on every address.
  - The block moves it to `127.0.0.1`, so only this machine reaches it.
- **Modules the build left out.**
  - The example configuration loads `mod_verto`, `mod_signalwire` and
    `mod_av`.
  - The section "Install FreeSWITCH" did not build them.
  - Without this line, FreeSWITCH logs `Error Loading module` for each at
    every start.
- **Where the test call goes.**
  - The dialplan is FreeSWITCH's routing.
  - FreeSWITCH bridges a call to `echo` in the `public` context to a test
    callee on this machine, `127.0.0.1:5070`.
  - `absolute_codec_string=PCMU` makes FreeSWITCH offer the callee PCMU only.
    That is the one codec SIPp's callee answers with.

`sofia status` lists the profiles. Both are `RUNNING`:

- `internal` shows `sip:mod_sofia@192.0.2.10:5060`.
- `external` shows `sip:mod_sofia@192.0.2.10:5080`.

## Place a test call

SIPp plays both ends:

- a callee on this machine that echoes audio back,
- a caller that calls `echo` on FreeSWITCH's `external` profile and plays a
  recorded G.711 sample.

So the call carries real audio both ways. The caller uses port 5090, because
FreeSWITCH holds 5060 and 5080:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo apt-get install -y sip-tester jq
mkdir -p ~/sipp/pcap && cd ~/sipp
ln -sf /usr/share/sip-tester/*.pcap pcap/
sipp -sn uas -i 127.0.0.1 -p 5070 -rtp_echo -m 1 -bg
sudo sipp -sn uac_pcap 192.0.2.10:5080 -i 192.0.2.10 -p 5090 -s echo -m 1 -timeout 90s
```

- The caller needs `sudo` because it plays the audio sample through a raw
  socket.
- It sends about 7 seconds of audio, then a short DTMF clip, and hangs up.
- At the end SIPp's statistics screen shows `Successful call` at 1.

SIPp's built-in caller sends its `ACK` and `BYE` straight to FreeSWITCH.
FreeSWITCH is the far end of the caller's dialog. Unlike the proxy guides,
this guide needs no edited scenario.

Each leg has its own audio.

- The caller offers PCMA, and FreeSWITCH answers it in PCMA.
- On the callee's leg FreeSWITCH offers PCMU.
- FreeSWITCH converts the audio between the two codecs.

[Run sipnab beside
FreeSWITCH](freeswitch-sipnab.md) shows all four streams.

## Operate it

**See a call's two legs while it is up.** FreeSWITCH calls each leg a
channel. Start a call in the background and list the channels:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
cd ~/sipp
sipp -sn uas -i 127.0.0.1 -p 5070 -rtp_echo -m 1 -bg
sudo sipp -sn uac_pcap 192.0.2.10:5080 -i 192.0.2.10 -p 5090 -s echo -m 1 -timeout 90s -bg
sleep 3
fs_cli -x 'show channels as json' | jq -r '.rows[] | "\(.direction) \(.name) \(.read_codec)"'
sleep 12
```

```text
inbound sofia/external/sipp@192.0.2.10:5090 PCMA
outbound sofia/external/echo@127.0.0.1:5070 PCMU
```

- The `inbound` channel is the caller's leg, in PCMA.
- The `outbound` one is the callee's, in PCMU.
- The last line waits for the call to end.

**Check health and read the logs.**

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
systemctl is-active freeswitch
fs_cli -x status
sudo tail -n 30 /usr/local/freeswitch/log/freeswitch.log
```

- `fs_cli -x status` prints:
  - FreeSWITCH's version,
  - its uptime,
  - the number of sessions since it started.
- FreeSWITCH writes its log to `/usr/local/freeswitch/log/freeswitch.log`, not
  to the journal.

**Apply a configuration change.**

- A change to the dialplan or the users takes effect with `reloadxml`.
- A change to `vars.xml` or a SIP profile needs a restart:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
fs_cli -x reloadxml
sudo systemctl restart freeswitch
fs_cli -x status | head -2
```

`reloadxml` prints `+OK [Success]`.

**Uninstall.** Remove FreeSWITCH, its user, and the two libraries:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo systemctl disable --now freeswitch
sudo rm -rf /usr/local/freeswitch /etc/systemd/system/freeswitch.service /usr/local/bin/freeswitch /usr/local/bin/fs_cli
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo userdel freeswitch
sudo make -C /usr/local/src/voice/sofia-sip uninstall
sudo make -C /usr/local/src/voice/spandsp uninstall
sudo rm -rf /usr/local/include/sofia-sip-1.13 /usr/local/include/spandsp /usr/local/share/sofia-sip
sudo ldconfig
rm -rf /usr/local/src/voice/sofia-sip /usr/local/src/voice/spandsp /usr/local/src/voice/freeswitch-1.11.3.-release*
```

## When something does not work

- **The test call fails, and SIPp reports `Aborting call on unexpected message
  ... received 'SIP/2.0 488 Not Acceptable Here`.**
  - The callee answered with a codec FreeSWITCH had not offered it.
  - Without `absolute_codec_string`, FreeSWITCH offers the callee the caller's
    codec, PCMA.
  - SIPp's callee answers PCMU whatever FreeSWITCH offers.
  - FreeSWITCH's log shows `Originate
    Failed.  Cause: INCOMPATIBLE_DESTINATION`.
  - Keep `{absolute_codec_string=PCMU}` in the `bridge` line, or offer your
    callee a codec it supports.
- **`fs_cli` prints `[ERROR] fs_cli.c:1699 main() Error Connecting []`.**
  - Nothing answers on the event socket. One of these is true:
    - FreeSWITCH is not running.
    - Its `listen-ip` is not the address `fs_cli` connects to, `127.0.0.1`.
  - Check `systemctl status freeswitch`.

---

<!-- source: docs/freeswitch-sipnab.md -->

# Run sipnab beside FreeSWITCH

sipnab reads the SIP and the audio that pass through FreeSWITCH off the wire.
So it needs nothing from FreeSWITCH: no module, no configuration change.

FreeSWITCH is a back-to-back user agent (B2BUA).

- It answers the caller's call.
- It places a second call, with a Call-ID of its own, to the callee.

On the FreeSWITCH machine sipnab sees:

- both calls, which it calls dialogs,
- the four audio streams.

It can tie the two dialogs together as one call.

FreeSWITCH can also send sipnab a copy of its SIP over HEP. HEP is the
protocol SIP servers use to send Homer their traffic.

This guide adds sipnab to the FreeSWITCH machine from
[Use FreeSWITCH in your voice stack](freeswitch.md).

## Tested on

Every block on this page ran as written, in order, on 2026-10-12.

- It ran with sipnab 0.5.211 from its release package.
- It ran on the Debian 13 (kernel 6.12.63) and Ubuntu 24.04 (kernel 6.8.0)
  machines that [the FreeSWITCH guide](freeswitch.md) had set up, with
  FreeSWITCH 1.11.3.
- Each test call carried audio both ways on both legs.
- On both, causing each fault under [When something does not
  work](#when-something-does-not-work) produced the message it quotes.

The examples use `192.0.2.10` as the machine's address.

## Install sipnab

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
V=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/NormB/sipnab/releases/latest \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["tag_name"].lstrip("v"))')
curl -fsSLO https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/releases/download/v$V/sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb
curl -fsSL https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/releases/download/v$V/SHA256SUMS.txt \
  | grep " sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb$" | sha256sum -c -
sudo apt-get install -y ./sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb
sipnab --version
```

## Watch a call through FreeSWITCH

sipnab watches SIP ports 5060-5061 unless you give it others.

- FreeSWITCH's `external` profile takes the test call. It listens on 5080.
- So give sipnab the range from 5060 to 5080 with `--portrange`.

Start sipnab on every interface for 30 seconds. It prints:

- each SIP message as it passes,
- a report of the calls at the end,
- a copy of what it captured in `/tmp/freeswitch-call.pcap`, for the next
  steps.

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d any --portrange 5060-5080 --duration 30 --report -O /tmp/freeswitch-call.pcap
```

sipnab writes the capture file after it has dropped its root privileges, as
the user `nobody`. So the file goes in `/tmp`, where `nobody` can write.

While it runs, place a test call from a second terminal. Do it as in
[Place a test call in the FreeSWITCH guide](freeswitch.md#place-a-test-call):

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
cd ~/sipp
sipp -sn uas -i 127.0.0.1 -p 5070 -rtp_echo -m 1 -bg
sudo sipp -sn uac_pcap 192.0.2.10:5080 -i 192.0.2.10 -p 5090 -s echo -m 1 -timeout 90s
```

sipnab prints, in order:

- the caller's `INVITE` to FreeSWITCH at `192.0.2.10:5080`,
- FreeSWITCH's own `INVITE` to the callee at `127.0.0.1:5070`, with a
  different Call-ID,
- the replies, `ACK`s and `BYE`s of both.

When the 30 seconds are up, the report lists two dialogs, both `Completed`:

- the caller's leg, whose Call-ID SIPp made (`1-...@192.0.2.10`), with 7
  messages,
- the callee's leg, whose Call-ID FreeSWITCH made, with 6.

FreeSWITCH answers the caller's `INVITE` with `100 Trying`. The callee does
not. That is the seventh message.

Below them, the `RTP Streams:` table holds the call's audio. All of it goes to
or from FreeSWITCH:

```text
RTP Streams:
SSRC         PT   Codec    Clock  Source                Destination           Pkts    Lost   Loss%   Jitter   Dur    Kbps
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0xdee0ee8f   8    PCMA     8000   192.0.2.10:6000       192.0.2.10:32348      236     0      0.0%    0ms      7s     64
0xeed25cad   0    PCMU     8000   192.0.2.10:25690      127.0.0.1:6000        360     0      0.0%    32ms     8s     54
0xeed25cad   0    PCMU     8000   127.0.0.1:6000        192.0.2.10:25690      360     0      0.0%    32ms     8s     54
0x02d49cad   8    PCMA     8000   192.0.2.10:32348      192.0.2.10:6000       236     0      0.0%    52ms     9s     50
0x0e05384e   101  telephone-event 8000   192.0.2.10:6000       192.0.2.10:32348      10      0      0.0%    6ms      0s     2
```

- The caller sends 236 PCMA packets and 10 DTMF (`telephone-event`) packets
  to FreeSWITCH.
  - They go to a port FreeSWITCH chose for the call.
  - FreeSWITCH sends PCMA back.
- On the callee's side the audio is PCMU, both ways.
  - FreeSWITCH converts between the two codecs.
- The callee's answer offered no `telephone-event`.
  - So no DTMF stream goes to the callee.
- FreeSWITCH chooses new ports for each call.

## Read one call: timing and audio quality

The capture file holds the whole call. Find the caller's leg and print
sipnab's report of it. The caller's leg is the dialog whose Call-ID starts with
`1-`, as SIPp names its calls:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
CALL=$(sipnab -N -I /tmp/freeswitch-call.pcap --portrange 5060-5080 --json-dialogs --no-cli-print --quiet \
  | jq -r 'select(.call_id | startswith("1-")) | .call_id')
echo "$CALL"
sipnab -N -I /tmp/freeswitch-call.pcap --portrange 5060-5080 --call-report "$CALL" --no-cli-print --quiet
```

A file you read takes `--portrange` too. The report gives:

- the call's timing,
- its SIP transactions,
- a line for each of its audio streams. Each line has:
  - the jitter,
  - the packet loss,
  - an estimated MOS (mean opinion score, from 1 to 5).

```text
Media Streams:
  RTP 192.0.2.10->192.0.2.10 PCMA SSRC=0xdee0ee8f pkts=236 jitter=0ms loss=0.0% mos=4.36 R=90.8
  RTP 192.0.2.10->192.0.2.10 PCMA SSRC=0x02d49cad pkts=236 jitter=52ms loss=0.0% mos=4.33 R=89.5
  RTP 192.0.2.10->192.0.2.10 telephone-event SSRC=0x0e05384e pkts=10 jitter=6ms loss=0.0% mos=unknown (unpublished)
```

The callee's leg's report adds a line FreeSWITCH supplies. FreeSWITCH puts a
`Reason` header in the `BYE` it sends. sipnab reads it:

```text
Cause:      Q.850 cause 16 "NORMAL_CLEARING" [Reason]
```

## See both legs as one call

FreeSWITCH gives the callee's leg a Call-ID of its own.

- Its `INVITE` carries nothing that names the caller's leg.
- It has no `Session-ID` header, the one
  [RFC 7989](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7989.html) defines for that.

sipnab still ties the two together, from their addresses and their start
times. It says so.

**In the terminal interface.** Open the capture:

```bash
sipnab -I /tmp/freeswitch-call.pcap --portrange 5060-5080
```

The call list shows the two dialogs, `Dialogs: 2 shown of 2`.

- Press `Enter` on the first to open its ladder.
  - The ladder is the diagram of its messages between the caller at
    `192.0.2.10:5090` and FreeSWITCH at `192.0.2.10:5080`.
- Press `x` for the extended flow, `Extended flow: on (multi-leg)`.
  - It adds the callee's leg and the callee, `127.0.0.1:5070`, as a third
    column.
- Press `Esc` to go back to the call list.
  - There, `Esc` asks `Are you sure you want to
    quit?`, and `Y` quits.

**Over the REST API.** sipnab answers HTTP requests about what it captured.
The route `/correlated` names the other legs of a call:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
CALL=$(sipnab -N -I /tmp/freeswitch-call.pcap --portrange 5060-5080 --json-dialogs --no-cli-print --quiet \
  | jq -r 'select(.call_id | startswith("1-")) | .call_id')
export SIPNAB_API_KEY="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
sipnab -N -I /tmp/freeswitch-call.pcap --portrange 5060-5080 --api 127.0.0.1:8080 --no-cli-print --quiet &
sleep 2
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/dialogs/$CALL/correlated" | jq .
kill %1
```

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "source_call_id": "1-114198@192.0.2.10",
  "legs": [
    {
      "call_id": "3c33fca7-40b8-1240-48b2-bc24119de73a",
      "score": 50,
      "strategy": "timing_heuristic",
      "identifier_match": false,
      "observed_gap_ms": 2
    }
  ],
  "total_matched": 1,
  "heuristic_only": true
}
```

`timing_heuristic` and `identifier_match: false` say how sipnab matched the
leg:

- from its addresses and its start, 2 ms after the caller's,
- not from an identifier both legs carry.

On a busy FreeSWITCH, calls that start close together can match the same way.
The [REST API
reference](rest-api.md) describes the other
strategies.

**Over MCP.** sipnab's [MCP server](mcp.md) answers the same questions for an
AI agent. This block does the following:

- It takes the caller's leg's Call-ID from sipnab's report.
- It sends sipnab the messages a client would.
- It asks the `render_ladder` tool for that leg as a Mermaid diagram.

The `sleep` gives sipnab time to read the whole file first:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
CALL=$(sipnab -N -I /tmp/freeswitch-call.pcap --portrange 5060-5080 --report --no-cli-print --quiet \
  | awk '$1 ~ /^1-/ {print $1}')
{ printf '%s\n' \
    '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"shell","version":"0"}}}' \
    '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}'
  sleep 2
  printf '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"render_ladder","arguments":{"call_id":"%s","format":"mermaid"}}}\n' "$CALL"
} | sipnab --mcp -N -I /tmp/freeswitch-call.pcap --portrange 5060-5080 --quiet \
  | jq -r 'select(.id == 2) | .result.content[0].text'
```

The answer is a Mermaid `sequenceDiagram` of the caller's leg.

- It runs from the `INVITE` to the `200 OK` of the `BYE`.
- Each message has its time from the first.
- sipnab fences it as untrusted text taken from the capture. The fence is the
  `⟦untrusted-capture-data⟧` lines:

```text
⟦untrusted-capture-data⟧sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant p0 as 192.0.2.10:5090
    participant p1 as 192.0.2.10:5080

    p0->>p1: INVITE
    Note right of p1: +0.000s
    p1-->>p0: 100 Trying
    Note right of p0: +0.001s
    p1-->>p0: 180 Ringing
    Note right of p0: +0.003s · PDD 3ms
    p1-->>p0: 200 OK
    Note right of p0: +0.041s
    p0->>p1: ACK
    Note right of p1: +0.041s
    p0->>p1: BYE
    Note right of p1: +9.047s
    p1-->>p0: 200 OK
    Note right of p0: +9.054s
⟦/untrusted-capture-data⟧
```

- `PDD` is the post-dial delay. It is the time from the `INVITE` to the first
  ringing reply.
- The MCP tool `find_correlated` returns the same legs as the `/correlated`
  route.

## Receive FreeSWITCH's own copy of its SIP (HEP)

FreeSWITCH's SIP stack can send a HEP copy of every SIP message it sends and
receives. It sends the copy to a collector, such as Homer or sipnab. Then sipnab
needs no capture of the SIP at all.

Turn it on for both profiles. Send to `127.0.0.1:9060` with the capture id
`100`:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
cd /usr/local/freeswitch/conf
sudo sed -i 's|^    <param name="debug-presence" value="0"/>|&\n    <param name="capture-server" value="udp:127.0.0.1:9060;hep=3;capture_id=100"/>|' autoload_configs/sofia.conf.xml
sudo sed -i 's|<param name="sip-capture" value="no"/>|<param name="sip-capture" value="yes"/>|' sip_profiles/internal.xml sip_profiles/external.xml
grep -h -E '^ *<param name="(capture-server|sip-capture)"' autoload_configs/sofia.conf.xml sip_profiles/internal.xml sip_profiles/external.xml
sudo systemctl restart freeswitch
```

- `capture-server` names:
  - the collector,
  - the HEP version,
  - the capture id. That is a number that tells a collector which sender a
    copy came from.
- `sip-capture` turns the copies on for a profile.

Start sipnab's HEP listener for 30 seconds. `-d any` adds the call's audio
from the wire. HEP does not carry it:

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -L 127.0.0.1:9060 -d any --duration 30 --report --hep-senders
```

While it runs, place the test call from a second terminal, as in
"Watch a call through FreeSWITCH".

- sipnab prints each message as it arrives, marked `origin=hep`.
- The report lists:
  - the same two dialogs, with 7 and 6 messages,
  - the same five audio streams.
- Below them it names the sender:

```text
  SOURCE                                PACKETS  LAST SEEN                    IDLE  STATE
  hep:100@127.0.0.1                          13  2026-10-12T08:18:49.166Z      14s  sending
```

`hep:100` is the `capture_id` from `capture-server`.

- The capture id is what the sender claims. Nothing proves it.
- What keeps other senders out here is the address.
  - sipnab listens on `127.0.0.1`, which only this machine can reach.

## Without FreeSWITCH

sipnab does not depend on FreeSWITCH.

- The sections from "Watch a call through FreeSWITCH" to
  "See both legs as one call" read SIP and RTP off the wire or from a capture file.
  - They work the same on any SIP traffic, from any SIP server or none.
- The section "Receive FreeSWITCH's own copy of its SIP (HEP)" is the one that needs FreeSWITCH.
  - That is because FreeSWITCH sends the HEP.
- A capture file you take on the FreeSWITCH machine, such as
  `/tmp/freeswitch-call.pcap`, works on any machine with sipnab installed.
  - It works with "Read one call: timing and audio quality" and "See both legs as one call".

## When something does not work

- **sipnab reports `No SIP signaling found, but ... RTP packets across ...
  stream(s) were parsed`.**
  - It saw the call's audio, but none of its SIP.
  - FreeSWITCH's `external` profile is on 5080.
  - That is outside 5060-5061, the range sipnab watches by default.
  - Give sipnab the range with `--portrange
    5060-5080`.
- **Reading a capture file, sipnab warns `SIP outside --portrange 5060-5061 is
  being skipped` and names `Busiest port(s): 5080`, then says `Call-ID '...'
  not found in tracked dialogs`.**
  - The same range applies to a file.
  - Add `--portrange 5060-5080` to the command that reads it.
- **The MCP answer ends with `INCOMPLETE RUN — this report does not describe
  the whole capture` and `the capture is still being read`.**
  - The question reached sipnab before it had read the whole file.
  - Keep the `sleep` before the `tools/call` line.
  - Or make it longer for a larger file.

---

<!-- source: docs/fail2ban.md -->

# Ban SIP scanners with fail2ban

[fail2ban](https://github.com/fail2ban/fail2ban) reads your servers' logs. It
bans the addresses that show up in them for the wrong reasons. It does that by
adding them to a firewall rule.

- Make your SIP server write one log line for each scanner request and each
  wrong password.
- fail2ban then bans SIP scanners and password guessers.

It is the firewall alternative to [TFPS](tfps.md):

- TFPS reads the SIP traffic itself and drops attackers with an XDP program.
- fail2ban acts on what your SIP server logged. It bans with an ordinary
  nftables rule.

This guide does the following:

- It sets up OpenSIPS as a registrar that logs scanners and failed passwords.
- It has fail2ban ban on those lines.
- It proves it from this machine with:
  - a scanner,
  - a password guesser,
  - a phone that keeps working.

This guide does not use sipnab. When fail2ban is working,
[Feed fail2ban from sipnab](fail2ban-sipnab.md) adds sipnab as a second source
of bans.

Three terms used below:

- **Filter**: the patterns that pick the failure lines out of a log, and the
  address in each.
- **Jail**: one filter put to work. A jail sets:
  - which log it reads,
  - how many failures within how long earn a ban (`maxretry`, `findtime`),
  - how long a ban lasts (`bantime`),
  - what a ban blocks.
- **Ban action**: what fail2ban runs to ban and unban.
  - Here it adds the address to an nftables set.
  - A rule beside the set refuses that set's SIP traffic.

## Tested on

Every block on this page ran as written, in order, on 2026-10-01. So did every
command in the table in "Operate it".

- The machines were clean x86_64 virtual machines with 2 cores and 3 GB of
  memory.
- They ran Debian 13 (kernel 6.12.111) and Ubuntu 24.04 (kernel 6.8.0).
- The scanner and the phone were on the same machine, as
  "Give this machine a scanner and a phone to test with"
  sets them up.
- On Debian 13, each fault under
  [When something does not work](#when-something-does-not-work) happened
  during these runs, with the message it quotes.

| Software | Version |
|---|---|
| fail2ban | the distribution's: 1.1.0 on Debian 13, 1.0.2 on Ubuntu 24.04 |
| OpenSIPS | 4.0.2, from the OpenSIPS project's packages |
| SIPp (for the test call) | the distribution's `sip-tester` |

The examples use `192.0.2.10` as the SIP server's address. Replace it with
yours everywhere it appears.

- The scanner (`198.51.100.60`) and the phone (`203.0.113.70`) are test
  addresses.
- The section "Give this machine a scanner and a phone to test with"
  creates them on this machine.

## Before you start: OpenSIPS

- Run [Install OpenSIPS](opensips.md#install-opensips) in the guide "Use OpenSIPS as your voice stack's SIP server".
  - It installs the 4.0 packages.
- Then come back here.
- The section "Make OpenSIPS log scanners and wrong passwords" below replaces that guide's configuration.
  - The new configuration authenticates phones.
  - It logs what fail2ban needs.

## Make OpenSIPS log scanners and wrong passwords

Password checks need OpenSIPS's `auth` module. It is in its own package. The
configuration below does three things:

- It registers one test account, `1001`.
- It routes its calls to a test callee on this machine.
- It writes a log line for two things:
  - a request whose `User-Agent` names a known scanner tool.
    - OpenSIPS answers it with nothing.
  - a request whose credentials are wrong: a wrong password, or a user that
    does not exist.
    - OpenSIPS does not log a request that carries no credentials yet. Such a
      request is the normal first half of a login.

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo apt-get install -y opensips-auth-modules
sudo tee /etc/opensips/opensips.cfg >/dev/null <<'EOF'
# OpenSIPS as a registrar that logs what fail2ban bans on.
log_level=3
stderror_enabled=no
syslog_enabled=yes
syslog_facility=LOG_LOCAL0
udp_workers=2

socket=udp:192.0.2.10:5060

mpath="/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/opensips/modules/"

loadmodule "proto_udp.so"
loadmodule "signaling.so"
loadmodule "sl.so"
loadmodule "tm.so"
loadmodule "rr.so"
loadmodule "maxfwd.so"
loadmodule "sipmsgops.so"
loadmodule "usrloc.so"
modparam("usrloc", "working_mode_preset", "single-instance-no-db")
loadmodule "registrar.so"
loadmodule "auth.so"
modparam("auth", "username_spec", "$var(username)")
modparam("auth", "password_spec", "$var(password)")
modparam("auth", "calculate_ha1", 1)

loadmodule "mi_fifo.so"
modparam("mi_fifo", "fifo_name", "/run/opensips/opensips_fifo")

route {
	if (!mf_process_maxfwd_header(10)) {
		send_reply(483, "Too Many Hops");
		exit;
	}

	# Scanner tools that name themselves: log, and answer nothing.
	if ($ua =~ "friendly-scanner|sipvicious|sipcli|VaxSIPUserAgent") {
		xlog("L_WARN", "SIP scanner from $si: User-Agent \"$ua\"\n");
		exit;
	}

	if (has_totag()) {
		if (is_method("ACK") && t_check_trans()) {
			t_relay();
			exit;
		}
		if (!loose_route()) {
			send_reply(404, "Not here");
			exit;
		}
		t_relay();
		exit;
	}
	if (is_method("CANCEL")) {
		if (t_check_trans())
			t_relay();
		exit;
	}
	t_check_trans();

	if (is_method("OPTIONS")) {
		send_reply(200, "OK");
		exit;
	}

	# The one test account. Your registrar reads its accounts from a database.
	$var(username) = "1001";
	$var(password) = "correct-horse-1001";

	if (is_method("REGISTER")) {
		if (!pv_www_authorize("")) {
			$var(rc) = $rc;
			# -1: no such user, -2: wrong password
			if ($var(rc) == -1 || $var(rc) == -2)
				xlog("L_WARN", "SIP auth failure from $si for \"$au\"\n");
			www_challenge("", "auth");
			exit;
		}
		consume_credentials();
		if (!save("location"))
			sl_reply_error();
		exit;
	}

	if (is_method("INVITE")) {
		if (!pv_proxy_authorize("")) {
			$var(rc) = $rc;
			if ($var(rc) == -1 || $var(rc) == -2)
				xlog("L_WARN", "SIP auth failure from $si for \"$au\"\n");
			proxy_challenge("", "auth");
			exit;
		}
		consume_credentials();
		record_route();
		# Where the call goes. Here, a test callee on this machine.
		$du = "sip:127.0.0.1:5070";
		t_relay();
		exit;
	}

	send_reply(405, "Method Not Allowed");
}
EOF
sudo opensips -C -f /etc/opensips/opensips.cfg
sudo systemctl restart opensips
systemctl is-active opensips
```

OpenSIPS writes these lines to the systemd journal. There they look like this:

```text
... /usr/sbin/opensips[15830]: WARNING:SIP scanner from 198.51.100.60: User-Agent "friendly-scanner"
... /usr/sbin/opensips[15830]: WARNING:SIP auth failure from 198.51.100.60 for "1001"
```

## Install fail2ban

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo apt-get install -y fail2ban nftables
fail2ban-client --version
```

The jail below bans with nftables, so the command installs it too.

## Tell fail2ban what to look for, and what to ban

The filter reads OpenSIPS's lines from the journal. The jail bans an address
after 3 matching lines within 10 minutes.

- The ban lasts for an hour.
- It covers the SIP ports only.
  - Its rule names ports 5060 and 5061.
  - So a banned address can still reach your other services, SSH included:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo tee /etc/fail2ban/filter.d/opensips.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[INCLUDES]
before = common.conf

[Definition]
_daemon = \S*opensips
failregex = ^%(__prefix_line)sWARNING:SIP scanner from <HOST>: User-Agent
            ^%(__prefix_line)sWARNING:SIP auth failure from <HOST> for
ignoreregex =
journalmatch = _SYSTEMD_UNIT=opensips.service
EOF
sudo tee /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/opensips.local >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[opensips]
enabled   = true
filter    = opensips
backend   = systemd
banaction = nftables[type=multiport]
port      = 5060,5061
protocol  = udp,tcp
maxretry  = 3
findtime  = 10m
bantime   = 1h
EOF
sudo systemctl restart fail2ban
sleep 3
sudo fail2ban-client status opensips
```

- The status shows the jail with
  `Journal matches: _SYSTEMD_UNIT=opensips.service`.
- It shows nobody banned yet.
- When it starts, the jail also reads the last `findtime` of the journal.
  - So failures logged before it ran can earn a ban.

`_daemon` matches the program name the journal records. For the packages, that
is `/usr/sbin/opensips`.

## Give this machine a scanner and a phone to test with

Each test address lives in a network namespace.

- A network namespace is a separate network stack on this machine with its own
  address.
- A virtual cable links it to this one.
- Its requests reach OpenSIPS from that address, as if from another machine:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
for n in scanner:198.51.100 phone:203.0.113; do
  ns=${n%%:*} net=${n#*:}
  sudo ip netns add $ns
  sudo ip link add f2b-$ns type veth peer name eth0 netns $ns
  sudo ip addr add $net.1/24 dev f2b-$ns
  sudo ip link set f2b-$ns up
  sudo ip -n $ns link set lo up
  sudo ip -n $ns link set eth0 up
done
sudo ip -n scanner addr add 198.51.100.60/24 dev eth0
sudo ip -n scanner route add default via 198.51.100.1
sudo ip -n phone addr add 203.0.113.70/24 dev eth0
sudo ip -n phone route add default via 203.0.113.1
```

A small SIP client sends the test requests and prints each answer. It uses
only Python's standard library:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
mkdir -p ~/f2b-test
cat > ~/f2b-test/sipreq.py <<'EOF'
"""Send SIP requests and print each final answer.
usage: sipreq.py SERVER METHOD COUNT [USER-AGENT] [USER PASSWORD]"""
import hashlib, re, socket, sys, uuid

srv, method, count = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], int(sys.argv[3])
ua = sys.argv[4] if len(sys.argv) > 4 else "sipreq"
user, pw = (sys.argv[5], sys.argv[6]) if len(sys.argv) > 6 else (None, None)
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.settimeout(2)
s.connect((srv, 5060))
me, port = s.getsockname()


def request(n, ext, auth=""):
    return (f"{method} sip:{srv} SIP/2.0\r\n"
            f"Via: SIP/2.0/UDP {me}:{port};branch=z9hG4bK{uuid.uuid4().hex}\r\n"
            f"Max-Forwards: 70\r\nFrom: <sip:{ext}@{srv}>;tag={n}\r\n"
            f"To: <sip:{ext}@{srv}>\r\nCall-ID: {cid}\r\nCSeq: {n} {method}\r\n"
            f"Contact: <sip:{ext}@{me}:{port}>\r\nExpires: 300\r\n"
            f"User-Agent: {ua}\r\n{auth}Content-Length: 0\r\n\r\n").encode()


def answer(data):
    s.send(data)
    while True:
        try:
            reply = s.recv(65535).decode(errors="replace")
        except socket.timeout:
            return "no answer"
        except ConnectionRefusedError:
            return "refused"
        if int(reply.split(" ", 2)[1]) >= 200:
            return reply


for i in range(count):
    cid = uuid.uuid4().hex
    ext = user or str(100 + i)
    reply = answer(request(1, ext))
    if reply.startswith("SIP/2.0 401") and user:
        c = dict(re.findall(r'(\w+)="([^"]*)"', reply.split("WWW-Authenticate:", 1)[1].split("\r\n", 1)[0]))
        ha1 = hashlib.md5(f"{user}:{c['realm']}:{pw}".encode()).hexdigest()
        ha2 = hashlib.md5(f"{method}:sip:{srv}".encode()).hexdigest()
        resp = hashlib.md5(f"{ha1}:{c['nonce']}:00000001:0a4f113b:auth:{ha2}".encode()).hexdigest()
        auth = (f'Authorization: Digest username="{user}", realm="{c["realm"]}", '
                f'nonce="{c["nonce"]}", uri="sip:{srv}", response="{resp}", '
                f'qop=auth, nc=00000001, cnonce="0a4f113b", algorithm=MD5\r\n')
        reply = answer(request(2, ext, auth))
    print(f"{method} {ext}: " + reply.split("\r\n", 1)[0])
EOF
```

## Check that a phone registers and calls

The phone at `203.0.113.70` registers as `1001` with the right password:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec phone python3 ~/f2b-test/sipreq.py 192.0.2.10 REGISTER 1 MicroSIP 1001 correct-horse-1001
```

It prints `REGISTER 1001: SIP/2.0 200 OK`.

Then it places a call through OpenSIPS. SIPp plays both ends:

- a callee on this machine,
- the phone, which answers OpenSIPS's challenge with its password:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo apt-get install -y sip-tester
cd ~/f2b-test
cat > call.xml <<'EOF'
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="ISO-8859-1" ?>
<scenario name="Call with digest authentication">
  <send retrans="500">
    <![CDATA[
      INVITE sip:[service]@[remote_ip]:[remote_port] SIP/2.0
      Via: SIP/2.0/[transport] [local_ip]:[local_port];branch=[branch]
      From: <sip:1001@[remote_ip]>;tag=[pid]SIPpTag00[call_number]
      To: <sip:[service]@[remote_ip]:[remote_port]>
      Call-ID: [call_id]
      CSeq: 1 INVITE
      Contact: <sip:1001@[local_ip]:[local_port]>
      Max-Forwards: 70
      Content-Type: application/sdp
      Content-Length: [len]

      v=0
      o=user1 53655765 2353687637 IN IP[local_ip_type] [local_ip]
      s=-
      c=IN IP[media_ip_type] [media_ip]
      t=0 0
      m=audio [media_port] RTP/AVP 0
      a=rtpmap:0 PCMU/8000
    ]]>
  </send>
  <recv response="100" optional="true"/>
  <recv response="407" auth="true"/>
  <send>
    <![CDATA[
      ACK sip:[service]@[remote_ip]:[remote_port] SIP/2.0
      Via: SIP/2.0/[transport] [local_ip]:[local_port];branch=[branch]
      From: <sip:1001@[remote_ip]>;tag=[pid]SIPpTag00[call_number]
      To: <sip:[service]@[remote_ip]:[remote_port]>[peer_tag_param]
      Call-ID: [call_id]
      CSeq: 1 ACK
      Max-Forwards: 70
      Content-Length: 0
    ]]>
  </send>
  <send retrans="500">
    <![CDATA[
      INVITE sip:[service]@[remote_ip]:[remote_port] SIP/2.0
      Via: SIP/2.0/[transport] [local_ip]:[local_port];branch=[branch]
      From: <sip:1001@[remote_ip]>;tag=[pid]SIPpTag00[call_number]
      To: <sip:[service]@[remote_ip]:[remote_port]>
      Call-ID: [call_id]
      CSeq: 2 INVITE
      Contact: <sip:1001@[local_ip]:[local_port]>
      [authentication]
      Max-Forwards: 70
      Content-Type: application/sdp
      Content-Length: [len]

      v=0
      o=user1 53655765 2353687637 IN IP[local_ip_type] [local_ip]
      s=-
      c=IN IP[media_ip_type] [media_ip]
      t=0 0
      m=audio [media_port] RTP/AVP 0
      a=rtpmap:0 PCMU/8000
    ]]>
  </send>
  <recv response="100" optional="true"/>
  <recv response="180" optional="true"/>
  <recv response="200" rtd="true" rrs="true"/>
  <send>
    <![CDATA[
      ACK [next_url] SIP/2.0
      [routes]
      Via: SIP/2.0/[transport] [local_ip]:[local_port];branch=[branch]
      From: <sip:1001@[remote_ip]>;tag=[pid]SIPpTag00[call_number]
      To: <sip:[service]@[remote_ip]:[remote_port]>[peer_tag_param]
      Call-ID: [call_id]
      CSeq: 2 ACK
      Max-Forwards: 70
      Content-Length: 0
    ]]>
  </send>
  <pause milliseconds="2000"/>
  <send retrans="500">
    <![CDATA[
      BYE [next_url] SIP/2.0
      [routes]
      Via: SIP/2.0/[transport] [local_ip]:[local_port];branch=[branch]
      From: <sip:1001@[remote_ip]>;tag=[pid]SIPpTag00[call_number]
      To: <sip:[service]@[remote_ip]:[remote_port]>[peer_tag_param]
      Call-ID: [call_id]
      CSeq: 3 BYE
      Max-Forwards: 70
      Content-Length: 0
    ]]>
  </send>
  <recv response="200" crlf="true"/>
</scenario>
EOF
sipp -sn uas -i 127.0.0.1 -p 5070 -m 1 -bg
sudo ip netns exec phone sipp -sf call.xml 192.0.2.10:5060 -i 203.0.113.70 -p 5080 -s 2000 \
  -au 1001 -ap correct-horse-1001 -m 1 -timeout 20s -trace_screen -screen_file call.screen >/dev/null
grep -E 'Successful call|Failed call' call.screen
```

The output shows these events:

- OpenSIPS challenged the call.
- The phone answered the challenge.
- The callee answered.
- The phone hung up:

```text
  Successful call        |        0                  |        1
  Failed call            |        0                  |        0
```

The phone's first `INVITE` drew a challenge. That is the normal first half of
a login. So OpenSIPS logged nothing for it.

## Watch fail2ban ban a scanner

The scanner walks extensions the way SIPVicious's `svwar` does. It announces
itself as `friendly-scanner`. Then it tries once more:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo ip netns exec scanner python3 ~/f2b-test/sipreq.py 192.0.2.10 REGISTER 5 friendly-scanner
sleep 2
sudo fail2ban-client status opensips
sudo nft list table inet f2b-table
sudo ip netns exec scanner python3 ~/f2b-test/sipreq.py 192.0.2.10 OPTIONS 1
```

OpenSIPS answered none of the scanner's `REGISTER`s.

- Each prints `no answer`.
- Or it prints `refused` if the ban was already in place.

The jail lists the scanner:

```text
   `- Banned IP list:	198.51.100.60
```

nftables holds it in the jail's set. It refuses its SIP traffic:

```text
	set addr-set-opensips {
		type ipv4_addr
		elements = { 198.51.100.60 }
	}
	...
		udp dport { 5060, 5061 } ip saddr @addr-set-opensips reject with icmp port-unreachable
```

The last request prints `OPTIONS 100: refused`.

- The firewall answered with an ICMP port unreachable.
- OpenSIPS never saw it.

The phone is not affected. It still registers:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec phone python3 ~/f2b-test/sipreq.py 192.0.2.10 REGISTER 1 MicroSIP 1001 correct-horse-1001
```

## Lift a ban

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo fail2ban-client set opensips unbanip 198.51.100.60
sudo ip netns exec scanner python3 ~/f2b-test/sipreq.py 192.0.2.10 OPTIONS 1
```

- `unbanip` prints `1`, the number of addresses it unbanned.
- The scanner's `OPTIONS` gets an answer again: `OPTIONS 100: SIP/2.0 200 OK`.

## Watch a password guesser get banned, and the ban run out

A password guesser uses an ordinary `User-Agent` and a real user name.

- You can see a ban end on its own without waiting an hour.
  - Shorten this jail's `bantime` to 60 seconds while it runs.
  - Then put it back.
- `fail2ban-client set` changes the running jail only.
  - The jail file still says an hour:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo fail2ban-client set opensips bantime 60
sudo ip netns exec scanner python3 ~/f2b-test/sipreq.py 192.0.2.10 REGISTER 4 MicroSIP 1001 wrong-password
sleep 2
sudo fail2ban-client get opensips banip --with-time
sleep 70
sudo fail2ban-client status opensips
sudo ip netns exec scanner python3 ~/f2b-test/sipreq.py 192.0.2.10 OPTIONS 1
sudo fail2ban-client set opensips bantime 3600
```

- Each guess prints `REGISTER 1001: SIP/2.0 401 Unauthorized`.
- A guess or two past the third can still get an answer.
  - fail2ban acts on the log line after OpenSIPS has written it.
- `banip --with-time` shows when the ban started and ends, 60 seconds later:

```text
198.51.100.60 	2026-10-01 03:47:03 + 60 = 2026-10-01 03:48:03
```

The ban starts from the time of the failure that earned it. After the wait:

- `Banned IP list:` is empty.
- The `OPTIONS` gets an answer again.

## Operate it

The commands below do these things, in this order:

- ban a test address by hand,
- look at it,
- restart fail2ban,
- lift the ban.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `sudo fail2ban-client set opensips banip 198.51.100.61` | ban an address by hand, for the jail's `bantime`, and print how many it banned |
| `sudo fail2ban-client status opensips` | the jail's failures and its banned addresses |
| `sudo fail2ban-client get opensips banip --with-time` | each banned address, when its ban started and when it ends |
| `sudo systemctl restart fail2ban` | apply a change to the filter or the jail. Bans survive it, because fail2ban keeps them in its database and restores them |
| `sudo fail2ban-client set opensips unbanip 198.51.100.61` | lift a ban |
| `sudo fail2ban-regex systemd-journal opensips` | count the journal lines the filter matches, without banning anything |
| `sudo journalctl -u fail2ban -n 20` | the fail2ban service's messages, including a jail that failed to start |
| `sudo tail -n 20 /var/log/fail2ban.log` | fail2ban's own log: every ban and unban, by jail and address |

**Remove the test addresses** when you finish testing:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo ip netns del scanner
sudo ip netns del phone
rm -rf ~/f2b-test
```

**Uninstall.** Stopping fail2ban removes its nftables table. So no ban
outlives it:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo systemctl disable --now fail2ban
sudo rm -f /etc/fail2ban/filter.d/opensips.conf /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/opensips.local
sudo apt-get purge -y fail2ban
```

This keeps the OpenSIPS configuration from
"Make OpenSIPS log scanners and wrong passwords".
To uninstall OpenSIPS too, see [its guide](opensips.md#operate-it).

## When something does not work

- **The jail never bans.**
  - Check what the filter matches.
    `sudo fail2ban-regex systemd-journal opensips` reports `Failregex: 0 total`
    when it matches nothing.
  - OpenSIPS may run under another unit or another program name.
    - Then `journalmatch` or `_daemon` does not fit it.
    - See how the journal records the program with
      `sudo journalctl -u opensips -n 5`.
- **fail2ban does not start.**
  - `sudo journalctl -u fail2ban -n 20` names the jail and the reason.
  - One jail that fails stops fail2ban.
    - Every jail stops with it, SSH's included.

---

<!-- source: docs/fail2ban-sipnab.md -->

# Feed fail2ban from sipnab

[fail2ban](fail2ban.md) bans the addresses that a log names. sipnab can write
that log.

- sipnab has a scanner detector and a registration-flood detector.
  - Each finds attackers in the SIP traffic sipnab captures.
- With `--fail2ban`, sipnab writes one line for each detection.
- The filter and jail in sipnab's
  [`contrib/fail2ban`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/tree/main/contrib/fail2ban)
  turn those lines into bans.
- sipnab writes the lines. fail2ban decides and bans.

sipnab's lines come from the traffic it captures, not from your SIP server's
log.

This guide starts where [Ban SIP scanners with fail2ban](fail2ban.md) ends,
before its uninstall. OpenSIPS, fail2ban and the two test addresses are in
place.

## What sipnab writes

Two kinds of line, one per detection:

```text
2026-10-01 03:49:45 sipnab[17157]: scanner_detected src=198.51.100.60 ua="friendly-scanner" method="OPTIONS"
2026-10-01 03:51:13 sipnab[17540]: reg_flood src=198.51.100.60 count=51
```

- `scanner_detected` comes from the scanner detector, `--kill-scanner`.
  - sipnab quotes `ua` and `method`.
- `reg_flood` comes from the registration-flood detector, `--reg-flood`.
  - `count` is how many REGISTERs with credentials the registrar refused from
    that address within one second.
  - Out of the box the threshold is 50.
  - sipnab writes a line for each refusal past it.
  - So 80 refusals in a burst write 30 lines, `count=51` to `count=80`.

`--fail2ban` itself detects nothing. It only chooses the format. Without a
detector beside it, sipnab warns when it starts that `no detector is running,
so this run will emit nothing`.

**Know what `--kill-scanner` sends.**

- On a live capture, the scanner detector also answers the scanner requests it
  detects.
  - It answers from a separate process.
- The answer is a `200 OK`.
  - It carries your SIP server's address and port as its source.
- Watching the scanner's side, the request OpenSIPS ignored on purpose got an
  answer within milliseconds:

```text
03:50:04.370537 IP 198.51.100.60.54184 > 192.0.2.10.5060: SIP: OPTIONS sip:192.0.2.10 SIP/2.0
03:50:04.383978 IP 192.0.2.10.5060 > 198.51.100.60.54184: SIP: SIP/2.0 200 OK
```

So with sipnab running this way, a scanner learns that something answers on
your SIP port. That is true even when your SIP server answers nothing.

## Tested on

Every block on this page ran as written, in order, on 2026-10-01. So did every
command in the table in "Operate it".

- They ran with sipnab 0.5.199 from its release package.
- They ran with the `contrib/fail2ban` files as this version of the page
  describes them.
- They ran on the machines [the fail2ban guide](fail2ban.md#tested-on) ran on:
  - clean x86_64 virtual machines with 2 cores and 3 GB of memory,
  - Debian 13 (kernel 6.12.111) and Ubuntu 24.04 (kernel 6.8.0).
- They ran right after that guide's section
  "Watch a password guesser get banned, and the ban run out".
- The section "Ban with iptables instead of nftables"
  ran on both.
  - Debian 13's `iptables` package is 1.8.11 and reports `(nf_tables)`.
- A capture on both showed the answer `--kill-scanner` sends.

## Install sipnab

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
V=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/NormB/sipnab/releases/latest \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["tag_name"].lstrip("v"))')
curl -fsSLO https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/releases/download/v$V/sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb
curl -fsSL https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/releases/download/v$V/SHA256SUMS.txt \
  | grep " sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb$" | sha256sum -c -
sudo apt-get install -y ./sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb
```

The package installs a service that runs sipnab as the `sipnab` user. The
service captures on every interface. The package does not start it.

## Run sipnab with its detectors, writing the log

A drop-in does two things:

- It adds the two detectors and `--fail2ban` to the packaged command.
- It sends sipnab's standard output, where the lines go, to
  `/var/log/sipnab.log`.
  - That is the file the contrib jail reads.

sipnab's own messages, on standard error, stay in the journal:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/sipnab.service.d
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/sipnab.service.d/fail2ban.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[Service]
ExecStart=
ExecStart=/usr/bin/sipnab -N -d any --no-cli-print --syslog --metrics 127.0.0.1:9090 \
  --kill-scanner --reg-flood --fail2ban
StandardOutput=append:/var/log/sipnab.log
StandardError=journal
EOF
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now sipnab
sleep 3
systemctl is-active sipnab
sudo ls -l /var/log/sipnab.log
```

- `--no-cli-print` keeps every SIP message out of the log.
  - It does not hold back the detection lines.
- systemd creates the log file when the service starts.
- Start sipnab before the jail.
  - fail2ban refuses to start a jail whose log file does not exist.
  - It stops every other jail with it.

## Install sipnab's filter and jail

Fetch both files at the tag of the sipnab you installed:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
V=$(sipnab --version | awk 'NR==1 {print $2}')
sudo curl -fsSL "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NormB/sipnab/v$V/contrib/fail2ban/sipnab-scanner.conf" \
  -o /etc/fail2ban/filter.d/sipnab-scanner.conf
sudo curl -fsSL "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NormB/sipnab/v$V/contrib/fail2ban/sipnab-jail.conf" \
  -o /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/sipnab.conf
cat /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/sipnab.conf
```

The jail is `sipnab-scanner`.

- It reads `/var/log/sipnab.log`.
- It bans an address after 5 lines within 60 seconds.
  - The ban lasts for an hour.
  - It covers every port, UDP and TCP.
  - It uses nftables.
- `backend = auto` makes it read that file even where the distribution's
  default is the systemd journal, as on Ubuntu 24.04.

Load it:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo systemctl restart fail2ban
sleep 3
sudo fail2ban-client status sipnab-scanner
```

The status shows `File list: /var/log/sipnab.log`.

Before you leave this running on real traffic, measure who the detectors would
name on a capture of your own.
[Detect SIP scanners and auto-block via fail2ban](examples.md#detect-sip-scanners-and-auto-block-via-fail2ban)
shows how.

- Change the jail in a `sipnab.local` beside it.
- Never change it in `sipnab.conf`. The next download replaces that file.

For example, never ban the phone's network, and wait for 10 detections rather
than 5:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo tee /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/sipnab.local >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[sipnab-scanner]
ignoreip = 127.0.0.1/8 ::1 203.0.113.0/24
maxretry = 10
EOF
sudo systemctl restart fail2ban
sleep 3
sudo fail2ban-client get sipnab-scanner ignoreip
sudo fail2ban-client get sipnab-scanner maxretry
```

The jail now prints the three ignored ranges and `10`. Take the example out
again before "Watch sipnab's lines become a ban". That section counts to 5:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo rm /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/sipnab.local
sudo systemctl restart fail2ban
sleep 3
sudo fail2ban-client get sipnab-scanner maxretry
```

It prints `5`.

## Watch sipnab's lines become a ban

- Start with the scanner unbanned in every jail.
  - The fail2ban guide's tests may have left a ban behind.
- The OpenSIPS jail would also ban this scanner, after its third request.
  - So have that jail ignore it while you watch sipnab's.
  - Keep that until the end of "Watch a registration flood become a ban".
- Then the scanner sends four `OPTIONS` as `friendly-scanner`:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo fail2ban-client unban 198.51.100.60
sudo fail2ban-client set opensips addignoreip 198.51.100.60
sudo ip netns exec scanner python3 ~/f2b-test/sipreq.py 192.0.2.10 OPTIONS 4 friendly-scanner
sleep 3
sudo grep -c 'scanner_detected src=198.51.100.60 ' /var/log/sipnab.log
sudo fail2ban-client status sipnab-scanner
```

- The first three print `SIP/2.0 200 OK`.
  - That is sipnab's answer, not OpenSIPS's.
- The fourth prints `no answer`.
  - sipnab answers one source at most three times a minute.
- sipnab wrote a `scanner_detected src=198.51.100.60` line for each of the
  four.
- The jail counts them, `Total failed: 4`.
  - But it has banned nobody: `Banned IP list:` is empty.

The fifth inside 60 seconds earns the ban:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo ip netns exec scanner python3 ~/f2b-test/sipreq.py 192.0.2.10 OPTIONS 1 friendly-scanner
sleep 3
sudo fail2ban-client status sipnab-scanner
sudo nft list set inet f2b-table addr-set-sipnab
sudo ip netns exec scanner python3 ~/f2b-test/sipreq.py 192.0.2.10 OPTIONS 1
```

- The jail lists `198.51.100.60`.
- nftables holds it in `addr-set-sipnab`.
- The next `OPTIONS` prints `refused`.

The phone is not affected, and sipnab wrote nothing about it:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo ip netns exec phone python3 ~/f2b-test/sipreq.py 192.0.2.10 REGISTER 1 MicroSIP 1001 correct-horse-1001
sudo grep -c 203.0.113.70 /var/log/sipnab.log || true
```

It prints `REGISTER 1001: SIP/2.0 200 OK`, then `0`.

## Watch a registration flood become a ban

- Lift the scanner's ban first.
- The OpenSIPS jail still ignores the address, so only sipnab's jail acts.
- Afterwards, the OpenSIPS jail stops ignoring it:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo fail2ban-client set sipnab-scanner unbanip 198.51.100.60
sudo ip netns exec scanner python3 ~/f2b-test/sipreq.py 192.0.2.10 REGISTER 80 MicroSIP 1001 wrong-password | sort | uniq -c
sleep 3
sudo grep -c 'reg_flood src=198.51.100.60' /var/log/sipnab.log
sudo fail2ban-client status sipnab-scanner
sudo fail2ban-client set opensips delignoreip 198.51.100.60
```

- All 80 guesses print `REGISTER 1001: SIP/2.0 401 Unauthorized`.
- sipnab wrote 30 `reg_flood` lines for them.
- The jail lists `198.51.100.60`.

## Ban with iptables instead of nftables

The shipped jail bans with nftables. That worked on both systems this guide
ran on.

- You may manage the firewall with the `iptables` command on a host.
- There, give the jail fail2ban's iptables action.
  - The shipped file shows it in a comment.

This block does three things:

- It installs `iptables`.
- It switches the jail to it in a `sipnab.local`.
- It bans the scanner again with five `OPTIONS`:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo apt-get install -y iptables
sudo iptables -V
sudo tee /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/sipnab.local >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[sipnab-scanner]
action = iptables-allports[name=sipnab, protocol=all]
EOF
sudo systemctl restart fail2ban
sleep 3
sudo fail2ban-client unban 198.51.100.60
sudo ip netns exec scanner python3 ~/f2b-test/sipreq.py 192.0.2.10 OPTIONS 5 friendly-scanner
sleep 3
sudo fail2ban-client status sipnab-scanner
sudo iptables -S f2b-sipnab
sudo ip netns exec scanner python3 ~/f2b-test/sipreq.py 192.0.2.10 OPTIONS 1
```

- `iptables -V` names its backend in brackets.
  - `(nf_tables)` is the iptables command writing nftables rules for you.
  - `(legacy)` is the old kernel tables.
- The jail lists `198.51.100.60`.
- The `f2b-sipnab` chain holds a rule rejecting it.
- The next `OPTIONS` prints `refused`.

To go back to nftables, remove the override:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo rm /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/sipnab.local
sudo systemctl restart fail2ban
sleep 3
sudo fail2ban-client status sipnab-scanner
```

## Operate it

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `sudo fail2ban-client status sipnab-scanner` | the jail's failures and its banned addresses |
| `sudo fail2ban-client set sipnab-scanner unbanip 198.51.100.60` | lift a ban |
| `sudo fail2ban-regex /var/log/sipnab.log sipnab-scanner` | count the lines of sipnab's log the filter matches, without banning anything |
| `sudo journalctl -u sipnab -n 20` | sipnab's own messages, including an `[ALERT]` line for each detection |

**Uninstall.** Remove the jail and the drop-in, and put the packaged service
back:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo rm -f /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/sipnab.conf /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/sipnab.local /etc/fail2ban/filter.d/sipnab-scanner.conf
sudo systemctl restart fail2ban
sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/sipnab.service.d/fail2ban.conf
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl disable --now sipnab
sudo rm -f /var/log/sipnab.log
```

To remove sipnab too:

```bash
sudo apt-get purge -y sipnab
```

## When something does not work

- **fail2ban does not start, and `journalctl -u fail2ban` says `Have not found
  any log file for sipnab-scanner jail`.**
  - `/var/log/sipnab.log` does not exist yet.
  - Start sipnab as in "Run sipnab with its detectors, writing the log".
  - Then restart fail2ban.
- **The log stays empty.**
  - Run `sudo journalctl -u sipnab -n 20`.
  - sipnab warns there when `--fail2ban` has no detector beside it.
